title: Julia og Seth har førebudd seg til gravferda med dikt og samtalar om døden
content:
Skulane i Noreg markerer gravferda til kong Harald. Gravferdsdagen er ikkje ein offisiell fridag, og Utdanningsdirektoratet råder skulane til å halde ope.
Men det er opp til kvar enkelt skule og kommune korleis dei markerer dagen.
Julia Bjørgeengen Monguzzi og Seth Hunter Arcangeles i sjette klasse ved Østbyen skule i Bodø følger gravferda saman med klassen sin frå klasserommet.
Dei har blitt brukt etter dødsfallet til å snakke om kongen og skrive dikt.
– Kong Harald, du var veldig snill, og du hadde eit godt hjarte. Du var rettferdig og lét alle elske alle. Vi var og er veldig glade i deg. Kong Haakon, eg håpar at du blir like snill og rettferdig som kong Harald, les Julia høgt frå diktet sitt.
Sjølv om ho ikkje kjende kongen personleg, synest ho han verka som ein skikkeleg snill og morosam type. Også Seth har skrive eit dikt for å hylle den avdøde monarken:
– Tusen takk, kong Harald. Du var respektfull, snill og rettferdig. Tusen takk, kong Harald, og lukke til, kong Haakon.
Viser sendinga i klasserommet
Fleire skuler i landet vel å vise TV-sendinga frå bisettinga på storskjerm eller leggje til rette for eigne opplegg i klasseromma. Sendinga startar kl. 12.00 og varer til om lag kl. 14.40.
I klassen til Julia og Seth ser nesten alle sendinga samen i klasserommet. Men skulen har også opna for at elevar kan dra heim for å sjå sendinga heime.
For lærar Margrethe Vinje på sjette trinn er det viktig at skulen tek seg tid til å markere hendinga og formidle historia til elevane.
– Som elevane har sagt, så er dette ei historisk hending. Det er kongen vår, og eg synest det er viktig å skrive seg inn i minnebøkene, fortel ho.
Elevane har også den siste tida snakka ope om døden og kva som faktisk skjer under gravferda.
Julia fortel at ho mellom anna har lært at kongen ikkje skal gravast ned i jorda, men leggjast i ein sarkofag i Akershus slottskapell.
Sidan Østbyen er ein internasjonal skule, påpeikar Vinje at det er ekstra viktig å vise korleis ein praktiserer ei slik statleg gravferd i Noreg, då dette er ukjent for fleire av elevane.
Gravferda blir også vist i fleire kyrkjer og kommunale bygg i Noreg. Her kan du sjå kva ho blir vist nærast deg:
Eitt minutts stille i skuledagen
Heile landet markerer gravferda med eitt minutts stille. Det gjer dei òg på Østbyen skule i Bodø.
Tre klokkeslag vil lyde like før kl. 13.00, etterfølgt av eitt minutt stille som blir avslutta kl. 13.01.
Sjølv om skuledagen blir prega av gravferda, følgjer skulen Bodø kommune sine retningslinjer, som seier at elevane sjølve kan velje om dei vil sjå TV-sendinga.
– Vi oppmodar sjølvsagt elevane til å delta, men vi har respekt for at dei kan ha lyst til å gjere ein annan type aktivitet, fortel lærar Vinje på Østbyen skule.
Skulen har laga eit eige hefte om kongehuset med det som har vore og det som kjem. Alle elevane jobbar med dette, men dei som ikkje vil sjå gravferda på TV kan velje å berre halde på med det.
Skuledagen vart sett på pause for historia
På Rygge ungdomsskule i Østfold vart skulekvardagen sett på pause for å la elevane ta del i den nasjonale sorgmarkeringa. For lærar Samuel Nybråten var det eit naturleg val å la elevane følgje gravferda tett.
– Vi snakkar ofte om at samfunnsfag er dagsaktuelt, og det finst kanskje ikkje noko meir dagsaktuelt enn dette. Elevane får sjå noko som er historisk, og dei får lov til å vere med på det, fortel læraren.
Han understrekar kor viktig det er at dei unge får kjenne på fellesskapet i ei slik stund.
– Det er viktig at vi som klasse, skule og framtidige samfunnsborgarar får ta del i noko så stort. Eg trur dette tyder mykje for dei. Det er noko dei kjem til å sjå tilbake på som noko stort og som dei neppe kjem til å gløyme, seier han.
Øvd på Kongesongen
I forkant av gravferda har klassen førebudd seg godt. Elevane har blant anna øvd på Kongesongen, og dei har brukt tid på å sjå på kong Harald sine mange talar og gjerningar gjennom ei lang regjeringstid.
Elev Johannes Storhaug Pettersen i klasse 9B fortel at det var spesielt å følgje sendinga.
– Det er veldig fint, og det er litt rart. Det er jo eigentleg ganske trist, og det er ikkje alle som får vere med på noko slikt når dei er så unge, seier han.
For Johannes gjev det likevel meining å markere dagen saman med medelevane sine.
– Det er leit at han er død, men det er hyggeleg å vite at han er på ein betre stad. Dette er ein del av samspelet i samfunnet, så det er viktig for oss å lære om, reflekterer han.
Midt i sorga over kong Harald sitt bortgang, vert blikket òg retta framover mot Noregs nye monark, kong Haakon.
Johannes har trua på framtida for kongehuset.
– Eg tenkjer han kjem til å bli ein god konge. Eg tippar han kjem til å gjere mykje bra for landet og rett og slett leve opp til faren sin.
Tenkjer på den nye kongen
I Bodø tenkjer elevane i sjette klasse også på korleis dagen er for den nye kongen, kong Haakon, som skal følge faren sin til grava.
– Det er kanskje litt vanskeleg for han å prosessere alt. Han kjende faren sin veldig godt, og han er kanskje veldig lei seg no, seier Seth.
Han legg til at det nok kan vere vanskeleg å måtte opptre som konge midt i sorga. Julia deler den same omtanken.
– Eg tippar det er veldig trist for Håkon og Sonja. Det er jo litt vanskeleg å vere konge og prøve å vere glad for landet medan pappaen hans nettopp har døydd.
Sidan dødsfallet har flagget på halv stong møtt elevane og dei tilsette kvar morgon, noko som har ført til daglege samtalar. Dagen etter gravferda skal flagga heisast til topps igjen, og sørgjeperioden er over.
– Eg tenkjer at ein ny epoke startar då, men vi skal òg vere obs på at nokre elevar framleis er der at dei vil trenge å snakke om dette i tida framover, avsluttar lærar Vinje.

title: 'Ever evolving': PNG's unifying language celebrated in Tok Pisin Wik
content:
Members of Wellington's Papua New Guinea community say Tok Pisin is a versatile language that many people can use with relative ease.
Tok Pisin Wik is underway this week with a series of events around New Zealand celebrating Papua New Guinea's national language and traditional cultures.
The Ministry of Pacific Peoples has provided some useful resources for the week - Tenkyu tru!
Ancey Wamiri, a school teacher, told RNZ Pacific she uses Tok Pisin every day with family and friends, also teaches it during Tok Pisin Wik sessions.
Describing Tok Pisin as being in her blood and bones, Wamiri explained that the language has been been an "essential unifying factor" for people in a country of many diverse cultures.
"The wonderful thing about Tok Pisin is it has united us as a country, to be able to connect amongst ourselves as a nation.
"If we didn't have Tok Pisin then we'd be a completely divided people. So it was essential to have Tok Pisin become a part of the unifying language for our people.
Wamiri said Tok Pisin is very much a living language that is never stagnant.
"It's ever developing and ever evolving and changing," she explained.
"The great thing is it is a recognised language and not just a creole or a slight version of the English language - because it does have quite a bit of English in it - but somehow along the way it's gone into waves, dips and highs to be a language that we can speak."
Living language
If you're nervous about giving it a go, don't be. As the Wellington community say, it's versatile, and there's often no one right way to say something.
A common exchange may go: "Yu olrait? (How are you?)" responded to with "Mi olrait, tenkyu (I am good, thank you)"
Tommy Poliap Posangat told RNZ Pacific that from its origin, Tok Pisin was created as a way to bridge diversity.
"I believe Tok Pisin was created during he plantation period, when they brought all the islanders, Melanesians, together to work the plantations," Posangat said.
"And because PNG's got a variation of languages, over 800 languages, they've had to come up with a language that they can all speak and understand each other - not just the Papua New Guineans but you have the Solomon Islanders, Fijians and the Vanuatuans coming together, so that's how Tok Pisin was formed backed then, and it's just been evolving ever since."
Every day use
College student Naimah Leahy said the majority of her wider family still lives in PNG, so she makes an effort to stay in touch, which in turn helps keep her use of Tok Pisin alive.
"Apart from the time difference (two hours), I almost call them every day, message every day, make sure that I still am connected to those who are in Papua New Guinea because that's like my home," Leahy said.
Another college student from Wellington who is Papua New Guinean is Dziewanna Wamiri-Cokataki who said Tok Pisin is a beautiful language.
"It's like a wave, it's very up and down. You talk with a lot of emotion," she said, adding that using it with friends was a good way to keep growing the language.
"It's very cool to try and converse and learn, so that's what we try and do."
Em nau (that's right).

title: Reflections on Suquamish and Nisqually Canoe Journeys
content: Reflections on Suquamish and Nisqually Canoe Journeys Country United States agnes Wed, 09/02/2026 - 09:21 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Phoebe Farris (Powhatan-Pamunkey) Annual inter-Tribal celebrations involving Pacific Northwest Indigenous communities were sparked by the 1989 Paddle to Seattle event, held as part of Washington State’s Centennial celebration. Since then, many canoe journeys from Canada, Alaska, and Washington State have voyaged from their traditional homelands to states in the Pacific Northwest. These canoe journeys have grown to about 100 participating canoe families from Native communities around the world, including the Māori from Aotearoa/New Zealand and other Indigenous Peoples from Japan, Mexico, South America, and Guam. After morning arrivals at the Tribal hosts’ shorelands, families request permission to land, offering prayers and short speeches in their traditional languages. Evening activities involve more prayers, music, dancing, gifting, and honoring. These ceremonies are designated as Protocol and can be in a longhouse-type environment or in an outdoor, tent-like enclosure. Inside Nisqually Protocol Tent. The host Tribe receives gifts from the participating families as a token of gratitude, and traditional foods are served during breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Participating Tribes share and explain their cultural practices and request that non-Native guests honor these practices by standing when asked during certain prayers and by refraining from photographing some dance performances, specifically those featuring dancers wearing large, wooden face masks. The first canoe journey I observed was hosted by the Suquamish Tribe from July 27-29. Indoor activities took place at the House of Awakened Culture in Suquamish, Washington. At this particular landing, the ocean was right below the Protocol building. Phoebe Farris with Cynthia Lozier. On my first day at Suquamish, I met Chaplain Cynthia Lozier (Muckleshoot and Puyallup), a retired Army veteran whose role as Chaplain is to comfort grieving Indigenous families during funerals, at hospitals, and in home or hospice settings. Her husband, Franklin Ross (Puyallup and Muckleshoot), is also a veteran. Lozier sang songs in her traditional language, and her husband drummed during Protocol. Chaplain Cynthia Lozier (Muckleshoot and Puyallup) and husband Franklin Ross (Puyallup and Muckleshoot). That same day, I met an Elder named Leona Canuta (Pacheedaht First Nations), who asked me to take photos of her family’s canoe, “People of the Sea Foam”—also the name of their family drum group—and her daughter, Emily Harmony (Pacheedaht), her nephew, Mike Smith, and her grandchildren. She said that Professor Sarah Wright-Cardinal at Northwest University helped secure grants for carving canoes from Macawmah Land. I ran into her the next week at Nisqually and watched her dance with other women at Protocol, in their red-and-white regalia. Leona Canuta (Pachedahtt) standing next to her family’s canoe. Phoebe Farris with Aimee Phair. While wandering around Suquamish, I met Aimee Phair (Lummi Nation), who has tattoos on her face, neck, arms, and hands. She briefed me on the differences between tattoo shops that use electronic tools and artificial dyes and those that use nature-based dyes and no electrical machinery. She explained that the colors are sometimes less bright and don’t last as long as commercial tattoos, but the pain is minimal, similar to the very mild sensation of an acupuncture needle. Aimee Phair showing her hand tattoos. Later in the evening, Phair danced in Protocol and said she was heading to participate as a puller for the Muckleshoot canoe landing in Muckleshoot territory. I would see her again at Nisqually, where she discussed the Lummi nonprofit film “Children of the Setting Sun” and encouraged me to visit the nearby nature reserve dedicated to the late Billy Frank Jr. (Nisqually), a social-justice fishing-rights advocate. Calina Lawrence (Suquamish) with “Looking Eagle” tattoo. I also ran into an old friend, Calina Lawrence (Suquamish), whom I had not seen in years. She has a shoulder tattoo titled “Looking Eagle,” created by tattoo artist Kyle Twiddy (Skokomish). It is called Looking Eagle because by moving his head fast, he can see in all directions and understand all perspectives. Canoe landing at Sequalitchew Creek. A few days later, I witnessed the canoe landing “Medicine Creek Potlatch: Healing Through Our Waters,” hosted by the Nisqually Tribe from July 31 to August 5. The landings took place on Sequalitchew Creek and involved a one-and-a-half-mile walk down a trail from the local park to the water landing. The Protocol ceremonies took place inside a large tent on the Nisqually reservation, several miles from the creek. Per custom, the host Tribe was honored and gifted by the various canoe families. Guests observed traditional dancing and were offered meals. In addition to the beautiful surroundings and the excitement of watching colorfully decorated canoes landing, the experience was marked by the warmth of the people involved—the pullers (rowers), the performers, the volunteers, the Tribal staff, and the visitors and guests from all over Turtle Island and beyond. Canoe landing at Sequalitchew Creek. I met John Halliday (enrolled Muckleshoot, Duwamish, Yakama, and Warm Springs descent), a visually impaired artist and retired BIA administrator. Halliday’s artist name is Coyote. He was introduced to me by his caretaker, Lucas Patricio, also an artist, whose Tribal heritage is southwest Pueblo. They explained some of the techniques involved in making the traditional vest Halliday was wearing. John Halliday (Muckleshoot). At both landing sites, the host Tribes provided campsites with outdoor showers and toilets. For the first time in my life, I engaged in activities I will probably never repeat: helping set up a tent, crawling on my knees in the dirt, digging holes, pulling out squiggly earthworms, and nailing down posts—all while destroying my newly manicured nails. It was sort of fun, but I am an urban Indian and stayed at the Suquamish Tribal Casino Hotel and two other local hotels. I would like to express special gratitude to Kelvin Penn, a musician whose day job is managing sound equipment and other technical responsibilities at events like the Nisqually Protocol. Penn respectfully stood up for the Blessing the Floor prayers and all other significant prayers, making sure that the entire film crew turned off their cameras when requested. Protocol events were livestreamed and shown in the Elders’ tent, but certain activities were not allowed to be filmed, and Penn was on the case. I would also like to thank Cheebo Frazier (Nisqually), Tribal Council Vicechairwoman; Kyles Gemmell (Suquamish), Cultural Activities Coordinator; and Hazle Pacquette (Suquamish), Activities and Events Planner, for graciously responding to all of my emails, text messages, and phone calls regarding press passes, transportation, and housing. And all the volunteer cooks for the free salmon, crabs, elk stew, bison burgers, fresh fruit and vegetables, strong coffee, homemade pastries, and bottles of water available day and night that kept us nourished. --Phoebe Farris (Powhatan-Pamunkey descent) is Contributing Arts Editor for the Cultural Survival Quarterly magazine. An art critic, curator, author, and photographer, she has written extensively on Indigenous visual, literary, and performing arts for over two decades. Farris is also a Professor Emerita of Art and Design at Purdue University and has curated and contributed to exhibitions highlighting Native and global Indigenous artists. Her work bridges scholarship, creative practice, and advocacy, amplifying Indigenous voices in contemporary art and media. Top photo: Suquamish canoe landing site. All photos by Phoebe Farris.

title: New assessment finds five EU Missions are driving systemic change
content:
All five EU Missions are making steady progress towards their objectives – with the Climate Adaptation Mission having already met and surpassed its 2030 targets.
The five EU Missions were launched in 2021 under Horizon Europe 2021-2027. They are designed to translate scientific and technological innovation into practical solutions that can be tested and deployed in real-life settings across Europe, addressing pressing societal challenges – climate change, soil and waters health, and cancer – by going beyond traditional instruments and giving research and innovation a new role. Their time-bound objectives help mobilise coordinated action and support long-term societal transformation.
According to the assessment, all five EU Missions are making good progress towards their 2030 goals:
Climate Adaptation:
The goal of this mission is to support at least 150 European regions, local authorities and communities to become climate resilient. The target has already been largely surpassed, with 292 regional and local authorities having already implemented climate adaptation measures.
Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities:
Its objective is to support at least 100 cities in achieving climate neutrality, and to inspire other cities across Europe. Currently, already 107 cities have Climate City Contracts. They are projected to cut emissions by 76% by 2030, backed by more than €13 billion in supported or developing investment.
Cancer:
Its aim is to improve the lives of more than 3 million people through prevention, early detection, treatment and care for not only those affected by cancer, but also their families. The current actions show that it will be able to improve the lives of 2.3 million people by 2030. Upcoming projects expected to raise this figure beyond the target of 3 million.
Restore our Ocean and Waters:
The goal is to restore the health of our ocean and waters by protecting and restoring aquatic ecosystems, reducing pollution and making the blue economy carbon-neutral and circular. It has delivered 121 innovative solutions tested in 349 real-world demonstration sites, engaged 86 regions in replication efforts and secured over 1,000 Charter Actions from stakeholders. Under the Mission, the design of the core infrastructure of the European Digital Twin Ocean – expected to be fully operational by 2030 – was completed and is now accessible to all.
A Soil Deal for Europe:
The Mission is progressing towards its goal of 100 Living Labs, with 45 already established. It involves over 500 real sites (such as farms) across Europe, and 60 to 70 additional ones are expected to become operational by 2028.
According to a mid-term assessment published by the European Commission, the five EU Missions in Horizon Europe are delivering tangible positive results in addressing some of Europe’s most pressing societal challenges through scientific and technological innovation.

title: Vietnã completa 81 anos: o que o país socialista conquistou após triunfar na resistência contra os EUA
content:
Há 81 anos, em 2 de setembro de 1945, na Praça Ba Đình, em Hanói, o revolucionário vietnamita Ho Chi Minh lia a Declaração de Independência do Vietnã. As forças comunistas resistiram primeiro à França e, em seguida, a uma das maiores e mais brutais agressões militares estadunidenses da história, que terminou com a derrota dos invasores, em 1975.
Hoje o Vietnã registra um dos processos de desenvolvimento social mais acelerados do mundo, tendo conseguido em apenas cinco décadas reduzir a pobreza de 58% para 4% da população, eliminando a fome crônica e se tornando um dos maiores exportadores de arroz do planeta, segundo dados do governo vietnamita e do Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD).
A estabilidade atual, no entanto, tem raízes em um passado marcado por guerras e pela resistência vietnamita às potências do Norte Global.
A França ocupava a região, incluindo Laos, Camboja e a cidade chinesa de Zhanjiang, desde o final do século XIX, sob o nome de Indochina. Durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial, a partir de 1940, o Império do Japão passou a co-ocupar a Indochina mediante acordo com a França. Em agosto de 1945, com a derrocada japonesa, o movimento Liga pela Independência do Vietnã, comandado por Ho Chi Minh, assumiu o poder na Revolução de Agosto.
O país europeu não reconheceu a declaração de independência vietnamita em 1945 e no ano seguinte passou a combater as forças comunistas lideradas por Ho Chi Minh. A chamada “Guerra da Indochina” foi de 1946 a 1954, quando as forças vietnamitas derrotaram o exército francês em Dien Bien Phu.
A presença militar francesa começou a se enfraquecer só em 1954, quando Paris decidiu negociar uma saída da região. A partir de então, os Estados Unidos, que já vinham financiando a França militarmente de forma significativa, decidiram se envolver mais diretamente na ocupação do Vietnã.
Em 1955, os Estados Unidos boicotaram as eleições previstas nos Acordos de Genebra do ano anterior para decidir sobre a reunificação, já que acordos anteriores haviam definido a divisão do país ao longo do paralelo 17, que cortava o país praticamente “pela metade”, como medida temporária.
O governo dos EUA, sob a presidência de Dwight D. Eisenhower, determinou que o Grupo Consultivo de Assistência Militar (MAAG, na sigla em inglês), que antes apoiava as tropas francesas na região, passasse a treinar o Exército da República do Vietnã, aliado dos EUA. Isso se efetivou em 1º de novembro de 1955, o que é tido como a data oficial do início da chamada “Guerra do Vietnã”.
Apenas três décadas depois, em 30 de abril de 1975, o Exército de Libertação do Vietnã, comandado pelo governo de Ho Chi Mihn, tomaria Saigon, no sul do país.
A destruição pelos Estados Unidos
A guerra de invasão promovida pelos estadunidenses contra o governo socialista deixou um saldo nefasto. Segundo dados oficiais citados pela agência de Notícias do Vietnã, no total, as ações dos Estados Unidos causaram a morte de quase 3 milhões de pessoas. Cerca de 175 mil soldados continuam desaparecidos e quase 300 mil túmulos seguem não identificados.
Entre os crimes de guerra mais destacados, está o “Massacre de My Lai”, cometido em 16 de março de 1968. Soldados estadunidenses massacraram 504 civis na comuna de Tinh Khe, província de Quang Ngai: 182 mulheres, 173 crianças e 60 idosos com mais de 60 anos, conforme documentos preservados no Museu de Vestígios de Guerra, em Cidade Ho Chi Minh, no sul do país. O caso é um dos mais documentados entre, pelo menos, 320 crimes contra civis registrados num relatório de 9 mil páginas do exército dos Estados Unidos, desclassificado em 1994 e citado por múltiplas fontes vietnamitas.
Além disso, as sequelas são sentidas até hoje. O Corpo Químico das Forças Armadas do Vietnã estima que o exército estadunidense pulverizou cerca de 80 milhões de litros de produtos químicos tóxicos sobre territórios no sul do Vietnã, dos quais 61% eram formados pelo material extremamente tóxico chamado “Agente Laranja”, contendo 366 kg de dioxina, segundo o general Ha Van Cu, comandante do Corpo Químico.
Cerca de 4,8 milhões de pessoas foram expostas à dioxina presente nesses produtos. Entre 3 e 3,2 milhões são consideradas vítimas diretas, sofrendo cânceres, malformações congênitas ou doenças neurológicas.
Os efeitos continuam sendo observados até a terceira e quarta gerações de famílias afetadas. Só na província de Nghệ An, mais de 600 pessoas da terceira geração de ex-combatentes expostos apresentam sequelas. O número de mortes desde 1975 atribuíveis ao Agente Laranja chega a quase 1 milhão, segundo a Previdência Social do Vietnã.
Os militares dos Estados Unidos também lançaram cerca de 15 milhões de toneladas de bombas, minas e projéteis sobre o território vietnamita, segundo a rádio estatal Voz do Vietnã. O país calcula que ainda há 800 mil toneladas de artefatos não detonados que cobrem 20% do território do país; desde o fim do conflito, esses resíduos causaram mais de 40 mil mortes e 60 mil feridos. No ritmo atual de desarmamento de minas, serão necessários 300 anos para eliminá-las completamente, segundo a emissora estatal.
A reconstrução
Em 1975, o Vietnã era uma economia completamente destruída, com campos envenenados e infraestrutura em ruínas. Em 1986, o VI Congresso Nacional do Partido Comunista do Vietnã aprovou as reformas do Đổi Mới (“renovação”), que combinaram planejamento estatal com abertura econômica controlada. De 1990 a 2004, o PIB quase triplicou, com crescimento médio de 7,5% ao ano, segundo dados oficiais. A participação da agricultura no PIB caiu de 38% para 21,7% em duas décadas de reformas, enquanto a indústria e a construção subiram de 28,9% para 40,1%.
Em 1993, 58,1% da população vivia na pobreza. Em 1998, a cifra caiu para 37,4%, e em 2004, para 24,1%, segundo o Escritório Geral de Estatísticas do Vietnã.
Em 2024, a pobreza multidimensional atingiu 4,06%, com a pobreza extrema em 1,3%, segundo o Diário do Povo, jornal oficial do Partido Comunista do Vietnã.
A redução da pobreza foi mais lenta entre as minorias étnicas. Em 1993, a taxa de pobreza entre os grupos minoritários era de 84,6%; em 1998, recuou para 75,2%, enquanto a população de etnia Kinh reduzia a pobreza em ritmo mais acelerado, segundo o Escritório Nacional de Estatísticas do Vietnã. A desigualdade entre as planícies e as províncias montanhosas ainda é o principal desafio distributivo do modelo vietnamita.
Em dezembro do ano passado, a 15ª Assembleia Nacional aprovou 423 trilhões de VND (mais de R$ 83,7 bilhões) do Programa Nacional de Metas para Áreas Rurais de Novo Estilo, Redução Sustentável da Pobreza e Desenvolvimento Socioeconômico em Regiões Étnicas Minoritárias e Montanhosas para o período de 2026 a 2035.
Já o Índice de Desenvolvimento Humano (IDH) passou de 0,499 em 1990 para 0,766 em 2023, alta de 53,5% em 33 anos, conforme o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD). O Vietnã ocupa hoje a 93ª posição entre 193 países no grupo de desenvolvimento humano.
A taxa de alfabetização entre pessoas de 15 a 60 anos é de 99,1%, e a cobertura de seguro-saúde ultrapassa 95% da população, segundo o Partido. A expectativa de vida média chegou a 74,7 anos, segundo o Escritório Geral de Estatísticas do Vietnã, com base na Pesquisa Intermediária de População e Habitação de 2024.
Em 2025, o Vietnã exportou mais de 8,06 milhões de toneladas de arroz para cerca de 80 países e territórios, faturando cerca de 4,1 bilhões de dólares (mais de R$ 21,1 bilhões), segundo o Departamento de Alfândega.
Vietnã e Cuba: internacionalismo
Cuba foi o primeiro país do hemisfério ocidental a estabelecer relações diplomáticas com o Vietnã e enviou conselheiros e especialistas militares para auxiliar as forças vietnamitas na resistência a agressão estadunidense. Seis deles inclusive morreram por um ataque aéreo dos EUA em Hanoi em 1966.
Fidel Castro é lembrado no Vietnã como um grande amigo do país. Em 1973, Fidel visitou o país e declarou: “Por Vietnam, Cuba está disposta a dar o seu próprio sangue”.
Nessa visita, Cuba entregou ao Vietnã cinco obras socioeconômicas avaliadas em cerca de US$ 80 milhões: o Hotel Thang Loi em Hanói, o Hospital Vietnã-Cuba em Dong Hoi, a estrada que liga Son Tay a Xuan Mai, uma fazenda de criação de gado em Moc Chau e uma fábrica de frangos em Luong My.
Cuba também doou mais de 1.000 vacas leiteiras para o desenvolvimento da pecuária vietnamita e forneceu mais de 6 milhões de dólares para a aquisição de equipamentos destinados a ampliar a rodovia Ho Chi Minh.
Os laços históricos se mantém e hoje, quando Cuba atravessa uma das piores crises de sua história, o Vietnã tenta retribuir.
Nas comemorações dos 65 anos de relações diplomáticas, em 2025, a Cruz Vermelha do Vietnã lançou uma campanha com meta inicial de 65 bilhões de dongs vietnamitas ( cerca de R$ 12,8 milhões), atingida em 20 dias. A campanha encerrou com 657,5 bilhões de dongs (mais de R$ 130 milhões) entregues a Cuba em duas parcelas, segundo a Cruz Vermelha do Vietnã.
Em 2026, uma nova campanha mobilizou quase 590 mil pessoas e arrecadou mais 537 bilhões de dongs (mais R$ 106 milhões), em homenagem ao centenário de Fidel Castro. O país também doou, em fevereiro de 2026, 250 toneladas de arroz, segundo a Agência de Notícias do Vietnã.
Além disso, o país estreitou suas relações comerciais com Havana e implementou neste ano um projeto conjunto entre a empresa estatal de arroz de Granma, em Cuba, e a companhia vietnamita Thai Binh — presente há anos no setor comercial da ilha —, que recentemente realizou sua primeira colheita no município de Yara.
A iniciativa conjunta, denominada TBAgri, ainda está em fase inicial e atualmente abrange cerca de 160 hectares nos terraços planos da comunidade José Martí. No entanto, o plano prevê uma expansão gradual até alcançar 25 mil hectares destinados ao cultivo de arroz.
O projeto opera sob um modelo de capital 100% estrangeiro e utiliza terras concedidas em usufruto pelo Estado cubano, com duração estimada de 25 anos. Em uma primeira etapa, a produção será destinada principalmente ao consumo interno, tendo como principal objetivo o autoabastecimento territorial.

title: Mariachi: la tradición que resiste y evoluciona
content:
Mariachi: la tradición que resiste y evoluciona
¡De México para el mundo! Este género musical ha sabido transmitir la esencia de nuestro país a través de sus letras, melodías y la imagen inolvidable del charro mexicano.
Hablar de México sin mencionar al mariachi es imposible. Más que un género musical es un elemento cultural tan relevante, que en 2011 fue reconocido como Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Humanidad por la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Educación, la Ciencia y la Cultura (UNESCO).
Su origen es difuso. Las teorías dibujan sus antecedentes en los conjuntos de cuerdas del occidente mexicano que interpretaban sones, jarabes y otras piezas.
Pese a su presencia en diferentes estados, el título de la cuna del mariachi lo tiene Jalisco, específicamente Cocula, donde es una forma de vida que se manifiesta en sus plazas, monumentos y las generaciones de músicos dedicados a este arte.
Porque más allá del tiempo, la tradición perdura y el mariachi ha sabido evolucionar. Pasó de tocar en celebraciones populares y familiares, a tener una representación en el cine, la televisión y ser un símbolo de México en el mundo.
Hoy el mariachi no solo se escucha en el extranjero, sino que han nacido agrupaciones en diferentes países, desde Latinoamérica, hasta Europa, Asia y Medio Oriente.
Esto resume su valor musical y cultural, y reafirma la importancia de mantener viva la tradición. Transmitirlo de generación en generación va más allá de seguir cantando sus canciones, se necesita buscar nuevas voces y músicos dispuestos a interpretarlas.
Un arte que necesita nuevas voces
“El mariachi es esencia de México en el mundo, presencia de Jalisco en México”, así describe la importancia de este género musical Don Ángel Martínez, representante del Mariachi Nuevo Tecalitlán.
Por eso es importante conservar la tradición, algo que se ha buscado impulsar en Jalisco, la meca del mariachi, con el objetivo de que los jóvenes mantengan el cariño hacia esta música y la transmitan con dignidad y orgullo.
Y los frutos se ven en los mariachis infantiles que tienen muchas agrupaciones, incluyendo el Mariachi Nuevo Tecatitlán, que también tiene su rama femenil. De esta forma, se vuelven semilleros de las próximas generaciones.
Pero, aunque no todos se conviertan en músicos profesionales, “el hecho de tener un contacto con el arte y la cultura de México, los hace ciudadanos más sensibles y empáticos con la sociedad”, explica Don Ángel.
Ser mariachi no es algo improvisado. En México existen escuelas de mariachi que permiten estudiar esta carrera de forma profesional, algo que puede llevar alrededor de cuatro años.
Sin embargo, como señala el músico, lo más importante es la práctica. Un mariachi profesional tiene ensayos múltiples días de la semana, con varias horas cada uno, pues la técnica para tocar los instrumentos, incluyendo la voz, debe trabajarse continuamente.
De esta forma se logra lo más importante para este género: transmitir diferentes emociones al público, pues “la música de mariachi no solo se escucha, se siente”, apunta Don Ángel.
Esto es lo que ha permitido romper las barreras del idioma y llevarlo a diferentes partes del mundo, pues, aunque las personas no entiendan lo que dicen las letras, sí sienten lo que expresan.
El traje, la identidad del mariachi
Si hay algo que identifica a estos músicos es su traje. Su inspiración es la ropa que usaban los campesinos con adornos de vestimenta española.
Como explica Don Ángel, se compone por el moño, la chaquetilla, la botonadura, botines charros especiales con fuelle, el fajo de vaqueta y la hebilla de plata, todo esto como parte del traje clásico de los charros hacendados.
Aunque hoy el mariachi se encuentra en casi cualquier rincón de México, la experiencia completa se vive en Jalisco. Desde la Plaza de los Mariachis en Guadalajara, donde se reúnen diferentes grupos, hasta los diferentes pueblos mágicos.
Un fin de semana en Cocula te acercará a las raíces de esta tradición, donde las presentaciones en vivo se unen al Museo de la Cuna Mundial del Mariachi, mientras en Tecatitlán te espera el Museo Silvestre Vargas con la historia del Mariachi Vargas.

title: La ciclovía de Bogotá, una revolución que inspiró al mundo hace más de 50 años
content:
La ciclovía de Bogotá, una revolución que inspiró al mundo hace más de 50 años
Hace 50 años, una protesta sobre dos ruedas cambió para siempre la forma de vivir Bogotá. Jaime Ortiz Marino impulsó la primera gran ciclovía de la ciudad, una idea que nació como una defensa del espacio público frente a los automóviles y que hoy inspira a cientos de ciudades del mundo.
Jaime Ortiz Marino, un barbudo aficionado a la bicicleta, lideró una revolución hace 50 años a punta de pedal. Es el inventor en Bogotá de la ciclovía, una contracultura al uso del automóvil que ha inspirado al mundo.
El 15 de diciembre de 1974, este arquitecto obtuvo un permiso para hacer una singular protesta contra la masificación de los autos: cerrar una zona de la capital colombiana a los coches y transitar en "bici" por el centro de la vía con otras 5,000 personas.
El primer evento importante de este tipo en el mundo se convirtió rápidamente en una tradición muy popular de todos los domingos.
La ciclovía que abarcaba la mayor parte de la ciudad ha sido imitada con modelos similares por unas 200 ciudades del planeta, según la alcaldía.
"Es el aula cívica al aire libre más grande del mundo", dice a la AFP Ortiz, que ahora tiene 78 años, y una barba blanca bien delineada, mientras observaba su creación con satisfacción.
Cada domingo alrededor 1.7 millones de bogotanos caminan, montan en bicicleta, patinan o realizan otras actividades físicas a lo largo de 127 kilómetros de calles sin autos, de acuerdo con cifras oficiales.
Los paseos dominicales son un respiro profundo para los habitantes de una de las mayores metrópolis de América Latina, con uno de los peores tráficos de la región y afectada por la contaminación del aire.
"La ciclovía es parte del alma de Bogotá", asegura Camilo Ramírez, un especialista en migración que trotaba junto a su esposa detrás de sus hijos de 5 y 12 años, ambos en bicicleta.
"Válvula de escape"
Desde Ciudad de México hasta Santiago y Sao Paulo, varias urbes latinoamericanas han puesto en marcha programas semanales de calles abiertas a la bicicleta en los últimos 20 años.
En Bogotá, a 2,600 metros sobre el nivel del mar, casi todos los domingos las nubes grises de contaminación se reducen.
En 2024, la ciclovía ha ayudado a reducir el equivalente a 444 toneladas de CO2, según cifras entregadas a la AFP.
Los deportistas disfrutan de la jornada soleada con paradas para refrescarse con diferentes bebidas y frutas, y comer empanadas y otros bocadillos.
Los más entusiastas recorren desde el norte, en los barrios más acomodados, hasta el sur, más pobre, o viceversa.
"¡Esto es lo que me da vida!", dice Jhon Lozano, un fanático del ciclismo de 89 años, que sale de casa a las 4:30 de la mañana cada domingo en su bicicleta de carreras para reunirse con amigos a lo largo de la ruta.
Ortiz describe la ciclovía como una "válvula de escape" para la cuarta ciudad más grande de América Latina, cuya población se ha multiplicado por diez en los últimos 50 años, pasando de 800.000 habitantes a ocho millones.
El crecimiento demográfico y la mala planificación urbanística hacen de Bogotá una ciudad con cada vez más autos, pero menos espacio para que transiten.
De las grandes urbes de la región es la única que aún no tiene metro, cuya construcción apenas está iniciando.
El Índice TomTom de Tráfico Urbano sitúa a Bogotá como la segunda área metropolitana más congestionada del mundo en 2023, después de Manila.
Locos por la "bici"
La tercera capital nacional más alta del mundo, después de La Paz y Quito, podría parecer un lugar poco amable para iniciar una revolución a bordo de una "bici".
Pero la pasión de los colombianos por el ciclismo se remonta a varias generaciones atrás, alimentada por las hazañas de leyendas de los pedales como Luis "Lucho" Herrera, ganador de la Vuelta a España en 1987, y Egan Bernal, primer latinoamericano en ganar el Tour de Francia, en 2019.
Como los padres de varios de esos ídolos, en Colombia los campesinos y la clase trabajadora usan la bicicleta para llegar a sus trabajos.
Antes de la ciclovía, "sabíamos que (...) en la mayor parte de las casas había una bicicleta", pero no espacios dónde montar, recuerda Ortiz.
Hoy Bogotá tiene cerca de 600 km de carriles construidos solo para ciclistas.
Las dos ruedas se convirtieron en un símbolo de emancipación, "permitiendo a todo el mundo desplazarse de forma accesible", analiza el psicólogo y urbanista Carlos Efe Pardo.
Además de su aporte para el ejercicio físico y el medio ambiente, la ciclovía se convirtió también en fuente de empleo, en un país cuya informalidad alcanza al 55% de los trabajadores.
"Aquí he ganado lo que necesito para pagar la educación de mi hija, mi propio bienestar y mi casa", afirma Eladio Gustavo Atis, mecánico de 56 años que lleva 32 arreglando pinchazos e inflando neumáticos para los ciclistas.

title: Fiction Park: They left a city and found a home
content:
Culture & Lifestyle
Fiction Park: They left a city and found a home
When an old friend tells a family about an empty ancestral property, a family decides to leave Kathmandu and start anew.LB Thapa
The dice of fate had never rolled in Bire’s favour. His insatiable appetite for gambling had finally consumed the last vestiges of his inheritance.
When Bire announced his intention to seek fortune in Kathmandu, Chhabilal, Bire’s elder brother, did not intervene. He simply watched his brother disappear over the horizon, knowing that some journeys must be undertaken alone.
Kathmandu greeted Bire with its characteristic chaos—a cacophony of honking vehicles and the ceaseless rhythm of survival. Bire found himself among the daily wage labourers who gathered at construction sites. He worked hard under the scorching sunlight. He carried bricks and mixed cement under the unforgiving sun, trying to adjust to the new environment.
In the evenings, when the work was done, and the labourers gathered around flickering lanterns to share their meagre dinners, Bire would join them in their rituals of escape. A bottle of local liquor passed from hand to hand, and a deck of cards would appear, the familiar symbols of his downfall drawing him back like a moth to flame. It was during one such evening that he first noticed Sita—not among the drinkers, but moving with quiet grace through the shadows of the labour settlement.
Sita was the daughter of Hom Bahadur, a weathered labourer who had raised his child with values as solid as the walls he helped construct. Unlike many in their circumstances, Hom Bahadur had insisted on education for his daughter. Sita had passed her School Leaving Certificate examination, but the halls of higher education held no appeal for her. She preferred the simple rhythms of domestic life—the warmth of the kitchen, the comfort of her mother's company, the quiet dignity of caring for their modest home.
Bire and Sita’s paths crossed with increasing frequency, their conversations beginning with shy glances and progressing to stolen moments between work shifts. However, Sita, through her own observation, glimpsed the man he could become. When Bire finally gathered the courage to propose, Sita's acceptance came with conditions as firm as the mountain stone that surrounded their village.
"I am also willing to marry you, Bire," she said with unwavering intensity. "But you must forsake three things: the gambling that has destroyed you, the drink that clouds your judgment, and the smoke that will blacken your lungs. These are not merely requests—they are the foundation upon which our life together must be built."
Bire agreed without hesitation, but Sita, wise beyond her years, demanded more than empty promises. She led him to the sacred precincts of Pashupatinath Temple, where the ancient Shiva lingam stands as a silent witness to countless vows. Bire knelt before the lord of destruction and creation, swearing with all the sincerity his soul could muster to honour his word.
When Sita finally confided in her father, Hom Bahadur agreed with her daughter’s decision.
The wedding was modest but filled with joy. Bire and Sita began their married life in a single room in Kathmandu's labyrinthine alleys, their possessions few but their dreams abundant. In that cramped space, Sita insisted on creating a small shrine, a corner of sanctity where she could offer her daily prayers. Bire, who had once lived only for the next gamble, now found himself drawn to the quiet peace of devotion.
Two daughters arrived in quick succession—tiny bundles of joy who filled their parents’ hearts while straining their already limited resources. The single room that had once seemed sufficient now felt like a cage. Bire watched his daughters sleep as Sita performed her evening rituals, and his heart ached for something more—a home where they could breathe, where the sacred could have its own space, where his children could play without knocking against the walls that confined them.
It was during one of his restless walks that Bire encountered Hikmat, an old friend whose own life had taken unexpected turns. Hikmat listened patiently as Bire poured out his frustrations—the impossibility of affording a proper home in the city, his unwillingness to let Sita work while their daughters were so young, the constant pressure that threatened to crush the fragile peace they had built.
"I have an idea," Hikmat said, his eyes gleaming with the light of revelation. "My ancestral village—Timirkot—lies about eighty kilometers from Gorkha Bazaar. We sold our property to a man named Captain Chitra Bahadur, a Gurkha serving in the British Army. He lives in England now and hasn't visited in years. The house stands empty, surrounded by land that once bloomed with abundance. You could live there. The village is nearly deserted now—no one would bother you."
Bire's heart quickened at the prospect. The village life he had known in his childhood called to him like a forgotten melody. He rushed home to share the proposal with Sita, who agreed immediately.
The journey began with a day's rest in Gorkha. The next morning, they boarded a battered jeep that carried them through winding mountain roads, the vehicle groaning with each turn. At Chisapani Bhanjyang, the road ended, and their true journey began.
For twenty kilometers they walked—Bire carrying their belongings, Sita with the younger daughter strapped to her back, the older girl clinging to her mother's hand. The path wound through rhododendron forests and alongside rushing streams, past terraced fields that clung to impossible slopes, and over suspension bridges that swayed treacherously above deep gorges.
When they finally reached Timirkot, Bire had no trouble locating Hikmat's ancestral home. It stood at the edge of the village, a structure of stone and timber that had once been grand but now wore the melancholy of abandonment. Vines crept over its walls, and the courtyard had surrendered to weeds and wild grass. The village itself seemed frozen in time—a handful of houses scattered across the hillside, many of them roofless and decaying, their former inhabitants having fled to the cities in search of opportunity.
But Bire and Sita saw not decay but potential. With determination born of necessity, they set to work. They cleared the undergrowth, scrubbed the stone floors until they shone, and repaired what they could with the limited tools they possessed. Sita cooked their meals over an open fire while Bire worked by the light of their kerosene lantern.
Within weeks, the house began to transform. The barren land around it responded to Bire's labor with generous yields—vegetables of every variety, grains and eventually, livestock that filled the empty stalls. Bire established connections with traders in Gorkha, who made the arduous journey to collect his produce. He was building not just a home but a legacy.
The villagers who remained were curious about the newcomers. Some came to offer help; others simply to observe. Bire received them all with the hospitality. When they asked who he was and how he had come to live in the captain's house, he would smile and say, "This is my home now, and you are all my neighbours."
His daughters grew strong and healthy, their laughter echoing through the valleys. A primary school lay five kilometers away—a journey they would make when they reached the proper age. For now, their education came from their mother's stories and their father's lessons about the land. Sita had never been happier; she had space for her shrine, room to breathe, and the peace that comes from living in harmony with nature.
Then, on an ordinary morning, everything changed.
Bire was working in his fields when he heard angry voices echoing from the house. He dropped his hoe and ran, his heart pounding with a premonition of disaster. When he arrived, he found a distinguished-looking man and his wife confronting Sita, their faces contorted with rage.
"How dare you occupy my property without permission!" the man thundered. "I will summon the police immediately!"
Bire stepped forward, his hands raised in a gesture of submission. "Sir, I beg your forgiveness," he said, his voice steady despite the turmoil within.
"We meant no disrespect. We will vacate your property at once. Please, there is no need for the authorities—we will leave peacefully."
Captain Chitra Bahadur, a British Army officer, was momentarily disarmed by Bire's humility. Sita, meanwhile, had recovered her composure and was already ushering the captain and his wife inside. She offered them fresh yogurt and insisted they rest while she prepared a proper meal. The captain's wife, impressed by Sita's grace under pressure, began to soften.
Over the course of the day, Bire showed the captain the fields he had cultivated, the livestock he had raised, and the repairs he had made to the property.
That night, as the family huddled together in the kitchen, preparing for their departure, Captain Chitra Bahadur and his wife held their own conversation.
The next morning, as the captain and his wife prepared to leave, he called Bire and Sita before him. His stern visage had been replaced by something warmer, something approaching gratitude.
"My wife and I have discussed the matter thoroughly," he said. "And we have reached a decision. You will stay. The property is mine, yes, but I have no intention of living here. The previous caretaker abandoned his duties—he hasn't paid the taxes in two years. You, however, have shown greater care for my land than I could have hoped for. I ask only one thing: pay the taxes promptly and send me the receipts on WhatsApp. Consider this as your home, for as long as you wish."
Bire and Sita stood frozen, the weight of the captain's words slowly penetrating their consciousness. Tears streamed down their faces—tears of relief, of gratitude, of vindication. They had ventured into the unknown with nothing, but they had been rewarded beyond their wildest expectations.
As the captain departed, waving from the winding path, Bire turned to Sita, who was still in tears. Their daughters emerged from the house, their small faces full of curiosity at their parents' display of emotion.

title: Tribes hit hard by wildfires face health effects, cultural losses
content:
Nada Hassanein
Stateline
Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior.
Now it’s gone.
Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said.
“I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.”
Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen.
Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires.
“What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel, executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert.
An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks.
This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service.
The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires.
Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said.
“The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.”
By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015.
Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres.
In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed.
The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands.
Health effects
Faith Zacherle-Tonasket has seen how the wildfires have affected perinatal health. Founder of xa?xa? Indigenous Birth Justice, which offers perinatal and doula support across the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said three of her clients went into early labor during this year’s fires. She and her team believe stress amid displacement due to evacuations contributed to the early labor. Emerging research is also showing how wildfire smoke is a primary pollutant affecting pregnancy.
Zacherle-Tonasket also helps lead the River Warrior Society, a nonprofit offering wildfire relief for tribal and non-tribal members. The group has been coordinating shelter placements for elders, donations and food assistance.
“This is one of the biggest fires our reservation has had,” she said. “The biggest need we have on our reservation is air purifiers.”
Respiratory health has been a major concern post-wildfires amid smoke and poor air quality. American Indian and Alaska Native people disproportionately have chronic respiratory health conditions exacerbated by wildfire smoke, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Matilda Bob’s father, a veteran who is now displaced with her, has COPD.
Along with respiratory distress, there’s been “tremendous stress, anxiety, grief, trauma — and we expect and know that those behavioral health needs are going to continue beyond this current emergency. Post-fire recovery creates additional health concerns,” said Dayna Seymour, the Colville Tribes’ health and human services chair. “Our members are going in now to clean up the ash and debris, and aren’t really always sure what’s in that ash and debris, whether there’s hazardous materials, heavy metals, asbestos or other contaminants.”
Seymour added that community members helped deliver medications to their displaced neighbors and helped each other dig fire lines.
Research shows disproportionate smoke exposure among tribes in California, noted University of Kansas Assistant Professor Melinda Adams, a cultural fire practitioner and scholar who teaches in the Department of Earth, Energy, and Environment.
“Because wildfire is increasing in frequency and intensity,” said Adams, a member of the N’dee San Carlos Apache Tribe of Arizona, “we must look at cumulative effects and identify patterns in human and environmental health while investing in climate and wildfire mitigation strategies that include Indigenous knowledge.”
Prescribed burns, carefully controlled fires to reduce brush that could fuel megablazes, are crucial tools in preventing dangerous wildfires and preserving ecosystem health. But regulatory barriers have made implementing traditional Indigenous burn practices difficult, Desautel and Adams said.
This week, the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee advanced legislation that would streamline approval of prescribed burns, while the EPA issued guidance last year.
Funding and staffing limitations are also a barrier, Desautel added. The Indian Forest Management Assessment Team found that Indian trust forest lands are funded at about a third per acre of comparable federal forests.
Waterway pollution, cultural art lost
Seymour added that traditional foods including huckleberries and herbs and roots, such as bitterroot and camas, that the tribes rely on were scorched across the land.
“Those are things that we utilize to help us in ceremony, that we utilize to eat for subsistence. So that was a huge loss for our people,” Seymour said.
In Oregon, while no homes were lost on the Klamath Tribes’ lands, leaders still have concerns and uncertainty around environmental aftereffects, particularly on traditional food systems the tribes were finally in the process of regenerating.
The tribes had just started restoring their ancestral salmon after removal of four dams two years ago. Last year, the tribes documented the first adult Chinook salmon in the Williamson River, and earlier this year detected the first salmon hatch in over a century in the tributaries of the Upper Klamath Lake.
“The biggest (wildfire) impact is the effects on hunting and gathering that may be felt in the future. …With this high-intensity, high-severity wildfire, there’s likelihood of sedimentation into the streams that could serve as spawning grounds for that new salmon,” said Tim Sexton, Wildland Fire Program Manager at the Klamath Tribes. Research is showing how wildfires affect fish habitats.
Klamath Tribes Chairman William Ray Jr., a former firefighter of 40 years, said he’s been advocating for tribal control of the waterways amid pollution that already existed before this year’s wildfires.
“We have ecological collapse going on. Our water quality in our lake and rivers isn’t very good,” he said.
At the Colville Reservation, Zacherle-Tonasket said many of her community members are holding off on traditional hunting and instead her nonprofit has gotten discounts from local butchers to help families.
“We don’t want to hunt this year,” she told Stateline. “It’s just ethically not right to hunt when our own animals are suffering the way we are.”
Bob said that many cultural heirlooms burned — her own traditional beadwork, a 100-year-old berry basket passed down from her great grandmother, and her nephew’s handmade attire worn during special dances at powwows.
But her family will continue to dance as they do “for the people who can’t,” she said, on their ancestral land.
“Every time your foot hits the floor’s a prayer,” she said. “We were raised to respect the land. … We’re still standing in the fact that we’re all OK, that we all made it, that we didn’t lose anybody.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

title: From Karnataka Midwife To Padma Shri: Remembering Sulagitti Narasamma’s Extraordinary Journey
content:
Sulagitti Narasamma, a traditional midwife from Karnataka, spent nearly seven decades helping women through childbirth, drawing on knowledge she learnt through observation, experience and her grandmother, Marigamma. Born on 16 June 1920 in Thimmenayapete village in Pavagada, Tumkur district, Narasamma began learning childbirth practices as a young girl by accompanying her grandmother, who was also a midwife. She later became known as ‘Sulagitti Narasamma’, with ‘sulagitti’ being the Kannada word for a traditional midwife.
She travelled across villages and remote communities to assist women in labour, including difficult deliveries. Her work continued despite social rejection and caste barriers. She was recognised with the Vayoshreshtha Samman in 2013, Karnataka’s Rajyotsava award the same year, an honorary doctorate from Tumkur University in 2014 and the Padma Shri in 2018. She died on 25 December 2018, aged 98. Looking back on her life, Narasamma described midwifery as a sacred responsibility and said, “The work of a Sulagitti was given to me by God.”
Not Just A Profession
Narasamma’s relationship with midwifery began within her family. Her grandmother Marigamma had worked as a traditional midwife in the village of Madakasira after being widowed at a young age. She did not charge families for her services. Instead, villagers supported her with food, clothing and the implements she needed. Narasamma accompanied her grandmother when she went to assist women in childbirth and gradually absorbed what she observed.
The apprenticeship shaped the way she later understood childbirth. She learnt to use her hands to assess the baby’s position and sense when birth was approaching. She also learnt about traditional herbs and plants, including knowledge shared by communities she encountered during her work. Narasamma recalled that she was still an adolescent when she delivered her first baby. Her aunt-in-law, Kanumakka, went into labour while other women in the neighbourhood were away at work.
Narasamma summoned a young girl for assistance and delivered the baby. According to Narasamma’s account, Kanumakka blessed her afterwards and encouraged her to continue the work. Over time, Narasamma’s reputation spread beyond her village. Families travelled to seek her help, while she herself travelled by foot, bullock cart and other vehicles to reach women in labour. She was sometimes called upon for difficult births, including by a Brahmin doctor who, according to Narasamma, sought her assistance after hospital medicines and injections had not helped.
Crossing Social And Geographical Boundaries
Narasamma’s work was not always accepted by the people around her. Some members of her family considered midwifery ‘polluting’ work, while her husband’s income from selling buttermilk was affected as some people stopped buying from him because she continued her work. She also encountered caste-based restrictions. In some upper-caste homes, she was asked to conduct deliveries in courtyards, while strict social boundaries governed who could enter certain homes. Yet Narasamma continued to help women regardless of their caste or community. She recalled travelling through heavy rain and difficult terrain to reach the temporary settlement of a nomadic tribal community near a forest.
The journey took several hours, but she eventually reached the woman in labour and safely delivered the baby. Narasamma also described how she viewed women’s suffering during childbirth as something shared across social divisions. Her understanding of service extended beyond delivery itself. In her recorded consent statement, she spoke about advising pregnant women and new mothers about diet and breastfeeding, while also recalling traditional knowledge of herbs, leaves and roots.
She strongly rejected the practice of blaming women who could not conceive. She argued that responsibility should not automatically be placed on women and said both husband and wife should be considered. Her statement reflected the values she had developed through decades of lived experience. “Under no circumstance should the woman be called ‘barren’,” she said in the account.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Sulagitti Narasamma’s story is not only about childbirth. It is also about how knowledge is learnt, preserved and passed between generations. Her training did not take place in a classroom; it began by watching her grandmother and developed through years of experience within the community. Her story also shows how care can cross boundaries created by caste, geography and social convention.
At the same time, traditional practices and community knowledge should be understood responsibly alongside the importance of safe, evidence-based maternal healthcare. Narasamma herself described her work through the language of service and compassion, saying, “Delivering a woman from labour pain is more sacred than a puja.” Her life invites us to look beyond formal recognition and ask what happens to valuable community knowledge when the people who carry it are no longer there to pass it on.
How can we preserve such lived knowledge while ensuring every mother has access to safe and dignified healthcare?
