title: Arapaho Tribe Wants Christian Pastor Off Reservation After She Calls Their Ceremonies 'Idol Worship'
content:
ARAPAHOE, Wyo. (AP) — Every Sunday morning on the Wind River Reservation, congregants gather at Foundations for Nations Church to pray while protesters outside do the same.
The two rituals have unfolded in parallel since the Christian church’s pastor, Sarah Lucas, preached a sermon condemning Arapaho ceremonial ways.
The Northern Arapaho and Eastern Shoshone Tribes that share the reservation have made clear that Lucas is no longer welcome. Lucas, who is not Native American but owns the land under her church, says she isn’t going anywhere. The standoff tests the boundaries of religious freedom and the right of a tribal nation to govern according to its own values and protocols.
The conflict stems from a video that circulated in July as Arapaho people surfaced from their weeklong sundance ceremony. In it, Lucas called that cornerstone of Arapaho spiritual life “idol worship.”
“Jesus is the chain breaker. He is the only God that we should be praying to,” Lucas said.
Lucas says her words reflect her interpretation of the Bible and are constitutionally protected. Many Arapaho people say she took aim at something central to who they are, reopening wounds from a not-so-distant era of religious assimilation and abuse.
With the smell of coffee and sweetgrass swirling, regular Sunday demonstrators were recently joined by activists from the American Indian Movement and Arapaho Chairman Keenan Groesbeck as they marched past ranchland and scattered homes toward the church.
“We brought in our ceremonial elders. We heard them loud and clear,” said Groesbeck. “They don’t want them here no more.”
Lucas condemned the highest Arapaho ceremony
The sundance marks a time of connection, offering and collective renewal. As Arapaho people closed this year’s ceremony and welcomed a new year according to their traditions, Lucas and her smaller-than-usual congregation prayed for them.
“You have generations, centuries of people doing this offering, going in and making vows to change,” Lucas said. “Father God, we see no fruit.”
Many Arapahos were stunned to hear an outsider not only disparage the ceremony but talk about closely held details that aren’t meant to be discussed openly.
Big Wind Carpenter, who was among the protesters, said Lucas couldn’t have chosen a more painful target.
“There’s nothing I could say to make non-Arapahos understand,” Carpenter said.
Lucas said she regrets her sharp delivery captured in clips that went viral but not the message itself. Since founding her church nine years ago, she said she has had “hard conversations” urging Native congregants to renounce sundance, sweat lodges and burning cedar during prayer, traditions she equates to idolatry.
“The Bible makes it very clear to only worship one God,” Lucas said.
Some members of her mixed Native and white congregation were unaware of her stance. Lucas said Sunday turnout is down half from 150. Some weeks, the protest crowd has rivaled church attendance.
Arapaho congregant Tearany Black, who considers Lucas a stand-in parent, said she agrees Native Christians should turn away from ceremony but found the tone of the sermon racist.
“She cares for our people,” said Black. “I just don’t think she understands where we’re coming from.”
On Wind River, ceremony and Christianity coexist
DJ Gardner grew up praying in sweat lodges and reading the Bible. He joined Lucas’ congregation last year and didn’t anticipate being asked to choose.
“I thought they accepted us,” Gardner said. “In my view, why else would you be on a reservation?”
The 28-year-old, who has walked away from Foundations for Nations, associates Lucas’ rhetoric with assimilationist boarding schools like the one his grandfather survived.
In part to repair that dark history, the Episcopal and Catholic missions that have been active on Wind River since the late 1800s now embrace ceremonial practices.
“It’s an irony of colonialism, the degree to which Native people have remade Christianity according to their own values,” said Michael McNally, a professor of religious studies at Carleton College in Minnesota.
Lucas interprets the Bible differently.
“I don’t believe you can have mixture,” she said.
Foundations for Nations grew through community aid
Mary Rose Goggles was struggling with the costs of raising her grandchildren in 2017 when Lucas knocked on her door and warmly invited her to join her new church.
Goggles, who practices Arapaho ceremonial ways but dabbles in Christianity, liked the worship band and activities that kept her grandchildren busy. As Foundations for Nations grew, she visited its food bank, clothing giveaways and events like a fall harvest festival.
“It was good to see the kids enjoying themselves. It was good to see my relations getting help,” Goggles said.
Lucas built relationships on Wind River by filling gaps. Her church offers free after-school and summer day camps. Visiting missionaries fill tribal members’ gas tanks and replace their sagging roofs.
Foundations for Nations’ website solicits outside donations to “revive, raise up and restore” Wind River, listing grim statistics about addiction, sexual assault and unemployment. The Associated Press found those numbers were pulled from national studies not specific to the reservation or could not be traced to a verifiable source.
A page asking donors to “sponsor” a child in exchange for photos and letters was recently removed.
Goggles left Foundations for Nations several years ago after moving away but thought warmly of the church until seeing Lucas’ sermon, which she said left her “heartbroken.”
Jenea Mandan has cycled through feelings of anger and shame about sending her children to the church’s summer camp. An Arapaho traditionalist, Mandan had misgivings about the Christian program but needed childcare help.
“At that time I was a single mom, I was in a low-income situation,” Mandan said. “It feels like they took advantage of that.”
The church sits on private land. The tribe still wants it gone
Lucas believes God called her to Wind River. But she deliberately built her church on private property within the reservation’s boundaries rather than tribal land where, she said, the tribes would effectively be her landlords.
Foundations for Nations is located amid a patchwork of federal, tribal and private property — the legacy of 19th century federal policies designed to eliminate tribes by breaking up collective land bases.
“That era has cascading effects that are devastating for tribal sovereignty,” said Jessica Shoemaker, a professor at the University of Nebraska College of Law.
Shoemaker said tribes have broad civil authority over non-Natives on tribal land, including to banish them. But jurisdiction over private property within reservations is litigated case-by-case.
Lucas and her attorneys with the Liberty Counsel, a conservative Christian legal organization, assert that her ownership of the property shields her from banishment.
In July, the Arapaho and Shoshone councils passed ordinances requiring religious groups to seek their approval before operating on Wind River.
“That’s the law of the land on our reservation,” said Groesbeck.
That has forced Foundations for Nations to suspend youth programming since it is now prohibited from picking up and dropping off children on the reservation.
In an Aug. 31 memo, the Arapaho council acknowledged that “jurisdictional limits” likely prevent it from regulating church activity on private land. And any tribal court enforcement of those ordinances could face federal review, where there’s a high bar for proving non-Native conduct threatens tribal well-being.
Meanwhile, the 21,000 square-foot (1,950 square-meter), steel-sided building that houses Foundations for Nations’ sanctuary, community spaces and indoor playground has been unusually quiet. Construction on a neighboring youth center continues.
“God would not have us build this and provided all of it to empty it out,” Lucas said.
Gardner has returned to the Catholic church of his childhood, where Arapaho geometric motifs adorn the sanctuary and he is welcome to burn cedar.
He has been praying for guidance on forgiveness.
“In order for me to strive to be like Jesus, I would have to forgive,” Gardner said. “But there are some lines you just don’t cross.” ___
This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Día Internacional de las Mujeres Indígenas: tres lideresas que siembran respuestas frente al cambio climático
content:
- Las historias de tres lideresas indígenas en México, Colombia y Perú tienen un punto en común: enfrentar la crisis climática también significa conservar los conocimientos y las condiciones que han permitido a sus pueblos vivir en esos territorios durante generaciones.
- Xananine Calvillo trabaja con niñas, niños y jóvenes ngiwa del Valle de Tehuacán, en México, para recuperar semillas, alimentos y conocimientos ligados a su territorio.
- Mayra Collantes representa a las mujeres de 14 comunidades de la cuenca del Ampiyacu, donde impulsan soluciones frente a las sequías y las dificultades de acceso al agua.
- María Taimal acompaña a las Abuelas y Seguidoras de la Medicina Tradicional Cofán en la restauración de áreas del Putumayo mediante plantas medicinales.
En distintos territorios de América Latina, prepararse para un clima cada vez más extremo puede significar cosas tan concretas como proteger una semilla, recuperar una planta medicinal o conseguir que el agua vuelva a llegar hasta una comunidad. Frente a sequías prolongadas, temperaturas más altas, lluvias cada vez menos predecibles y fenómenos climáticos como El Niño, las mujeres indígenas están impulsando respuestas que combinan conocimientos transmitidos durante generaciones con nuevas herramientas para cuidar sus territorios y sostener la vida de sus pueblos.
Este 5 de septiembre, Día Internacional de las Mujeres Indígenas, sus experiencias también permiten mirar el cambio climático desde quienes enfrentan sus consecuencias. En sus comunidades, las mujeres participan en la producción de alimentos, el cuidado del agua y la conservación de los ecosistemas, pero también ocupan cada vez más espacios de organización y toma de decisiones desde los que proponen cómo prepararse frente a un futuro climático incierto.
En Mongabay Latam compartimos las historias de tres lideresas indígenas en México, Perú y Colombia. Aunque sus territorios y experiencias son distintos, las tres trabajan para mantener vivos conocimientos y prácticas que fortalecen la capacidad de sus comunidades para decidir cómo cuidar a la naturaleza y sus culturas.
México: sembrar conocimientos para defender el territorio
En las milpas del Valle de Tehuacán, en Puebla, existen terrazas agrícolas construidas con piedras sobre las laderas de los cerros. Desde tiempos antiguos, estos sistemas han permitido aprovechar el agua en un territorio donde las lluvias son escasas. Allí, Xananine Calvillo camina con niñas y niños: recorren los cultivos de maíz, buscan quelites, reconocen distintas plantas y escogen mazorcas. Después, utilizan hojas y semillas para pintar y conversar sobre el territorio: cómo era antes, qué crece en él y cómo imaginan su futuro.
“Cada vez que llega la época de lluvias, los cerros cambian de color; es como si tuvieran otra piel”, describe Calvillo sobre este paisaje donde el semidesierto se mezcla con el bosque tropical seco. “Entender las estaciones es lo que nos puede hacer más conscientes de nuestra dependencia de la naturaleza y de los ciclos de la tierra”.
Para Calvillo, recuperar las dietas tradicionales también forma parte de la respuesta frente al cambio climático. Esto implica reducir la dependencia de la agricultura industrial y volver a alimentos y prácticas vinculados con el territorio, desde los cultivos de la milpa hasta las plantas que crecen en los cerros.
“Nuestras dietas tradicionales —que aportan incluso mejores nutrientes que las dietas occidentales— no solo nos pueden hacer sobrevivir al cambio climático, sino también nos pueden hacer reconocer de dónde venimos y qué es lo mejor para la tierra de la que dependemos”, agrega.
Calvillo es una joven del pueblo ngiwa y activista por la justicia climática. Originaria de la comunidad de San Mateo Zoyamazalco, creció en el Valle de Tehuacán y estudió Estudios Latinoamericanos en la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM). Su interés por estos temas comenzó desde niña, al observar a sus abuelos sembrar y conservar semillas y, al mismo tiempo, los cambios que ocurrían alrededor de las comunidades con la expansión de la agricultura industrial.
Años después, tras participar en movimientos climáticos, decidió regresar parte de esas discusiones y herramientas a su propio territorio.
Junto con otras jóvenes ngiwa creó el Colectivo Jna Tsjo —“Cerro de la flor”—, que trabaja para recuperar conocimientos vinculados con la milpa, las plantas comestibles y medicinales y las semillas nativas. Una de sus preocupaciones es que estos saberes puedan seguir siendo transmitidos a las nuevas generaciones y, al mismo tiempo, convertirse en herramientas para enfrentar un clima cambiante.
“Es necesario formarnos en qué podemos hacer desde las comunidades, desde los hogares y con las infancias, de crear estas habilidades para sostener la vida, pero a la vez defender las condiciones que ya sostienen la vida”, dice la lideresa. “Tradicionalmente, nuestra alimentación proviene de los cultivos de la milpa: de las calabazas, los frijoles, los chiles y el maíz, que se complementan con las hierbas silvestres que crecen en la misma milpa, pero también en los cerros”.
En un territorio semiárido, explica Calvillo, las semillas conservadas y seleccionadas durante generaciones están adaptadas a condiciones de poca agua y temporadas cortas de lluvia. Por eso, protegerlas tiene también un sentido de autonomía y supervivencia. En los intercambios de semillas organizados por el colectivo han encontrado familias a las que ya les resulta difícil conseguir variedades nativas, mientras aumenta la dependencia de semillas comerciales. Para ella, recuperar las primeras significa que las comunidades puedan conservar una herramienta propia para responder ante escenarios de escasez de agua y alimentos.
El colectivo lleva esta conversación especialmente a niñas, niños y jóvenes mediante recorridos por las milpas, intercambios de semillas, talleres al aire libre, murales y actividades artísticas. No se trata solamente de enseñarles cómo sembrar. Calvillo busca que pregunten a sus madres, padres y abuelos qué se cultivaba antes, qué plantas se comían o utilizaban como medicina y qué historias existen alrededor de ellas. Así, la recuperación de conocimientos también fortalece una relación con el territorio que, sostiene, será necesaria para que una nueva generación quiera permanecer en él y defenderlo.
“Nosotros entendemos que mucho del conocimiento ancestral ya está incrustado en la lengua misma, en la forma en la que se dicen las cosas, en la forma en la que se habla de la vida misma”, describe.
El agua atraviesa buena parte de esas preocupaciones. Calvillo cuenta que los agricultores ya enfrentan mayores dificultades para anticipar las temporadas a partir de las primeras lluvias y que los ciclos que antes servían para decidir cuándo sembrar o cosechar son cada vez menos predecibles. A ello se suma la presión que ejerce la extracción industrial de agua en una región donde los manantiales, ríos y acuíferos son fundamentales para las comunidades.
“Nuestras semillas se han adaptado a eso, pero ahora hay una dependencia de las semillas transgénicas, del agronegocio, de las industrias que al final están haciendo que nuestro pueblo pierda la soberanía alimentaria y su capacidad de sobrevivir a la escasez de comida y de agua, por toda esta extracción que las industrias han hecho al punto de secar pozos y manantiales”, explica Calvillo. “Solo la organización comunitaria es capaz de detener todos estos proyectos extractivos”.
Frente a las sequías y temperaturas más altas que podrían intensificarse con fenómenos climáticos como El Niño, plantea que las respuestas deben combinar prácticas tradicionales —como la captación de lluvia y el cuidado de los sitios vinculados al agua— con nuevas tecnologías y, sobre todo, con la defensa territorial.
“El movimiento de defensa del territorio está liderado por personas más grandes y nosotras decíamos: cuando ellos no estén, ¿quién va a seguir esta lucha?”, cuestiona Calvillo. “Esas mismas personas nos han respondido que se necesita involucrar a los jóvenes. Nosotras veíamos que podíamos usar lo que sabemos, no solo lo que hemos estudiado, pero también lo que los abuelos nos han contado, para transmitírselo a otras generaciones, a las infancias, e ir creando conciencia, y después en la capacidad de liderar estas luchas”.
Esa defensa intenta ahora trascender a cada comunidad. El Consejo Regional Ngiwa reúne a autoridades tradicionales, comuneros, colectivos y habitantes de 12 comunidades del Valle de Tehuacán para intercambiar conocimientos y organizarse frente a amenazas sobre el territorio. Algunas comunidades, explica Calvillo, conservan mejor sus semillas. Otras mantienen conocimientos sobre lugares sagrados o formas de cuidar el agua. Compartirlos puede fortalecer su capacidad colectiva para enfrentar periodos de sequía y calor.
Para Calvillo, la adaptación climática no puede reducirse a aprender a soportar condiciones cada vez más difíciles. “Uno tampoco se puede adaptar a perder la lengua, a perder lo que nos hace nosotros, a perder la cultura, a perder el territorio, a perder la vida misma”, sostiene.
Perú: agua, organización y liderazgo frente a la sequía
Cuando el nivel de los ríos baja en la cuenca del Ampiyacu, en la Amazonía peruana, las distancias se hacen más largas. Las lanchas ya no pueden llegar hasta algunas comunidades y dejan a sus pasajeros en las playas, mientras que transportar alimentos y mercancías se vuelve más difícil y costoso.
Río arriba, donde algunas comunidades todavía no cuentan con sistemas de abastecimiento de agua, la sequía también puede traer problemas de salud. Mayra Collantes conoce bien estas dificultades. Hace unos tres años, recuerda, una fuerte sequía se prolongó durante casi seis meses.
“Este ha sido uno de los cambios climáticos más fuertes que hemos tenido”, cuenta. Durante aquel periodo, dice, aumentaron los precios, murieron peces en las cabeceras de los ríos y el agua de las quebradas se deterioró. Incluso encontraron animales silvestres muertos por falta de agua. “Sí nos vimos afectados totalmente, tanto nosotros como los animales”, recuerda.
Collantes tiene el cargo de Mujer Líder de la Federación de Comunidades Nativas de la Cuenca del Río Ampiyacu (FECONA) y representa a las mujeres de 14 comunidades. Desde joven comenzó a participar en reuniones y capacitaciones comunitarias, hasta asumir responsabilidades dentro de su comunidad y, posteriormente, en la Federación. Hoy forma parte de una junta directiva integrada por seis mujeres y seis hombres, donde, explica, las decisiones se toman de manera conjunta.
Esa participación ha sido clave para definir algunas de las respuestas frente a los cambios del clima. Una de ellas fue mejorar los sistemas de abastecimiento de agua utilizando energía solar.
En la comunidad de Collantes ya existía un sistema instalado por el Estado, pero funcionaba con gasolina. El costo del combustible fluctuaba y las familias pagaban entre 15 y 20 soles mensuales sin garantizar que el sistema pudiera operar todo el mes. Con la incorporación de paneles fotovoltaicos, el gasto de mantenimiento bajó a unos cinco soles mensuales y el bombeo se volvió más constante. “Desde que se hizo con el sistema fotovoltaico, ha mejorado el sistema de agua para las familias”, explica.
Conservación Internacional Perú, organización que ha acompañado y financiado parte de estas iniciativas, señala que actualmente unas 250 familias de cinco comunidades cuentan con sistemas mejorados. En algunos casos se rehabilitó infraestructura que había quedado fuera de funcionamiento y se sustituyó el bombeo con combustible por energía solar.
En otros casos se implementaron sistemas utilizando infraestructura comunitaria. El agua es entubada, no potable, y las federaciones han buscado coordinación con gobiernos locales para su tratamiento.
Para las mujeres, el efecto va más allá de disponer de agua. En muchas familias son ellas quienes recorren las distancias necesarias para conseguirla y quienes asumen buena parte del cuidado cuando niñas y niños enferman por problemas asociados a su calidad o escasez. Por eso, explica Conservación Internacional, su participación en los espacios donde se deciden las prioridades climáticas permite incorporar necesidades que de otra manera pueden quedar fuera.
“Desde Conservación Internacional, hemos venido impulsando las Guarderías de Conservación”, explica Bibi Gutiérrez, coordinadora intercultural de esta organización. “Muchas veces, las mujeres no asisten a reuniones, talleres, convocatorias ni asambleas de la comunidad, por lo que no expresan sus necesidades, porque tienen que quedarse en la casa con toda la carga familiar”.
Al contar con guarderías durante las actividades comunitarias y organizativas, las mujeres pueden participar sin tener que asumir al mismo tiempo el cuidado de sus hijas e hijos. Conservación Internacional contrata a personas para atenderlos y acompañarlos mientras ellas intervienen en estos espacios, expresan sus preocupaciones y participan en las decisiones. “Al final, las mujeres son las que acarrean el agua y las que hacen los cultivos. Ellas son las que más viven las amenazas del cambio climático”, sostiene Gutiérrez.
Para Collantes, la adaptación también pasa por fortalecer la autonomía y organización de las mujeres. Como becaria del Programa Mujer Indígena de Conservación Internacional, impulsó la formalización de seis asociaciones de productoras y artesanas para que pudieran inscribirse en registros públicos y acceder a fondos concursables; algunas ya han comenzado a hacerlo. Esta también es una forma de resiliencia frente al cambio climático, sostiene.
“Porque si dependen de un solo producto o cultivo, por las condiciones climáticas que son tan impredecibles, se enfrentan a diversos riesgos y sus ingresos pueden disminuir”, coincide Yadira Díaz, gerente del programa Loreto de Conservación Internacional Perú. Diversificar sus actividades, explica, permite a las familias contar con distintas fuentes de ingresos frente a esas variaciones y, al mismo tiempo, reducir las presiones sobre el bosque. “Es decir, podrían recurrir a actividades ilícitas como tala ilegal o minería para poder tener un ingreso, pero no lo hacen porque ven el valor que hay en el bosque en pie”, sostiene Díaz.
Mayra Collantes sabe, sin embargo, que prepararse no significa tener todas las respuestas. “Adaptarnos al cambio climático es muy complejo todavía para nosotros”, reconoce. Por eso insiste en continuar gestionando recursos, fortaleciendo capacidades y compartiendo lo aprendido entre mujeres antes de que llegue el siguiente fenómeno extremo.
“Hay que seguir trabajando, preparándonos y seguir gestionando, tocando puertas en las instituciones”, concluye Collantes. “Las mujeres líderes que conocen mucho más de este tema deben compartir con más mujeres el mensaje sobre la adaptación al cambio climático para estar preparadas todas y poder enfrentarlo”.
Colombia: restaurar el bosque para que permanezca la medicina
Bajo la sombra de un árbol, María Taimal dice que el clima se siente distinto. En la hectárea que las mujeres Cofán han venido restaurando en el Putumayo, Colombia, también han comenzado a observar otros cambios: plantas que producen frutos atraen abejas y aves, o algunos animales que vuelven a acercarse al área. Para ellas, recuperar ese espacio no significa únicamente volver a tener árboles. Allí también están intentando recuperar plantas medicinales, fuentes de agua y conocimientos que sus mayores han transmitido durante generaciones como una herramienta para enfrentar los cambios del clima.
“Donde sembramos una planta estamos sembrando vida”, afirma Taimal. “Esto es lo que nos motiva a seguir en la reforestación de muchas especies”.
Taimal pertenece al pueblo cofán, vive en el resguardo Santa Rosa del Guamuez, en el municipio de Valle del Guamuez, y representa al grupo Abuelas y Seguidoras de la Medicina Tradicional Cofán. Son 70 mujeres: 35 abuelas —la mayor tiene unos 98 años— y 35 seguidoras más jóvenes, además de niñas y niños que participan en el proceso.
El proyecto nació frente a una pérdida concreta. La deforestación había reducido la presencia de plantas medicinales vinculadas con la cultura del yagé, explica Taimal. Las mujeres decidieron entonces conservarlas y llevar a niñas y jóvenes a esos espacios para que pudieran aprender directamente de las mayores. “Nuestras abuelas y seguidoras de la medicina tradicional son conocedoras, son artesanas y también médicas; transmiten el conocimiento de generación en generación”, dice.
Con apoyo del programa Mujer Indígena de la Amazonía de Conservación Internacional Colombia, el grupo comenzó a restaurar terrenos que habían sido afectados por cultivos ilícitos. La propuesta consistía precisamente en utilizar plantas medicinales para recuperar esas áreas y, a la vez, fortalecer la medicina tradicional dentro de las comunidades.
“A raíz de la deforestación que hemos tenido en el Putumayo hemos creado chagras medicinales —en un encierro de 15 por 20 metros— y también una hectárea de tierra que queríamos conservar y en ella tener muchas plantas medicinales, maderables y artesanales que hacen parte de nuestra cultura”, explica Taimal.
Pero el deterioro ambiental se cruza con otros cambios que las mujeres perciben en el territorio. Taimal recuerda que antes podían regresar a trabajar a la chagra después del almuerzo. Ahora, asegura, el calor puede ser demasiado intenso. También ha visto disminuir el tamaño de ríos y quebradas que conoció durante su infancia.
Frente a los impactos del cambio climático, la restauración se ha convertido también en una forma de responder. Las mujeres plantan especies captadoras de agua alrededor de nacederos y quebradas y han comenzado a identificar lugares que consideran importantes para recuperar el agua, como las lagunas y sus sitios sagrados.
“Con el apoyo de Conservación Internacional pudimos reforestar con 300 plantas medicinales, artesanales y maderables, con las cuales también estamos fortaleciendo las fuentes hídricas que son primordiales para nosotros y para el mundo entero, porque el agua va a desembocar a los ríos y los ríos van a bañar a todo Colombia y hasta donde tengan que llegar”.
Lo que comenzó principalmente como restauración ahora incluye la transformación de plantas en cremas, champús y otros preparados a partir de conocimientos de medicina tradicional. Las mujeres recibieron capacitación para elaborar productos que puedan vender y generar ingresos.
Sin embargo, para Taimal el centro del proyecto sigue siendo la continuidad del conocimiento. En la cultura cofán, explica, el yagé ocupa un lugar central. “Es la planta mayor —como le decimos— y la planta guardiana de nuestro territorio”. Alrededor de ella existen otras plantas asociadas a su cultura que las mujeres buscan cuidar y propagar, pero son cada vez más las y los jóvenes que comienzan a acercarse a esos conocimientos para replicarlos.
“Aunque el área que ellas están influyendo para mitigar o para realizar acciones en contra el cambio climático no sea tan grande, el impacto que están generando sí lo es, porque es escalable”, explica Ana Vieco, coordinadora de proyectos de Conservación Internacional Colombia. “No se mantiene solo con lo que ellas están haciendo en el presente, sino que es un impacto que se va transmitiendo a las nuevas generaciones que ya están interesadas en participar en el proyecto. Invertir en la mujer de la Amazonía es invertir en la conservación de la Amazonía”, sostiene.
Esa transmisión es una forma de asegurar que la cultura cofán continúe. Por ello, las abuelas y abuelos cofán crearon un santuario de plantas medicinales: Orito Ingi–Ande, un lugar que los mayores “visionaron como una universidad”, dice Taimal. Allí, como en las áreas que hoy restauran, sembrar significa algo más que recuperar vegetación: es dejar a quienes vienen detrás un territorio donde todavía puedan aprender de las plantas, del agua y de quienes las cuidaron antes.
“Para el futuro, creo que desde ya debemos empezar a entregarles —como dicen nuestras abuelas— la rienda a nuestros jóvenes para que también vayan transmitiendo ese conocimiento de aquí a mañana a sus hijos y a sus familiares”, concluye Taimal. “Lo que queremos es que sigan y valoren lo que hoy en día estamos trabajando con nuestras abuelas sobre ese conocimiento tan grande”.
*Imagen principal: Xananine Calvillo durante un recorrido por la milpa tradicional resguardada por su compañera María y su familia en la comunidad de San Marcos Tlacoyalco. Foto: cortesía Amos Trust

title: Scottish Holocaust victim recognised at Auschwitz
content:
Scottish Holocaust victim recognised at Auschwitz
- Published
The name of a Scot who died in the Holocaust after refusing to abandon Jewish children in her care has been added to a special memorial wall at Auschwitz.
Jane Haining is recognised in a renewed section of the Auschwitz Birkenau Memorial and Museum's main exhibition - devoted to hundreds of prisoners for whom no registration photographs were taken.
The new name plaques adorn the wall of a long corridor and are displayed next to many images of prisoners dressed in striped shirts with shaved heads.
Haining's death certificate said she died in hospital on 17 July 1944, aged 47, but it is widely accepted she died in a gas chamber and her remains are on the Auschwitz site.
- Hungarian march honours Auschwitz Scot - Published14 April 2019

- Auschwitz Scot recalled by former pupil - Published7 June 2017

Born and raised in the village of Dunscore in the south of Scotland, Haining was the matron at a Church of Scotland school in Budapest from 1932 to 1944.
The Scottish Mission School had around 400 day and boarder pupils aged from six to 16 years old, a mixture of Jewish and Christian girls.
The Church of Scotland said she helped keep the children safe for more than four years after the war broke out in 1939.
Despite numerous offers to return home she stayed on, saying: "If these children need me in days of sunshine, how much more do they need me in days of darkness?"
She was arrested by German officers in April 1944 and taken to Auschwitz the following month.
A spokesman for Auschwitz Birkenau Memorial and Museum said: "The corridor has two important purposes.
"It restores individual names and identities to people who were imprisoned and killed in Auschwitz, but it also helps visitors understand the complexity of the prisoner population."
Members of Haining's family - Kevin O'Brien, Liz Harrigan and Patricia Audis - visited the exhibition this week during a study tour to Auschwitz, organised by the Renfrewshire branch of the Unison trade union.
Her neice, Deirdre MacDowell, said: "To see Jane's name on a permanent memorial wall makes one ask how is it that she came to be in Auschwitz?
"And that's the beginning of her story and it can be told to all who ask about her.
"Her story is humbling, full of compassion and kindness and makes us think about how we live our own lives - it is a legacy for us all."
A Church of Scotland spokesman said it was "very moving" to see her name added to the corridor wall to keep her memory alive for "generations to come".
"It is more important than ever that people learn the lessons of history and do not make the mistakes of the past," he said.

title: Back-to-school rituals that help these families calm first-day jitters
content:
This week, Libby Barnicke and her family will engage in what has become, for them, an important tradition. She’ll dress up her two boys in their crisp new school uniforms and line them up on the front porch for their annual back-to-school photo.
It’s a tradition that is replicated in households from coast to coast. For many families, these early weeks of September are a major occasion. The end of summer, and the start of a new year.
“I always view September as the new year. Not January first,” said Ms. Barnicke, who lives in Toronto. “It feels like the beginning. Like a renewal. It’s excitement, but also a lot of anxiousness.”
It’s a month that brings new milestones in many families. The start of a new routine, or adventure, or challenge. A new step toward independence. For many, it will be their first day in a new place.
The Globe and Mail spoke with four families experiencing “first days” this week. Here’s what they told us about how they feel, and how they’re preparing:
First day of kindergarten: Aadhya Trivedi, 4 years old
Aadhya is a chatty preschooler who lives in Toronto with her family. She knows how to spell her own name, and how to count to four fingers when asked her age. She likes rainbow-coloured tutus, chapatis with curried vegetables and reading books with her mom. When she grows up, she plans on being a doctor and also a princess.
What she’s most excited about
Aadhya’s older brother already attends the school where she’s headed, so he’s given her some ideas on what to expect.
“Kindergarten,” she said, “is where you help your teachers. Cleaning. Putting books away. Sitting in the circle.”
She’s most excited to see the school library, which her brother has described in great detail. She can’t wait to pick out her own books and bring them home.
What she’s worried about
Aadhya will miss the comforts of daycare. “The teachers love me a lot. I love my teachers a lot.”
She’ll miss her daycare friends, too. “I love my friends,” she said. “We hug with each other and hold each other’s hands.”
She’ll be parting ways with almost all of them. Most are heading off to a different school, so she’ll have to make new friends. When asked if this makes her nervous, she gives the tiniest nod.
“The new friends might hate me, and might not love me,” she said. “They might not want to be best friends with me.”
How the family is preparing
“She’s already been in the daycare setting, so the routine is kind of the same,” said her mom, Sonali. They’ve been working as a family to drill the importance of that morning routine in to their children: Of waking up by a specific time and leaving plenty of room each morning to get ready and out the door without feeling rushed.
Beyond that, Sonali said she’s been focused on preparing Aadhya for the practical challenges of kindergarten such as how to get through a full day without an afternoon nap, how to recognize her own name at her cubby and how to tell the difference between her stuff and all the other kids’, which often look similar.
Aadhya is also practicing how to open and close her own lunch bag and food containers. It’ll be her first time bringing lunch from home, and she’ll have to figure out how to navigate that. “It’s all about keeping things simple and accessible,” said Sonali.
First day rituals
Each year, Sonali asks family and friends to send in short video messages for the kids with their well-wishes for the new school year. She compiles all of them into a larger video that the family watches the night before school. They make popcorn, settle into the couch and make a night of it.
“It’s a tradition that we all look forward to,” Sonali said.
The transition from summer to a new school year is always an anxious, nerve-wracking time. “And, honestly not just for the kids,” she said.
“It’s emotional for the parents too – seeing your babies going out into the world.”
First day of middle school: Taylor, 12
Until recently, Taylor attended a co-ed, public Catholic school in Toronto, where he lives with his family. But this week he is moving to an all-boys, private middle school that is connected to a high school. So he’ll be sharing the halls for the first time with kids who are much older, ranging from Grade 7 all the way up to Grade 12.
What he’s most excited about
Taylor is an athlete who plays soccer, football and hockey. “Any sport, basically.” So he’s looking forward to the new sports and activities available.
“It’s a lot bigger than my [former] school, so there’s lots of different types of activities and clubs,” he said. “It’s just a totally different environment.”
He’s also looking forward to the fact that he’ll be joined by many of his existing friends who are moving to the new school alongside him.
What he’s most worried about
“Probably the exams.” The curriculum in middle school, he expects, will be much more intense.
How they’re preparing
This week will represent a big step into independence for Taylor, said his mom Libby. Instead of getting dropped off and picked up by his parents each day, he’ll be responsible for getting himself to and from school.
For the first time, Taylor will have to navigate public transit on his own. He’ll also have to figure out where to buy his snacks after school, and how to pay for them. The family is having to discuss, for the first time, questions such as whether he’s ready for a debit card or a cellphone.
“It’s a change in tide,” said Libby. “We’re having meaningful conversations about what the new routine is going to look like – early adult conversations, I would say.”
Back to school rituals
This will be the seventh year that Libby has lined up her boys for their back-to-school photo (they missed one year because of the pandemic). “It’s just always been a marker for me to show the progress – to show just how big they’re getting.”
Still, beyond the anxiety and the nerves, she said, there’s a lot of excitement.
“I think there’s something very joyful about coming of age, and moving on,” she said. “I just can’t wait to see what he does with this next chapter.”
First day of high school: Arshia Purohit Singh, 13
At first glance, Arshia seems like a typical Vancouver teenager. She likes sushi and swimming, music by Olivia Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter and books from the popular ‘Powerless’ YA series by Lauren Roberts.
But, if you spend just a minute talking to her, it’s clear that she’s no ordinary kid. Arshia was the valedictorian at her elementary school and runs her own small business online. She organizes fundraisers for the local children’s hospital and intends to be a lawyer one day – after graduating from Harvard Law School, of course.
She’s made the difficult decision to attend a different high school (which, in her Vancouver school district, is grades eight through 12) than all of her friends. She’s opting instead for a school with an International Baccalaureate program, which she considers more academically challenging.
What she’s most excited about
Arshia is looking forward to the idea of a challenge. Of more intense classes, and the chance to join the basketball team, the debate club and the students’ council.
“I’m definitely feeling a little bit nervous, but I’m also just really excited for all the new opportunities and all the new people I’m going to meet.”
She’s excited, too, about having a bit more freedom.
“In elementary school, it’s a lot more structured. We were kind of taken to every class, things like that. But in high school, they’ll tell us to go to our different classes, and then it’s just entirely up to us.”
How the family is preparing
The family is big on organization and building good habits. Ever since they were little, Arshia’s mom Sophia Purohit Singh has taught her two kids how to balance their own schedules and make sure they’re staying on top of deadlines.
“The habits were developed way early on, where it was always about keeping yourself busy and organized. Having your own calendar and managing it,” said Sophia. “So there’s not time left over to go on their phone for hours.”
They’ve doubled down on this routine over the summer. Entirely of her own accord, Arshia has been working ahead on her math workbooks (“just to be ready for next year”), and has been talking through with her parents how she might juggle her many new assignments and responsibilities in high school.
Back-to-school rituals
Every year, the family spends at least one day combing through the house to see what school supplies they’ve left lying around.
“It’s stuff we’ve collected over the year, and figuring out how to reuse them,” said Arshia. And then they’ll go back-to-school shopping for everything else.
Back-to-school outfits, said Arshia, “are definitely still a thing.” For her first day of high school, she chose her outfit in advance: A new skirt she bought recently, with a t-shirt and hoodie, in case of cold. “I’m just going to wear what makes me comfortable,” she said.
She knows this is an important moment for her.
“This is kind of a big point of change in my life,” she said. “In a few years, my life is going to change a lot.”
First day of teaching: Nick Erickson, 41
Over the past few decades, Mr. Erickson has been a sawmill worker, a concrete labourer and a logging truck driver. But this week, the father of five from Lake Babine Nation in B.C. will take on a new career: A high-school teacher.
He’s a new graduate of NITEP, the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia, where, after going back to school in his late 30s, he recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in education. He’ll be teaching a small group of Indigenous students, grades eight through 12, at a high school in his community.
“My goal is to give Indigenous students the confidence to go on to bigger and better things. To show them they’re capable,” he said.
“If I can do it at the age of 41, there’s no reason why anybody else can’t do it.”
What he’s excited about
Mr. Erickson can only recall ever having one Indigenous teacher when he was growing up. “It was the only classroom where I felt like I wasn’t really being judged,” he said. Now, he’s excited to be that positive role model for his own students.
“I have a lot of life stories. I’ve had a lot of things happen in my life that I can relate with the kids.”
Plus, as the father of five daughters (who range in age from eight to 25), he has ample confidence and experience in dealing with teenagers.
As a teacher, he said, he won’t be “Mr. Erickson.” Just “Nick.”
“I want to help them and teach them,” he said. “But I also want to learn beside them.”
One more bonus? His wife, Marsha Erickson, completed the NITEP program alongside him. They’ll be sharing this experience as first-time teachers in the community together.
What he’s worried about
“I’m kind of nervous. I’m responsible for these kids. But if I’m my genuine, authentic self, I’m not going to have any problems. I’m just going to be the best person I can in front of them.”
Back-to-school rituals
Each year, the couple has taken back-to-school pictures of their five kids on the deck in front of the house. This year they’ll take photos again – only this time, with the addition of mom and dad.

title: From Leaking Roofs to Bright Learning Walls: How a Crumbling Govt School Became a Space Kids Love
content: “Earlier, when it rained, water used to fall from the roof. Now there is no such tension, and we can concentrate on our studies.” For years, rainy days at school meant something very different for Aastha Kohle and Yogeshwari Chamat. At Gardiner High School in Nagpur’s Civil Lines, the girls had watched rainwater seep through their classroom roof. Tiles had fallen, plaster had come off the walls, and parts of the building had grown unsafe. The school had stood there since 1933, and its age was beginning to show in ways that affected the children studying inside it. Then came the summer break. When Aastha and Yogeshwari returned to school in July 2026, the difference was impossible to miss. The roof had been repaired. The classrooms were brighter. Colourful illustrations from their syllabus covered the walls, and spaces that had once felt neglected had been thoughtfully redesigned. There was also a science lab, which soon became one of their favourite places in school. “Our walls look beautiful, and there are pretty paintings in our classrooms,” they say. From science concepts to mathematical formulae, the walls now turn everyday classroom spaces into extensions of the lesson. For the girls, the change has shaped how they feel at school too. Their confidence has grown, they say, and the lessons they once encountered only in books now surround them in their classrooms. Science concepts and mathematical formulae appear on the walls, turning the school itself into part of how they learn. That idea, of creating a school environment that supports children as they learn, is central to Zero Gravity’s work. It began with a girl erasing her notebook Zero Gravity is a youth-led initiative working under the Dr Shrikant Jichkar Foundation, founded by Maitri Jichkar in memory of her late father. Started in Nagpur in 2008, the organisation works across education, healthcare and rural development, with education at the heart of its work. Maitri’s decision to focus on school infrastructure grew out of a moment she witnessed years ago. Around 2010-11, while visiting a government school where her organisation was supporting students with stationery, she walked into a classroom with a leaking roof. Children had crowded into the part of the room where it was not raining. There was little furniture, and some students did not even have school bags. Then she noticed a girl carefully erasing something from her notebook. When Maitri asked her why, the girl replied that if she did not erase what she had written that day, she would have nothing to write on the next day. Maitri Jichkar’s journey with school transformation began with a girl erasing her notebook because she had no pages left to write on. “That just stuck with me,” Maitri recalls. “I realised the vast gap between opportunities.” For her, the question was also one of dignity. “Just because a child comes from an underprivileged family doesn't mean that our system has to offer him something that he thinks he deserves,” she says. “No child should have to live or learn this way.” The experience eventually led to the Happy School Project, which began around 2013 with a simple goal: transform government schools into places where children could learn with a sense of pride and belonging. What if the walls could help children learn? In its early years, Zero Gravity depended largely on volunteers who would pick up paintbrushes and work with local communities to brighten schools. But Maitri soon realised that painting walls addressed only one part of a school’s needs. Today, the organisation’s team of architects and designers looks at everything from lighting, ventilation, toilets and furniture to teaching aids, playgrounds and learning spaces. The building itself also becomes a teaching tool. Through what Zero Gravity calls ‘Building as a Learning Aid’, the team maps concepts from the school curriculum and incorporates them into the physical environment. A science concept might appear on a classroom wall. Mathematical formulae can become part of the design. Writing surfaces and interactive spaces are created so that teachers can use the building while teaching. For Zero Gravity, repairing a school is only the beginning — the team also rethinks lighting, ventilation, furniture, learning spaces and how children experience them. “The core is to integrate and increase the educational value of the school building,” Maitri explains. The process begins with a needs assessment, followed by a detailed study of the building, budgeting and design. Architects create drawings and 3D models, while the team works on curriculum integration, artwork and space optimisation. Artists, labourers, local vendors and volunteers then help bring those plans to life, with Zero Gravity supervising the work. The small volunteer-led effort now works alongside municipal corporations, Zilla Parishads, district administrations and CSR partners. The organisation has transformed more than 150 schools so far and currently has a waiting list of nearly 1,000 schools. Transformation began with a falling brick At Gardiner High School, the government school in Nagpur where Aastha and Yogeshwari study, the first challenge was safety. The 1933 structure had deteriorated to a point where two classrooms were no longer being used because the roof was considered unsafe. The principal, Mrs Shveta Dhalwale, remembers the school before the transformation as a place where leaking roofs, falling tiles, damaged plaster and waterlogged areas had become part of everyday life. In fact, one incident made the need for intervention even more urgent. A brick once fell from a ventilator in the last room of the building while children were playing outside. Thankfully, no one was hurt. Principal Dhalwale shares, “Whenever I go to that room, I thank God that nothing happened that day.” When Zero Gravity first came in May 2026, the school did not expect a transformation of this scale. “We thought they would fix the tiles and plaster a few rooms,” Dhalwale says. “But this is beyond our expectations.” The team first had to address the basics, including the roof and other structural repairs. Even seemingly simple work such as electrical wiring had to be carefully planned because the old walls could not safely be drilled into. At Gardiner High School, years of leaking roofs, falling tiles and damaged plaster gave way to classrooms designed with children and learning in mind. With the structure made safe, the team turned to the spaces where children would learn. Classrooms were redesigned with colourful, curriculum-linked artwork. Science concepts appeared on walls, along with visuals such as the solar system and the Arabian desert. The science lab and other learning spaces were also redesigned. The children joined in, too. They painted, created artwork and helped make the new spaces their own. ‘We have to preserve it for the next classes’ For Dhalwale, one of the most heartening changes has been the way students now interact with their surroundings. Earlier, children would sometimes draw on the walls. Today, they see those same walls as part of their learning space, and something worth protecting. “They know we have to preserve it for the next classes,” she says. She has noticed other changes too. Attendance has improved, and students have started bringing their friends to the school to seek admission. The difference is visible inside the classroom as well. Dhalwale says the transformed spaces have made teaching more joyful for teachers and students alike. The Building as a Learning Aid approach brings the curriculum into the classroom itself, turning walls and everyday spaces into teaching tools. “It is a happy teaching and learning place, both for the students and teachers,” says Dhalwale. “We enjoy teaching with a joyful atmosphere around.” And the transformation has continued beyond the renovation itself. Zero Gravity now works closely with the school, responding to its evolving needs. After spending about a month revamping the school space, the team is now developing a library, with plans to eventually use storytelling as a way to open conversations around healthcare and mental wellbeing with the children. ‘Create a space where children can explore’ For Samiran Ghodmare, a counselling psychologist and Zero Gravity volunteer, the work has changed how he looks at education. When he first joined the Happy School Project, he wondered how much changing a physical space could really mean to a child. His work had centred on children’s mental health, but Zero Gravity made him realise that the basics come first. “Before even working on anyone’s mental health, the basic needs should first be fulfilled,” he says. He began to see a school as both a place of learning and, for many children, their first comfortable space outside home. If that space feels neglected or unsafe, it becomes harder for them to be curious, creative or even open up. The children now see their walls differently — not as surfaces to draw on, but as learning spaces they want to protect for those who come after them. Samiran has also seen how change inspires people to contribute. Volunteers who arrive for a few days often stay on, taking responsibility for more schools, connecting donors or offering their professional skills. “You want the children to be more interactive with the space,” Samiran says. “We need to create a space where it gives them an opportunity to explore their mind, their creativity and their world.” That same thinking is shaping Gardiner’s next learning space. As Zero Gravity continues working with the school, Samiran is helping develop a library where storytelling can eventually open conversations around mental and physical health. When the neighbourhood started showing up The transformation at Gardiner also changed how the neighbourhood saw the school. As the work progressed, people began contributing in their own ways — from stationery and computers to furniture. A private school even donated its old furniture, which was still in good condition. Maitri has seen this ripple effect across other projects too. The transformation has also brought the neighbourhood closer, with people contributing stationery, computers and furniture to the school. At one government school, teachers had pooled money to buy scholarship-exam books, while children sometimes tore one textbook into three parts so they could share it. After Zero Gravity built and stocked a library, more students began preparing for scholarship exams, with several eventually earning scholarships. The space also became a study centre for young people in the community. In another village, a community hall that had remained unused for 15 years was repaired and painted. Soon, residents began organising cleanliness drives, while the administration decided to develop a library and study centre there. For Maitri, these moments show how a physical transformation can change what a community believes is possible. “We are just raising the standard of how these places should look,” she says. “So that becomes a minimum standard.” A place that tells a child: you matter Today, children at Gardiner High School walk into classrooms where the roof no longer leaks, lessons continue on the walls, and a library is being built for them. For Zero Gravity, a school is more than a building — it is a child’s first reminder that their learning, safety and dreams matter. Maitri believes that giving children the right opportunities today can shape generations to come. For her, the larger purpose of Zero Gravity is to create spaces that show children they are worthy of care. “I just want children to feel that the system, and society in general, knows how to care for them,” she says. “I want them to know that they matter. All images courtesy Zero Gravity

title: 190 Days Without a Homicide
content:
Jenee Gragston dropped to the ground and held on to the grass as if it could save her life. She yelled to her family members to get down. She later told me that she didn’t know where the bullets were coming from, but she knew they were close. When the firing stopped, the cries began. She could hear her 4-year-old nephew howling: “Get it off me! Get it off me!” She wasn’t close enough to see what had happened, but it looked like he had blood on his chest. A teenage boy was lying near the child. The teenager “never screamed or anything,” she said. “I can still see all of it.”
It was a Saturday afternoon, mid-August in Lexington, Kentucky. Hundreds of people had gathered in Charles Young Park to celebrate what’s called East End Day—a combination of family reunions, live music, and lots of food. I grew up going to festivals in that park, though I lived on the west side of town, in the Charlotte Court housing projects.
Kentucky isn’t the most dangerous place in America, but it’s up there, with the 14th-highest rate of gun deaths. Twelve years ago, my uncle was murdered in Lexington. Three years ago, my sister’s husband was shot and killed there. I worry about my brother, who still lives there. He had gotten himself off the streets for a while, but is now back living in the city. Lexington had recently seen a hard-won drop in gun deaths—last year was the fourth straight year of declines in gun violence among young people. This spring and summer set a record of 190 straight days without a homicide. Then came the East End Day shooting, which killed that teenager, 16-year-old Di’Zhon Robertson, and wounded four others—including the 4-year-old, who was shot in the leg. The next weekend, another person was killed. The weekend after that, four separate shootings left two more dead.
Gragston was selling Polish sausages in the park. She’d paid more than $300 for the grill, $300 for the sausages, more than $1,000 in fees, $75 for the booth. Business was good; some people returned for seconds. Her husband, her kids, and other family members had come to help her set up her tent. Her 4-year-old nephew was handing customers sodas and water bottles. On the basketball court nearby, Devine Carama was talking with a group of young people. Carama is the director of ONE Lexington, a city-funded program that tries to prevent gun violence by mentoring at-risk boys. He, too, threw himself down when he heard gunfire. “I almost got shot that day,” he told me. Two people near him were hit—a man and his girlfriend. Carama and others tried to bandage the man’s leg; he told me he could see a glimmer of bullet or bone through the blood.
A day later, 18-year-old Jametrius Griffin turned himself in and was charged with murder. According to court testimony, Griffin’s younger brother had gotten into an argument; punches were thrown, and the younger brother fell or was pushed. When Griffin saw that, he yanked out a gun and started firing.
For the past three years, Robertson had participated in ONE Lexington’s summer youth program, which offers workshops on building emotional and social skills, as well as college-campus visits. “He wasn’t a street kid,” Carama said. Griffin’s younger brother was in ONE Lexington, too—in its school mentoring program. The organization had also helped Griffin get a job at UPS. The group’s work seemed to be making a difference. And then a fight left one young man dead, one wounded, and one in prison.
In many ways, Lexington feels like a small town, where everyone knows everyone. I went to middle school with Griffin’s lawyer, Daniel Whitley, who has a big reputation locally for representing people accused of murder—and for winning their cases. The week after the shooting, I spoke with Whitley and with Griffin’s mother, Jay-Me Baxter, on a video call.
“A bunch of bullshit” was how Baxter described the park shooting, “because everybody’s friends and everybody’s family.” She said her youngest son told her he had been bullied by Di’Zhon Robertson and others. The day after the shooting, she made the same argument in a video she posted on Facebook that outraged many in the community. She suggested that her older son had had no choice and said she didn’t care “who makes it home as long as mine do.” (I tried to reach Robertson’s mother through family members to see if she would talk with me about what happened to her son; her sister replied that the family didn’t want to relive it. But friends and family members described the teenager as quiet, observant, and “very respectful.”)
“I’m like, Shit, I know Di’Zhon’s mama,’” Baxter told me—the other mother was close friends with her own sister. Baxter said she had had a conversation with her about the beef between the boys, and assumed the issue had been settled. Griffin loved football, and he had started college at Kentucky State University. “But you know them kids,” she said. “They be doing stuff in silence.” Her son must have been simmering with fury.
I knew Baxter’s family growing up—she’s a year older than me, and they, too, lived in the Charlotte Court housing projects. She didn’t remember me, but she knew my brother. Her mother was white, and had nine children. Baxter, the third-oldest, is half Black, like her younger siblings. But the oldest two are white. Her mother used to cry, Baxter told me, because “the white kids didn’t ever live with us.” In our majority-Black neighborhood, a white mother with mixed-race kids stood out. Baxter remembers people throwing rocks through their windows and a lot of name-calling—“white bitch.” Her family was poorer than many others, but people in the neighborhood assumed that she was privileged, and tormented her for it. “That white mama, man,” she said. “You know what I’m saying?”
That kind of bullying is part of the pain of being impoverished. You feel so low, you desperately want to make someone else feel lower.
Baxter is a single mother, and Griffin is the oldest of her five children. Like my own mother, she lost custody of her kids because of drugs—she signed over her parental rights to her mom. She told me the story as if she was discussing a character in a book: “Jay-Me got in trouble. Jay-Me started using drugs, cocaine specifically.” Like my mother, Baxter was a victim of sexual abuse. She grew up watching her mother “get beat by men. I done been touched by men, and I never told my mama until a couple months before she died.”
It took Baxter seven years to stop using drugs and get her kids back. Those kids needed her, yet she kept choosing drugs over them, she said, as her voice cracked and tears hit her cheeks. “That hurts, because I can’t believe I did that.” I’ve heard those same words from my own mother and watched her cry for the same reason.
Before Baxter signed over her rights, she said, she asked her mother to promise that what she’d experienced as a little girl wouldn’t happen to her kids. She wanted to break the cycle of violence, poverty, and dysfunction that is the inheritance of so many children. “I’m not a gun mama,” Baxter told me, but she believes in “stepping in the street” to fight. “I’ve been fighting all my life,” she said.
Backgrounds like these are so common in Whitley’s line of work that he seemed to tune out our conversation. At one point on the video call, we heard the sound of snoring. Baxter joked about it: “Listen to him. My lawyer tiiiiiired.” We continued talking for a few more minutes and never heard from him again. “Night night, Daniel,” she said before we hung up. He called me back later, apologized for not saying goodbye, and said he hadn’t been asleep.
Despite the pity I felt for Baxter and her family, I felt more for those shot by her son, and their families.
Di’Zhon Robertson’s uncle Tyrone Johnson officiated his funeral, and told me that the church was full of people “struggling with their emotions.” I was told by attendees that the teenager’s grieving mother had to be pulled off the coffin. Damon Williams Jr., a 14-year-old wounded in the shooting, was hit in the thigh. He had been planning on joining his middle school’s football team this season. Lakeisha Martin was shot in the stomach and the sternum. East End Day, her older brother Isaiah Barron told me, “is a day for our community that we look forward to every year.” Martin was in the hospital for 21 days and will be unable to work for months.
The day of the shooting, Jenee Gragston rushed to the hospital as her nephew went into surgery. She told me the police said she should leave her tent, and could return later to retrieve everything. But when her husband went back to the park, almost everything was gone. The cooler with the meat. The grill, the propane tank, even her prescription eyeglasses. Other tents had been robbed as well. Gragston told me that she was grateful her nephew was okay, but that she would never go to one of the park festivals again.
Lexington is trying hard to reduce this kind of gun violence. Mayor Linda Gorton told me the city has handed out free gun locks and offered to buy back guns from residents, among other interventions. Through ONE Lexington, it offers groceries, hotel stays, and educational funds to people affected by gun violence. The city relocated a family whose house had been shot up, Gorton said. Still, she conceded, “there are times when we cannot control every human being’s behavior.”
It doesn’t help that Kentucky has such lax gun laws. Just this year, state legislators dropped the age required to carry a concealed firearm from 21 to 18. When I was growing up in Lexington, gun violence was even worse. Whenever you have a community of young men who feel powerless and disrespected, who have been raised to protect themselves and their families from perceived threats, and who believe words can’t save them but a gun might, then death will follow. The story of what happened in Lexington this summer is particularly tragic because so many had worked so long and so carefully to make a difference. But a gun changes everything in a moment.
Carama, of ONE Lexington, told me he has more friends who are dead than alive. He, too, said that “a lot of it is out of our control,” and that there’s only so much someone from outside a young person’s family can do. You can monitor a kid all you like, but if he has a gun, “you got a split second to react.” Ultimately, he said, “you can’t prevent everything. It’s just not possible.”
In Jay-Me Baxter’s account, she tried, in her way, to intervene. “The mamas grew up together,” she told me. “This could’ve been prevented.” But it wasn’t.

title: Rescued bears begin new lives after years of captivity in Vietnam
content:
One of these centers is the Vietnam Bear Rescue Center in Bach Ma National Park in the central city of Hue, supported by Animals Asia. It covers 12 hectares.
The bears at the center have been rescued from captivity farms in Thai Nguyen, Hanoi, Nghe An and other localities.
For years, many were confined to cramped, suffocating metal cages.
At the rescue center, they are given individual indoor spaces of about 10 square meters, along with proper care, hygiene and nutrition.
A safe and happy final chapter for bears once kept captive. Photo: Animals Asia
Every morning, the center's young men and women rise early to begin caring for and monitoring the bears.
When they first arrive, the animals are often emaciated and in poor condition.
With time, proper food and attentive care, many regain their health and develop glossy black coats.
Whether a bear is allowed into the semi-wild enclosure each day depends on factors including the weather and its health.
The semi-wild habitat is surrounded by large mesh-covered structures.
Inside are swings, pools of water and climbing structures designed to encourage the bears to play and explore.
Tree trunks are secured at their bases to prevent the animals from climbing or damaging them.
In the semi-natural enclosure, the bears take part in activities designed to restore their natural instincts and improve their physical condition.
Rather than placing food in a single feeding trough, staff scatter it throughout the enclosure, putting treats on elevated poles or hiding them in hollows and bamboo stems.
The bears must move around and use their senses to find their meals.
“This helps bears recover their natural foraging instincts,” said Phan Thi Thuy Trinh, a manager at the center.
“Their environment and food are also varied as much as possible to stimulate them and partly recreate the vast and diverse conditions of a natural habitat.”
The center primarily cares for Asiatic black bears and sun bears.
Both are omnivores, although plants make up between 70 percent and 90 percent of a bear's natural diet.
Their food includes forest fruits, seeds, bamboo shoots, leaves, young shoots, roots and tubers.
Their diets change regularly with the seasons and are supplemented with other foods, including dry feed providing protein, calcium and minerals.
Menus are rotated so that it takes roughly two weeks before a particular meal is repeated.
In addition to their main meals, essential oils and honey are hidden in tree hollows throughout the semi-wild enclosure, encouraging the bears to use their senses and search for food.
Health monitoring is another essential part of their care.
Every bear receives a routine health examination at least once every two years.
Emergency examinations are conducted whenever caregivers notice signs of illness or other abnormal behavior.
Bears that have spent many years in captivity commonly suffer from dental problems, musculoskeletal disorders, high blood pressure and liver or gallbladder diseases.
Veterinarians are able to treat most of these conditions, while particularly complex cases may require assistance from leading specialists in Vietnam or abroad.
Two decades of efforts to end bear bile farming
According to Vietnam's Department of Forestry and Forest Protection, the country recorded 4,239 captive bears in 2005.
After more than two decades of coordinated management, rescue and public-awareness efforts, the number had fallen to 206 animals as of July this year, a reduction of nearly 95 percent from its peak.
Over the past two years alone, the captive population has fallen from 384 to 206, demonstrating the impact of cooperation among government agencies, forest rangers and conservation organizations.
Nevertheless, 129 bears remain in the hands of 46 households and private facilities.
These animals are considered a priority for continued efforts to persuade their owners to voluntarily transfer them to rescue centers.
The localities with the largest remaining populations include Hanoi, Nghe An, Hai Phong and Dong Nai, along with several northern provinces.
“The biggest challenge now is no longer rescue capacity, but shortening the time between reaching an agreement with an owner and safely bringing the bear to a rescue center,” said Nguyen Vu Linh, director of Bach Ma National Park.
For years, rumors about the supposed medicinal value of bear bile, bear paws, claws and gallbladder products as well as the practice of keeping bears as pets, have helped drive the species toward decline.
Although people involved in the illegal trade in bear bile continue to face penalties, demand among consumers has proved difficult to eliminate.
In mid-March, a court in Ho Chi Minh City sentenced D.M.H., born in 1997, to 18 months in prison for illegally possessing and trading 39 bear claws and teeth.
Education for Nature Vietnam (ENV) has warned that efforts to end bear bile farming cannot be completed as long as a market for bear bile remains.
Of particular concern is the growing availability of jewelry made from bear teeth and claws on online marketplaces.
The department has set 2026 as the target year for completely ending the bear bile farming industry.
Animals Asia began rescuing bears in Vietnam in 2007.
The organization has rescued 300 bears, including Asiatic black bears and sun bears.
Of these, 183 are currently living in lush semi-natural environments at two bear rescue centers, located in the buffer zone of Tam Dao National Park in Phu Tho Province, northern Vietnam and Bach Ma National Park in Hue City, central Vietnam.

title: Joe Salgado virou à direita no 11 de setembro e sobreviveu
content:
Um carro dos bombeiros, uma ambulância e um veículo de socorro ajudam a compor um solene triângulo, palco da homenagem da comunidade portuguesa às vítimas dos ataques de 11 de setembro. Ao final da tarde de sexta-feira, ouve-se português na confluência da Ferry Street com a Wilson Avenue, em Newark, New Jersey. Manhattan fica a meia-hora. Estes portugueses, que hoje colocam a bandeira nacional a meia-haste, também têm uma história para contar.
É o caso de Joe Salgado, um dos poucos sobreviventes portugueses do 11 de setembro. Trabalhava no 47.º andar da Torre Norte e conseguiu escapar do edifício com vida. Tinha chegado cedo ao trabalho no banco First Union. “Era um dia lindo. Lembro-me tão bem”, afirmou à Rádio Observador, entrevistado na emissão especial desta sexta-feira à tarde em Nova Iorque. Aos 65 anos, Joe Salgado recorda vividamente essa terça-feira, dia 11 de setembro de 2001. “Chegava cedo ao banco, entre as 7h30 e as 8h00. Dependia do trânsito, mas era um dos managers e, como manager, queria sempre chegar antes do pessoal”. Nesse dia fatídico não foi diferente.
Tinha começado uma reunião há poucos minutos quando sentiu um estrondo que fez abalar a torre. Do piso onde estavam, não se aperceberam logo do que tinha acontecido. Teria sido um embate na torre, mas pensaram num pequeno avião ou helicóptero. Mesmo assim decidiram começar a descer as escadas. Foi quando chegaram ao 22.º andar que ouviram muito barulho. Foi o momento em que o segundo avião se despenhou contra a torre sul.
Quando chegaram ao piso zero havia mais do que uma saída. Quatro colegas decidiram virar à esquerda. Joe e mais três funcionários viraram à direita. “Ainda hoje não sei porquê. Não sei por que virei à direita”, admite. Mas essa decisão salvou-lhe a vida. Os quatro colegas que foram pelo outro lado já não conseguiram sair.
Joe Salgado cruzou a rua e olhou para as torres. A segunda começou a ruir. “Começámos a correr pela rua abaixo o mais rápido possível. Não conseguíamos ver nada, tal era o pó nos olhos. Um bombeiro deu-nos uma garrafa de água, limpámos a cara e fomos a pé até Brooklyn”. Só mais tarde encontrou uma cabine telefónica e ligou para casa — para dizer que estava vivo. Durante todo esse tempo não faziam ideia se Joe tinha escapado. “Quando chegámos a Staten Island, houve uma carrinha que nos viu e parou. Viu que estávamos cobertos de pó e levou-nos a New Jersey”. Por essa altura, o mundo já estava em choque. Joe Salgado ainda não sabia exatamente o que tinha acontecido e só com a família, e com o que ia passando nas rádios e nas televisões, teve a verdadeira noção da tragédia a que tinha conseguido escapar: “Tive uma sensação de gratidão”.
Joe reúne-se todos os anos no dia 11 de setembro com os colegas que estavam juntos naquele dia no escritório. Esteve várias vezes no Ground Zero e assinalou lá o 10.º e o 20.º aniversário, mas não este ano. “Já faleceram 13 amigos. Ainda é um grande choque para todos”, justifica.
“Lembro-me dos apitos dos rádios dos bombeiros que tinham falecido”
Na Ferry Street, a meia-hora de comboio do World Trade Center, o português é uma das línguas mais faladas. Basta olhar para as montras e para as caras. Estamos num pequeno Portugal do outro lado do Rio Hudson. E muitos têm histórias para contar de um dia que não esquecem. É o caso do capitão da polícia de Newark, Maik Alexandre — a mãe não sabia escrever Michael, daí a opção menos óbvia na escolha do nome.
Maik Alexandre, que fala com o Observador impecavelmente fardado, lembra-se desse dia como se fosse ontem: “Estava a ter aulas na Academia de Polícia quando o primeiro avião embateu numa das torres e pensávamos que tinha sido um acidente. Quando o segundo avião se despenhou na torre sul, quase 20 minutos depois, soubemos que estávamos em guerra”.
Maik Alexandre começou por ir no carro da polícia, a fazer de batedor, para que as ambulâncias chegassem o mais rapidamente possível a um dos cinco hospitais que existiam em Newark na altura. “Fiz esse percurso mais de 60 vezes, para trás e para a frente”. Em 2001 tinha apenas 25 anos, mas lembra-se bem do nevoeiro de cinza no Ground Zero: “Não conseguia ver quase nada. O ar estava cheio de pó e vidro.” Depois, o que recorda melhor é do cheiro. “Era o cheiro de um corpo queimado, mas não era um… Eram milhares”.
As recordações vão surgindo à medida que conversa com a Rádio Observador. “Lembro-me dos apitos dos rádios dos bombeiros que tinham falecido. Alguns eram altos, significa que estavam por cima dos escombros. Outros baixinhos. Estavam enterrados e as baterias estavam a descarregar. Por isso, começavam a apitar”. Passados dias, ainda se ouviam esses apitos por entre os escombros.
Nesta emissão especial da Rádio Observador, em Nova Iorque, falámos com muitos portugueses e luso-descendentes. Em três horas de emissão em direto, foram feitas 11 entrevistas, que pode ouvir aqui.
Nova Iorque continua a ser a grande metrópole, uma cidade imensa, inundada de luz, cores, odores, mas tem uma ferida por sarar. Na zona de impacto daquele dia, abre-se um buraco para onde escorre água de forma ruidosa. Os nomes de 2.983 vítimas estão gravados em painéis de bronze do memorial dos atentados de 11 de setembro, onde os discursos estão proibidos. Entre essas quase 3 mil vítimas estão 9 portugueses: António Rocha, Raymond Rocha, Manuel da Mota, Christopher Mello, António Rodrigues, João Aguiar Jr., Dennis Gomes, Carlos da Costa e Mark Jardim.
A emissão especial da Rádio Observador em Nova Iorque teve o apoio da Fundação Luso Americana para o Desenvolvimento

title: Tourists put these sea turtle nests at risk. Local Mexicans intervened, and now 3,200 hatchlings are swimming free
content:
On August 30, a Mexican nonprofit dedicated to sea turtle conservation released between 3,200 and 3,500 sea turtles into the Gulf of Mexico from a beach in northern Veracruz.
The nonprofit, Tortugas Fundación Yepez A.C., was founded in 1967 by fisherman Don Marcelino Yepez and his wife Librada Gerón, affectionately known as “Mama Turtle.”
Their legacy lives on as their eldest son, Ricardo Yépez, continues their mission today.
“It’s already August 30, 2026, and well, the moment has arrived — the time has come to see the culmination of sleepless nights, hard work, patrols, [and] all-nighters,” Yépez said in an Instagram Reel.
According to Yépez, tourists were putting nesting sea turtles and their eggs at risk by approaching, touching, and even climbing turtles.
Patrols intensified in August after a pregnant green sea turtle was reported dead on a beach in Nautla, Veracruz. Afterwards, Yépez issued a public warning to tourists to give nesting sea turtles their space, according to reports by La Jornada.
In the weeks since, Yépez and his team of patrollers set up protected sites and moved nests from high-risk areas to small enclosures where they could hatch in peace.
“Today they are being released back into the ocean without any form of harm,” Yépez said, as he crouched on the beach, shoulder to shoulder with his volunteer team. “There aren’t enough words to express our gratitude to all the people who call us, who alert us, and who take responsibility for beach areas.”
“A huge thank you to all these angels whom God has placed in our path so that we can achieve our conservation goals for this endangered little animal,” he continued. “We’re celebrating 59 years of work — it’s easy to say, but it’s 59 years of continuous seasons, of persistence — and thanks be to God, and thanks to all of you, it’s possible for us to continue today. From my parents’ time until today — that’s 59 years now.”
At the end of his speech, Yépez said that there weren’t “enough words” to thank everyone who made the release possible.
“Well, today we’re going to release roughly 3,200 to 3,500 baby turtles,” he said. “Ready, guys? Uno, dos, vámonos!”
In unison, the Tortugas Fundación Yepez A.C. team released the sea turtles onto the sand from their respective buckets. As they raced to the water, the sea turtles tumbled on top of each other and wiggled their flippers, eager to reach the surf.
“Congratulations on your 59 years!” one Instagram user commented. “You say ‘it’s easy,’ but it's a lifetime of dedication and effort that not everyone does.”
