title: Tokyo leading the way in weather and disaster resilience
content:
France recorded one of the hottest days since statistics began in 1947, with temperatures exceeding 44°C in some locations, and the country's public health authorities reporting over 2,000 excess deaths due to the heatwave as of July 2026.
Tokyo is no stranger to heat and other extreme weather, as well as being one of the world's most densely populated cities, home to over 14 million people. Discover three ways Japan’s capital is working to keep people safe in the face of climate challenges, and see how resilience can be woven into everyday life, communities, and businesses.
Everyday readiness: making resilience part of daily life
As extreme weather becomes part of daily urban life, the Tokyo-based startup Sakigake Japan is working to get resilience built into everyday routines. The company connects disaster-preparedness and climate-adaptation solutions with real-world use, creating value in normal times and becoming essential when crises strike.
One of their solutions is an AI- and cloud-based platform that visualizes weather and flood risk, which is particularly important in Tokyo, where sudden, localized downpours can overwhelm infrastructure. The platform helps estimate inundation risks specific areas face, supporting earlier precautions and better planning.
The increasing heat is also a major concern that must be addressed, as if a large disaster hits in summer and air conditioning stops, temperatures in homes and other buildings can quickly become life-threatening.
Mobile cold-chain solutions could address that gap. Portable refrigeration units used for events and logistics in normal times, can then shift to evacuation support for food, beverages, and medicine during emergencies. In addition to being movable, they can operate off-grid when external power is lost, enabling faster, more localized responses when transport and utilities are disrupted.
Creating rain gardens and green infrastructure in the city
Setagaya City in Tokyo is a residential district known for its abundant greenery, and home to Setagaya Trust & Community Design, a new model for urban development, fostering community ties through green infrastructure initiatives, such as personal rain gardens.
A rain garden collects rainwater from roofs and paved surfaces, holds it temporarily, and allows it to gradually soak into the ground. This helps reduce urban flooding and ease the heat island effect, among other benefits. Rainwater stored in tanks can also be used for watering gardens or during emergencies.
The idea is that if each household created one, it could help reduce flood risk across the community, so the initiative focuses on making rain gardens easy to build and enjoyable as an extension of everyday gardening, using materials readily available at home improvement stores and planting a variety of species to help create habitat for local wildlife.
As climate change increases the risk of urban flooding around the world, expanding bottom-up environmental efforts that begin with small, individually built rain gardens—alongside government-led infrastructure—can help strengthen disaster resilience in high-density cities like Tokyo.
New cooling fabrics to help beat the heat
As temperatures continue to rise, finding practical solutions for keeping people safe and comfortable is becoming a major challenge for cities around the world. Selected as a finalist for the pitch contest held at SusHi Tech Tokyo 2026, Asia’s largest global innovation conference, startup Eztia Materials has developed "HydraVolt," a next-generation cooling material aimed at people working in extreme heat sectors.
HydraVolt can be printed on or sewn into garments and is designed to lower skin temperature through evaporative cooling by up to 10 degrees Celsius, for as long as 8 hours, no electricity or batteries required. The material is recharged through exposure to water and can be laundered just like regular clothing.
The company has had successful test results with cooling headwear for elementary school children, shirts and headbands with the Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters professional baseball team, and arm covers for drivers at Yamato Holdings Co., Ltd., a logistics and parcel delivery company. The results suggest strong potential for the technology to be scaled and incorporated into daily life.
With heatwaves battering Europe and the United States, weather patterns becoming more extreme and natural disasters becoming increasingly common, countries and cities across the globe are seeking ways to adapt to the problems caused by climate change. With centuries of experience dealing with everything from earthquakes to typhoon season, learn from Tokyo's urban strength and preparedness, and see how resilience can be built into the structure of a city.

title: As guardiãs da fé de todos
content:
Por Jenifer Alexandre*
Durante séculos, quase toda cidade brasileira conheceu ao menos uma mulher capaz de unir fé, cuidado e conhecimento ancestral. Eram elas, as rezadeiras e benzedeiras: referências de cuidado, espiritualidade e solidariedade. Hoje, porém, a presença dessas mulheres se torna cada vez mais rara.
Muitas envelheceram sem conseguir transmitir seus saberes às novas gerações. Outras foram silenciadas pelo preconceito religioso, pela urbanização acelerada e pela ideia de que apenas o conhecimento científico possui valor. Aos poucos, aquilo que antes fazia parte do cotidiano popular corre o risco de sobreviver apenas na memória dos mais velhos.
Falar sobre rezadeiras e benzedeiras é também falar sobre etnociência: o reconhecimento dos conhecimentos produzidos pelos povos por meio da experiência, da oralidade e da convivência com a natureza, conforme o estudo Identidades étnicas e etnociências nas práticas de rezadeiras, de Graciela Souza Almeida e Natalino Perovano Filho.
Mesmo com as particularidades que distinguem o saber acadêmico e o saber popular, é impossível negar a riqueza existente nesses conhecimentos tradicionais, pois, durante muito tempo, diferentes pessoas e comunidades guardaram práticas de cuidado desenvolvidas a partir da observação das plantas medicinais, das crenças espirituais e coletividade.
No entanto, reconhecer a importância delas não significa negar a ciência ou substituir tratamentos médicos. Pelo contrário, significa compreender que diferentes formas de conhecimento podem coexistir e dialogar. A medicina popular e os saberes tradicionais fazem parte da formação histórica e cultural do Brasil. Ignorar isso é apagar parte da identidade do próprio povo brasileiro. Embora essas práticas sejam frequentemente associadas às mulheres, também existem homens que exercem esse ofício e participam da preservação desses saberes tradicionais.
Contudo, destaca-se a atuação feminina devido à sua expressiva presença histórica e cultural nesse contexto. Essas mulheres representam muito mais do que práticas religiosas. Elas preservam uma memória coletiva construída por meio da oralidade. Cada reza aprendida com a mãe ou com a avó, cada planta colhida no quintal, cada orientação dada a quem chega em sofrimento faz parte de um patrimônio imaterial que resiste há séculos, de acordo com as autoras Danielle Gomes do Nascimento e Maria Ignez Novais Ayala.
Desse modo, o desaparecimento gradual dessas pessoas revela também uma transformação profunda nas relações sociais. Muitos jovens já não aprendem as rezas, não conhecem as ervas medicinais e sequer conhecem mulheres que exerçam esse papel.
Esse processo de esquecimento não está relacionado apenas às transformações religiosas ou ao avanço da ciência, mas também à desvalorização de práticas culturais que, durante séculos, constituíram importantes formas de cuidado, acolhimento e transmissão de saberes. Soma-se a isso o desconhecimento sobre a importância histórica dessas práticas e, por vezes, a falta de reconhecimento das mulheres que dedicaram suas vidas ao cuidado da comunidade. Ou seja, mais do que o desaparecimento de um ofício, observa-se o enfraquecimento de um patrimônio cultural construído ao longo do tempo, cuja preservação depende do respeito à memória, à diversidade de saberes e às experiências compartilhadas pelos diferentes grupos sociais.
Ademais, embora muitas vezes tratadas como se fossem a mesma coisa, rezadeiras e benzedeiras possuem diferenças sutis. Conforme a pesquisada Alaíze dos Santos Conceição, no seu artigo Notas sobre religiosidades populares no Recôncavo, as rezadeiras estão mais ligadas às orações e pedidos de proteção espiritual. Já as benzedeiras, além das rezas, costumam utilizar ervas, ramos, gestos e sinais da cruz em seus rituais de cura. Em comum, ambas carregam um conhecimento transmitido entre gerações, resultado da mistura entre tradições indígenas, africanas e portuguesas que ajudaram a formar a cultura brasileira.
Mulheres que se apoiam na fé: na própria fé e no poder do acolhimento. Recebem em suas casas, sem cobrar nada, aqueles que chegam carregando dores, medos e esperanças como as guardiãs da fé de todos. Para elas, cada pessoa atendida é acolhida com carinho e respeito, como alguém da própria família. Suas mãos, acompanhadas por orações sussurradas, buscam sempre o bem-estar de quem as procura. Dona Maria e Dona Maria Matias são exemplos dessas mulheres, cujo acolhimento se revela não apenas em suas palavras e gestos, mas também na serenidade de seus olhares.
No entanto, muitas das práticas que fazem parte desse ofício ainda passam despercebidas e raramente são reconhecidas como patrimônio cultural ou como formas legítimas de conhecimento ancestral. Entre elas estão o acolhimento de pessoas em momentos de sofrimento físico e emocional, a escuta atenta, os conselhos oferecidos a partir da experiência, as visitas a vizinhos, familiares e enfermos e, sobretudo, o cultivo e o conhecimento das plantas medicinais mantidos nos quintais e transmitidos entre gerações.
Como afirmam as pesquisadoras Nascimento e Ayala, caminhar pelos caminhos da cultura popular significa reconhecer a riqueza de conhecimentos preservados pelas pessoas mais velhas ao longo das gerações. Em acordo com as autoras, as rezadeiras e benzedeiras carregam muito mais do que orações e rituais: guardam memórias, experiências e formas de cuidado construídas ao longo de gerações. São mulheres que mantêm viva uma relação profunda com a escuta, com a fé, com a natureza e com o acolhimento comunitário.
Na perda de uma delas, perde-se mais do que uma prática tradicional. Perde-se uma parte da memória cultural brasileira e uma fonte viva de conhecimentos ancestrais. Portanto, preservar esses saberes é preservar a memória popular brasileira. É reconhecer que a cura também pode nascer da fé, da escuta, do cuidado e da ancestralidade.
Para saber mais

title: Tohono O’odham fight border wall on sacred, sovereign lands
content:
Standing near the pond at Quitobaquito Springs, Lorraine Marquez Eiler, a Hia-Ced O’odham elder, shared how her ancestors held ceremonies at the sacred site — a desert oasis in a national park that the federal government is set to bulldoze for a new border wall.
She pulled out a photo of her great-great grandparents and her great-grandparents, who would walk about 50 miles through the Sonoran Desert to the springs. The O’odham call the water flow A’al Vaipia. She showed the image of her ancestors to a group that included Indigenous leaders and a U.S. congressional representative — all there on Aug. 24 to condemn the border wall construction.
“All of my lifetime of work has been for the memories of my ancestors, of what they went through. With the incoming wall, should it be disrupted?” Marquez Eiler said in a determined voice, speaking of her ancestral lands. “That’s just another slap in the face, as far as I’m concerned, to my ancestors. And so I ask: Why?”
Surrounded by more than 100 community members at a town hall that followed the visit to Quitobaquito, Marquez Eiler hoped the federal government would pause border construction, as it did earlier this month in Texas after public backlash.
Quitobaquito is sacred to the Hia-Ced O’odham, the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous people in Southern Arizona and México, who have traveled to the site for generations to join religious pilgrimages and ceremonies. They fear the spring is at risk of drying up if another border wall is built on the protected lands about 30 miles west of Tohono O’odham Nation.
The tribal nation is now fighting to halt border construction on two fronts: On O’odham land, where the federal government plans to build a new 30-foot border wall; and on adjacent federal land where another new border fence threatens Quitobaquito.
The projects are part of the Trump administration’s push to spend nearly $50 billion in taxpayer funds on border wall construction.
This is far from tribal citizens’ first fight with the U.S. government over destruction and division of their sovereign tribal lands. From the beginning, people of the Tohono O’odham Nation have lived on lands that had no borders.
When the U.S. and Mexico governments agreed to separate territories, the Tribal Nation wasn’t informed.
For years and until today, O’odham citizens — on both sides of a border they never agreed to — travel freely across their nation. While they have tried to work with border officials to quell crime, they have fought border walls that separate their people and harm their ancestral lands.
The recent fights under the Trump administration have spurred a legal battle and a high-profile standoff between federal agents and law enforcement from the Tohono O’odham Nation. O’odham people are now fighting for tribal sovereignty in the face of a Republican-led federal government arguing for U.S. sovereignty.
Feds already razing the land
In the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, where Quitobaquito Springs sits about 13 miles west of the Lukeville port of entry, the Trump administration has proposed a 30-foot tall border fence 150 feet from the existing one. Marquez Eiler is worried she will no longer be able to access land that for generations has been part of her Tribal Nation’s religious traditions, if that wall is built.
Parts of Quitobaquito lands originally belonged to a family of Hia-Ced O’odham descent. In 1937, President Franklin Roosevelt signed a proclamation establishing the Organ Pipe National Monument as a way to preserve a vast swath of the Sonoran Desert. The new monument was part of a U.S. National Park Service effort to preserve “ecological wonders of the country,” the agency’s website states.
Now, a few miles east of the pond, construction equipment from federal government contractors sits next to the border, the land around it already cleared. Cactuses along the border are marked with a colored string, and a rope lines the proposed area where a second border wall may be built.
If that line continues west, the Quitobaquito pond is right in its path. If contractors bulldoze the cacti, they will destroy legally protected desert plants. They will destroy flora that is sacred to the O’ohdam people, who traditionally believe that plants and the earth are their ancestors.
When the U.S.-Mexico boundary was created through the 1854 Gadsden Purchase, it divided the Tohono O’odham Nation’s ancestral lands. Today, there are about 3,000 enrolled O’odham citizens living in Sonora, Mexico, and families often cross the border to visit family, visit cultural sites, and for religious ceremonies.
Tohono O’odham Nation sues federal government
About 30 miles east of Quitobaquito — on O’odham land — the administration has also proposed building a 30-foot fence in three areas where the border is currently marked by heavy steel fencing a few feet tall.
In June, the Tohono O’odham Nation filed a lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security in an attempt to block border wall construction on their land.
“While the Nation values its close relationship with the Department, it has long opposed construction of a border wall on the Reservation,” the lawsuit states.
“The Nation understands that construction of the wall would entail significant devastation on the Reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the O’odham,” the suit argues. “It would fray the ties between O’odham communities and families on opposite sides of the border, interfere significantly with O’odham religious rituals and practices, and destroy plant and animal resources sacred to the O’odham.”
The tribal nation’s lawsuit cited instances earlier in the year when federal contractors “destroyed ancestral sites of great importance while constructing the wall” adjacent to O’odham land.
In April, a Department of Homeland Security contractor damaged the Las Playas Intaglio, a 1,000-year-old fish-shaped geoglyph in Arizona’s Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge that pointed toward the Gulf of California.
Border Patrol continues construction
In a memorandum outlining opposition to the lawsuit, the federal government’s attorneys said the Tohono O’odham Nation failed to show that the border wall construction is being done in excess of the federal government’s legal authority. The document also emphasized the U.S. government’s “preexisting right to secure the border.”
“While the United States has worked — and will continue to work — cooperatively with Plaintiff to promote their shared interest in border security, Plaintiff does not hold veto power over the United States’ sovereign duty to secure its borders,” the memo said.
While waiting for a decision from the courts, tribal leaders put up “No Trespassing” signs on Aug. 7, saying in a news release that border wall contractors who attempted to enter the Tohono O‘odham Nation would be “illegally trespassing.” Early Aug. 25 morning, contractors entered the tribal nation accompanied by about 20 “masked, armed” border patrol agents, according to a news release from the Tohono O’odham Nation.
In an emailed statement to Arizona Luminaria, Rodney Scott, U.S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, said CBP is moving forward with the federal government’s border wall construction project along the 62 miles that cut through the Tohono O’odham Nation.
“The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border: remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity,” Scott wrote.
A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson in the same email said, “the worksites are inside the 60-foot Roosevelt Reservation,” referring to designated land north of the U.S.-Mexico border that the federal government manages.
“This is about tribal sovereignty”
At Quitobaquito Springs, Marquez Eiler, the tribal elder, led U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva toward the pond to share more with the congresswoman about the tribal communities’ fight.
“After standing here today, seeing this land, and directly hearing from the nation, I am more convinced than ever, this is not just a border construction project,” Grijalva said. “This is about tribal sovereignty, it’s about sacred land, it’s about history, culture and spiritual practices of the O‘odham people and others.”
Tohono O’odham Chairman Verlon Jose and Vice Chairwoman Carla Johnson organized the trip to Quitobaquito to stand against the Trump administration’s insistence on building a new border wall.
For the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous people, the land is their church, where they hold ceremony and prayer, Jose said. The federal government has a history of destroying the O’odham’s sacred land, he added.
When the first border fence went up between 2019 and 2020, contractors blasted through O’odham burial sites on Monument Hill.
“This is not ours to own. It is ours to protect, to protect for the people. To protect for you and I and everyone the creator has placed here on this earth,” Jose said.
“Why do we not want a wall?”
A few hours after their visit to Quitobaquito on Aug. 24, the International Sonoran Desert Alliance, which Marquez Eiler co-founded, hosted a town hall in Ajo, about 40 miles north of the springs. Grijalva, Jose and Johnson shared their efforts to stop the construction projects and listened to residents’ concerns.
More than 100 people filled the Ajo Plaza Rec Hall.
They shared worries over whether the wildlife would survive another construction project – the Quitobaquito pupfish, an endangered species, the Sonoyta mud turtle, the desert caper plant and the Quitobaquito tryonia, a tiny springsnail, call the springs their home.
They criticized the taxpayer cost for the border fence as too high – more than $46 billion in federal funding for projects from California to Texas. They urged Grijalva to push for comprehensive, humane immigration reform instead.
“Why do we not want a wall? Because we are not afraid of who is on the other side,” said Sara Mae Williams, Justice of the Peace in Ajo and a citizen of the Tohono O’odham Nation. “It’s us. It’s our people. It pains me when they try to divide us.”
On Aug. 25, Grijalva and other Democratic federal lawmakers who represent the borderlands – Reps. Veronica Escobar of Texas and Raul Ruiz and Juan Vargas of California – sent a letter opposing the wall to the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of the Interior.
The lawmakers urged the Trump administration to stop further construction of the border wall “until meaningful government-to-government consultation has occurred with the Tohono O’odham Nation and Congress has received a full accounting of the project’s impacts on Tribal lands, cultural resources, and surrounding communities.”
The fight continues
U.S. District Judge Richard J. Leon denied the Nation’s motion for a preliminary injunction on Aug. 14. In a written opinion explaining his decision, the judge said the Tohono O’odham Nation is “unlikely to succeed on the merits because the federal Roosevelt Reservation exists along the international border and, in any event, plaintiff has not established that construction of a border wall will indeed alter Reservation boundaries.”
“The international border is an area of great significance to both the United States and to the Nation,” Leon wrote. “While I have concluded that a preliminary injunction is unwarranted, I fully expect the Government in the months ahead to follow through on its guarantees of consultation and cooperation with the Nation to address the Nation’s concerns regarding border wall construction!”
The Tohono O’odham Nation appealed Leon’s decision to a higher court on Aug. 26. The day after, the Tohono O’odham again asked Leon’s lower court to stop border wall construction while the appeal was resolved. Leon had not responded by Sept. 10, and the federal government has said it plans to fight the injunction and appeal.
“We will not let this destroy our sacred sites, our burial sites, our holy places, the places of our ancestors,” Jose said at the town hall, pausing to stress his sentences. “We will not let it destroy our environment. We will not let it further divide our people. We will not let it divide our reservation.”

title: Witness for Wild Places: Being Rewilded by the Earth
content:
Witness for Wild Places: Being Rewilded by the Earth
September 4, 2026
This past week, the desert monsoon skies held towering clouds, dark with rain and lit with shafts of sunlight. My old jeep was creaking along the dirt road from Patagonia to Lochiel in southern Arizona’s San Rafael Valley when I saw six Border Patrol vehicles massing around a spur road. They were soon behind me, pushing for me to speed up on the dirt road that led into the San Rafael Valley. I didn’t speed up. They passed by at the first opportunity and sped down the road.
I knew in my gut that a confrontation was about to occur. I was making my way to Tierra Libre to bring a simple contribution of food and support and to listen to the stories of the protectors of Abuelita Cottonwood Tree. The great, old Grandmother tree was the last of her sisters standing in the way of the U.S. government’s rush to build a 27-mile section of steel bollard wall. This wall would run through a corridor where jaguars, ocelots, cougars, black bears, and a multitude of other animals have long moved freely. This Fremont Cottonwood tree, a living legacy and a spiritual bridge between the Earth and the sacred, now hosts treesitters high in her branches. Other protectors surround the tree, bearing witness to the impending destruction of this land and corridor.
Earlier in the week, a group gathered to hear the Protectors’ stories. The number of people gathering has begun to increase. Calls of support for the Protectors are rising. The day before our gathering, Julia Butterfly Hill called to encourage the people there on the ground. She shared her story, including waves of pressure intended to discourage her from her Redwood treesit. Her call came just in time, as increased pressure from Border Patrol was imminent.
When I arrived at the Grandmother Tree site, I saw a helicopter circling the camp, and the flashing lights from numerous Border Patrol vehicles that had passed me on the road confirmed the situation. The Protectors were told to clear the easement and the road, or risk ticketing and arrest. The treesitters were told to come down from Grandmother. The Protectors’ nonviolent response was to step aside while continuing to support their treesitters.
After my arrival, the Border Patrol left, and all was silent except for the singing birds, the rustle of Cottonwood leaves in the breeze, and the summer cicadas, who sang to endure the heat. Under a shade cloth, the Protectors gathered to share what they had experienced. I stood aside as they spoke, giving them quiet space to calm and clear their minds, hearts, and bodies. Later, several people greeted me and welcomed me to this place. This San Rafael Valley will rewild us as we join in protecting this last of our desert wilderness.
Everyone who gathered agreed that this increased pressure shows the effort to protect this precious ecosystem is working, as this witness shows, and that it may be wise to pause a moment to gain strength as they move this witness for the land forward. The planned border wall construction is the biggest obstruction to an essential wildlife corridor on this continent. The San Rafael Valley is a critical corridor for wildlife traveling north and south. This area is as precious as Big Bend National Park.
Join the effort to protect this place. When we speak up, our government will listen and stop this unnecessary destruction. More of us need to join the Protectors, be ready for the call, speak up, and join them in this wild place that will be further harmed if we don’t show up.
All photos by Jeanne Marie Mudd. For more on this treesit, listen to the Rewilding Earth Podcast Episode 180: Activists Take to the Canopy to Defend Centuries-old Cottonwood, Cats, and Connectivity.
Jeanne Marie Mudd works with non-profit and public sector organizations, writes, and leads retreats focused on rewilding where participants reconnect with the wild Light within and around us. This helps bring light to our relationship with the Earth and supports planetary rewilding. She serves on the Steering Committee of Quaker Earthcare Witness and is an Arizona delegation leader for the Friends Committee on National Legislation.

title: “Digital House of Artsakh Culture” Presented in Yerevan
content:
“Digital House of Artsakh Culture” Presented in Yerevan
Digital House of Artsakh Culture - artsakhian.org, a digital platform created to collect, preserve, and promote the intangible cultural heritage of Artsakh, was presented in Yerevan. The platform was initiated by the We Are Our Mountains Development Agency, founded by Ruben Vardanyan, with the support of the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.
Following the forced displacement of the Armenian population of Artsakh in September 2023, the natural continuity of cultural transmission was also disrupted. The dialect, folklore, rituals and customs, songs and music, traditional knowledge, and numerous expressions of everyday culture that had been passed down from generation to generation in their natural cultural environment now require particular attention, documentation, and preservation.
“It was important for us that Artsakh be represented in the digital world through the culture it has created. In this digital house, everything is interconnected — language, memory, people, and stories. Here, the culture of Artsakh is presented not as a closed chapter of the past, but as a living culture,” said Narine Aghabalyan, Deputy Director of the We Are Our Mountains Development Agency and Project Lead.
The structure of Digital House of Artsakh Culture is based on UNESCO’s five domains of intangible cultural heritage. It encompasses oral traditions and expressions, including folklore; performing arts; social practices, rituals and festive events; knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe; and traditional craftsmanship. The platform also serves as a digital repository, bringing together a library, video archive, photo archive, audio archive, and dictionary.
Lernik Hovhannisyan, a member of the scholarly team involved in creating the platform, emphasized the significance of the initiative in the context of the threats currently facing the cultural heritage of Artsakh.
“Against the backdrop of recent developments, as Azerbaijan pursues a policy of cultural ethnocide aimed at erasing the Armenian presence in Artsakh, with the tacit consent of the international community, this platform enables us to present our homeland and ensure that the story of Artsakh - every page of it - remains open to all of us and is never closed,” Hovhannisyan said.
During the presentation, the team introduced the concept behind the platform, its structure, the principles guiding its content, and directions for further development. The project team also invited people from Artsakh, researchers, and families holding private archives to share photographs, videos, audio recordings, personal accounts, and other materials that can contribute to preserving the cultural memory of Artsakh.
In his professional assessment of the platform, historian and cultural studies scholar Hamlet Petrosyan emphasized the importance of scholarly accuracy and professional responsibility.
“Our success lies in presenting our culture in a detailed, precise, and impartial way. Under these difficult circumstances, a professional approach is also a moral standard. This platform is an exceptional undertaking, and I am truly impressed by what has been accomplished,” Petrosyan said.
The public presentation of the platform does not mark the completion of the work. Rather, Digital House of Artsakh Culture is entering a new stage of development. Its content and digital repositories will continue to expand through the inclusion of new scholarly and private archives, oral testimonies, and other materials. The aim is for the platform to become a continuously growing, open, and reliable source of knowledge that preserves the living cultural memory of Artsakh and passes it on to future generations.

title: Pedro Miguel: Analfabetismo: porcentaje agridulce
content:
l martes pasado, el secretario de Educación Pública, Mario Delgado, anunció en San Juan Chamula, Chiapas, una reducción histórica del analfabetismo, que cifró en 3.8 por ciento de la población de 15 años y más (https://tinyurl.com/ymnbsm2c). Es un avance significativo en apenas dos años, pues en 2024 esa proporción era de 4.1 por ciento; muy notable en los seis últimos años, en comparación con 4.7 por ciento de 2020, y mucho más, en relación con 9.5 por ciento de comienzos de este siglo. Más allá de las estadísticas, como lo señaló el funcionario, “la alfabetización es uno de los actos de justicia, equidad y amor más profundos que se puedan realizar” y una aplicación de la consigna “Por el bien de todos, primero los pobres” (https://tinyurl.com/32tkh2cv).
En efecto, el analfabetismo afecta principalmente a mujeres pobres y a las entidades con mayores rezagos sociales del país: Chiapas, Guerrero y Oaxaca, y combatirlo significa una acción concreta de combate a la pobreza, la marginación y la desigualdad. De manera que alcanzar ese mínimo de 3.8 por ciento informado por el titular de la SEP es un logro nacional al que no debe escatimarse el mérito.
Pero, al mismo tiempo, los números esconden una realidad dolorosa e ina-ceptable. México tiene una población total de unos 134 millones 400 mil habitantes, de los cuales 101 millones tienen 15 años o más. El 3.8 por ciento de esa cifra significa que más de 3 millones 800 mil adolescentes y adultos en el país carecen de habilidades mínimas de lectoescritura y que, en consecuencia, ven reducidas sus capacidades de expresión, de comprensión del mundo, de pensamiento crítico y de participación política, social y económica. Desde esta perspectiva, el anuncio del secretario de Educación Pública es una noticia agridulce que debiera llevar a la reflexión y, sobre todo, a una acción radical, no para reducir, sino para erradicar el analfabetismo remanente.
No sería, desde luego, una tarea fácil, toda vez que la población afectada tiene un alto grado de dispersión, es rural en su gran mayoría y requiere de estrategias regionales diferentes; no es lo mismo abatir 1.4 por ciento de analfabetismo en la capital del país que enfrentar 13 por ciento en Chiapas. Incluso en entidades contiguas esos índices pueden brincar en forma significativa; así, son de 5.9 en Puebla y de 2.8 en Tlaxcala, o de 3.4 en Zacatecas y de 2 en Aguascalientes, o de 5.1 en Hidalgo y de 2.6 en el estado de México, lo que denota la existencia de realidades sociales particulares y de la necesidad de pensar en estrategias diferentes para cada localidad.
Por otra parte, eliminar el analfabetismo no se ha formulado como un objetivo explícito de los planes de gobierno, para los cuales este propósito se encuentra implícito en los compromisos del Plan Nacional de Desarrollo y en la política social de combate a la pobreza, superación de las brechas de género, fortalecimiento del sistema de educación pública y planes de justicia para el agro y las comunidades indígenas.
Sin embargo, la individualización de este problema podría permitir la definición de un objetivo nacional concreto: incorporar a casi 4 millones de personas al mundo del lenguaje escrito –y aquí uno debería preguntarse qué lenguaje o lenguajes en particular, porque el español no es el único de México–, lo que significaría un acto contundente de dignificación, es decir, de creación de condiciones para el ejercicio pleno de todos sus derechos, para su incorporación en circunstancias menos desfavorables a la economía y a la política.
Hace 65 años, en 1961, a Cuba le tomó un año alfabetizar a casi un millón de personas. No sería descabellado, entonces, pensar que en México podría lograrse la erradicación del analfabetismo, que numéricamente es cuatro veces mayor, en los más de cuatro años que le restan a este sexenio. Sería una obra social mucho más barata que cualquier gran proyecto de infraestructura y que la mayoría de los programas sociales, aunque tan benéfica como ellos, y sería además un objetivo difícilmente cuestionable en el terreno político (por más que las oposiciones ayunas de programa y los loros mediáticos inventaran algo que objetarle) y capaz de generar un amplio consenso social.
Se necesitaría, eso sí, una inequívoca voluntad política y un vasto esfuerzo de coordinación institucional de la propia SEP –por medio del INEA y el Conafe, por ejemplo– con las secretarías del Bienestar –para involucrar a los Servidores de la Nación–, del Trabajo –Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro–, de Cultura, Ciencia, Humanidades, Tecnología e Innovación, Defensa y Marina –por la logística– y Agricultura y Desarrollo Rural; por añadidura, habría que sumar esfuerzos con los gobiernos de los estados y municipales, y convocar a voluntarias y voluntarios de todas las edades, clases y condiciones sociales.
Pero valdría la pena. Llegar a 2030 sin analfabetismo sería un logro social magnífico para el Segundo Piso de la Cuarta Transformación.

title: Support Emergency Relief in Nepal
content: Support Emergency Relief in Nepal Country Nepal agnes Thu, 09/17/2026 - 12:13 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image Give Now to Double Your Impact! The devastating impacts of the sudden flash flood on August 26 that occurred in Nepal continue to be felt, and Cultural Survival continues to work to support our Indigenous community partners who are on their journey towards recovery. As we work to channel funds toward humanitarian aid that is Indigenous-led and locally determined, your gift continues to be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $10,000 through a grant from The Fund for Nonviolence. We express our deepest gratitude and appreciation to those who have already supported this cause - your contribution has helped ensure that urgent assistance reaches Indigenous communities whose livelihoods, territories, and cultural systems are under threat. Destruction from the flooding has been devastating, impacting all aspects of daily life, and getting assistance and information to the people who need it most has become one of the greatest challenges. Dipak Lama, a station manager based in the Dhunche district headquarters of Rasuwa, described how even local radio stations struggled to continue communicating with communities when the disaster struck. “On the very same morning, we had information from the police about the flood, and we were in the middle of sharing information through the radio, but the electricity went off, as the electricity office was destroyed by then,” Lama told Cultural Survival. Local FM radio is a vital source of information for communities cut off from conventional communication systems. Yet, even radio operations face challenges due to a lack of battery backup and solar power. In remote settlements, residents need information about rescue operations, safe routes, food distribution, and emergency services, but damaged infrastructure makes communication increasingly difficult. The disaster has also intensified debate over climate change and state responsibility. Environmentalists have classified the Bhotekoshi disaster as climate-induced, and Dr. Maheshwar Dhakal, Head of the Climate Change Management Division under the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Environment, said the catastrophic loss of life and property resulted from forces to which Nepal has contributed very little. “The loss of life and property we suffered in the Bhote Koshi flood is purely a climate-induced disaster,” Dhakal said, arguing that developed and industrialized countries have emitted vast quantities of carbon while Nepal’s contributions remain less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Indigenous Peoples’ rights activists are calling for disaster response and climate adaptation strategies to incorporate Indigenous knowledge and values. As development projects, including dams and hydropower facilities, make lands fragile, Indigenous Peoples are calling for Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), protection of traditional ecological knowledge, and greater attention to forests, biodiversity, soil conservation, and traditional practices that can reduce vulnerability to landslides and erosion. We continue to stand beside our partners in Nepal, channeling funds toward humanitarian aid that is Indigenous-led and locally determined, but we need your help to reach our $10,000 goal. Your gift will be matched dollar-for-dollar up to $10,000 through a grant from The Fund for Nonviolence, helping us respond to the needs of our partners. You can provide support and give Indigenous communities greater agency in determining their journey towards recovery. If you haven't already, please consider donating today – your contribution will help ensure that urgent assistance reaches Indigenous communities whose livelihoods, territories, and cultural systems are under threat. Thank you for standing with our Indigenous partners in Nepal. Support Indigenous communities in Nepal! Read more: "Deadly Flood, Dubbed “Himalayan Tsunami,” Leaves Over 1,300 Dead and Thousands Missing in Nepal" by Dev Kumar Sunuwar (Koĩts-Sunuwar, CS Staff)

title: An activist writes how the Chipko Movement inspired him to conserve forests in South India
content:
Parvatiya Navjeevan Ashram is situated on a small hillock overlooking the Bhilangana Valley along the Bhilangana River, one of the tributaries of the Bhagirathi, in Tehri Garhwal district, Uttarakhand (formerly Uttaranchal). This was the epicentre of the Chipko Andolan led by Sunderlal and Vimla Bahuguna. Unlike other Gandhian ashrams or communities, it had simple cottages and a small office from where Chipko activists worked, evolving strategies and creating hand-printed pamphlets to be distributed in the villages. There was a primary school on the campus run by the ashram and it had a small patch of agricultural land. As part of the ashram rules, those living on the campus had to participate in common activities like prayer and cleaning, but they also contributed towards the labour, working on the farm to produce food, or assisting in agricultural activities. The concept behind establishing the ashram was to prepare the younger generation of activists to fight for the cause of social and economic justice, based on Gandhian ideology. Thus, equal opportunity was given for both intellectual and physical work.
When I arrived at the ashram to learn from the Chipko movement, Sunderlal Bahuguna said to me, “If you are visiting the ashram to build a career for yourself then you have arrived in the wrong place. But if you want to become an activist to protect Nature and natural resources, to work with the hill people, then it is the right place for you”. Later I learnt that Vimla agreed to marry him only after he quit his career in politics to dedicate himself to the cause of the hill people and set up this ashram in a remote region. Thus, I was fortunate enough to be trained as an activist in the legacy of Gandhi.
I was an idealistic youth, fresh from my post-graduation training from Delhi School of Social Work, University of Delhi. The theories of social work and community development that I had learnt in the books were tested against the realities of Himalayan village life. I was enrolled on grassroots work with senior Chipko activists like Dhoom Singh Negi, a longtime colleague of Sunderlal Bahuguna, who had quit his secure profession as a high school teacher to join Chipko. Pratap Shikhar was another youth from Chhatra Yuva Sangharsh Vahini, the youth organisation motivated by the ideals of the late Jayaprakash Narayan. Thus it was a mix of young and old activists who had already put in their hard labour to organise the Chipko struggle in the remote hill regions, motivating people, especially the women, to save the forests from being cut down by contractors.
Often, we had to walk long distances in the hills to organise the villagers, most of the time establishing contacts and trying to convince them about the need to form a strong organised group to fight the government to stop the felling of trees. Many times we had to spend the nights in the villages and the rule was to not ask for food and accommodation. However, we never faced any problem as the farming communities in these villages were so warm and hospitable that they fed us and also provided us a place to sleep, sharing whatever they had. This helped us to understand the ground level reality of the socio-economic factors, and how village life was deeply linked to the surrounding forests from where they brought fodder, fuel, and water. In fact, instead of creating awareness, we were learning from the villagers how their lifestyle evolved through the interaction with surrounding natural resources like forests and streams which was the lifeline for their everyday living.
Having learnt the basic lessons of organising grassroots movements to protect forests, I was keen to launch a movement similar to Chipko in order to conserve the tropical forests in South India. The Trans-Himalayan Kashmir to Kohima foot march inspired me to start a similar foot march along the banks of the Kali River in Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka. I started walking alone from Karwar, the coastal town and district headquarters on the banks of Kali. I walked with the message of Chipko to Diggi, the origin of the Kali River on the border of Goa and Karnataka. Though local people joined me on the walk and provided accommodation and food, it was a challenging task to convey the message of forest conservation. The Kali valley was witnessing massive tree-cutting for building the Supa Dam that would help to harness the water of the Kali for generating power. However, the sight of the clearfelling of old-growth forests strengthened my determination to fight those policies that caused this destruction. By sheer coincidence, about a hundred kilometres from Kali, in the Sirsi region, there were spontaneous sparks of protest against the forest destruction as the village youth were keen to stop the felling of natural forests in order to establish teak plantations in the guise of “scientific forestry”.
Initially, the demand of the Appiko movement was to halt the clear-felling of natural forests and their conversion to monoculture plantations. The launching of the movement was a threat to the government policy. They tried every means to stop the spread of the movement. However, the hidden hardships of the people and the conflict over the natural resources led to the spread of the movement in numerous districts of Karnataka from Kodagu in the south to South Kanara and Shimoga districts.
Realising there was widespread people’s support to the movement, the government agreed to stop the clear-felling of the old-growth forests for teak plantations. However, the activists realised that the timber concessions given to wood-based industries and even the removal of two trees per hectare was causing large-scale damage to the existing forest resources. In order to halt the further process of deforestation and the threat to the existing forests, the movement put forth the demand for a moratorium on the felling of green trees in the natural forests of the Western Ghats.
Well-organised grassroots actions occurring over a decade and pressure from numerous groups forced the state government to change its forest policy. In 1989, the state government imposed a ban on the felling of green trees in natural forests. This ban continues till today thanks to the Appiko movement and the positive response of the state government, which has taken action to conserve the forests.
Excerpted with permission from ‘From the Himalaya to the Western Ghats: Relevance of Chipko’, Pandurang Hegde in 50 Years of Chipko: The Movement and Its Afterlives’, edited by Murali Sivaramakrishnan, Orient Black Swan.

title: Turtle Mountain chairman encourages civic, youth engagement
content:
This story was originally published by North Dakota Monitor.
Jack Dura
North Dakota Monitor
Tribal leaders should support their community’s youth to spur growth and break away from old politics that hinder opportunities, the leader of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians told college students, instructors and other tribal officials Thursday, Sept. 10.
Tribal Chairman Jamie Azure said he wanted to break away from that “standard approach” soon after his entry into tribal government as a council member in 2016. He outlined how his tribe worked to engage youth and drive toward goals for the Turtle Mountain community after trainings on strategic planning for Native nations showed why opportunities were lacking.
“We learned that if we are going to move forward as a nation, we needed to start planning on moving forward by using correct data, by using higher education, by showing people that our sovereign nations weren’t just little specks on a map,” Azure told an audience at the 29th Tribal Leaders Summit in Bismarck.
In 2018, Turtle Mountain leaders and the Native Governance Center organized a youth summit with roundtables to ask young people what challenges, opportunities or lack thereof they saw in the community, Azure said.
The tribe began a 10-year strategic plan based on that feedback, “and that’s still going through to today,” the chairman said.
The tribe built a water park for a safe, fun place for families and job opportunities for young people, and a recovery center to help people move forward from addiction, Azure said.
The tribe raised its minimum wage to $15 an hour and made youth employees eligible for a 401(k) retirement account and insurance after six months, he said.
“That to me is sustainable security for our people for the next 40, 50 years,” the chairman said.
Additionally, the tribe’s natural resources group and 25 to 50 youth workers cleaned up and transformed the beaches of Gordon Lake into Sky Chief Park. The youth asked the tribal council to prohibit alcohol at the lake, which passed, Azure said. And those teenagers began to enforce the rules, he said. Parking and camping areas got cleaner, he said.
“You can sit back and you can watch our young ones really just take a grasp and say, ‘This is who we are.’ That’s true sovereignty. That’s people coming together and saying, ‘We have the power,’” Azure said.
Tribes can take the example of the youth at Turtle Mountain and other tribes and “say we need to come together unitedly” and move forward on issues together, he said. He noted Turtle Mountain and Spirit Lake brought a voting rights lawsuit regarding North Dakota’s legislative redistricting that is ongoing.
“We continue to fight and we continue to move forward,” Azure said.
He said he’s become more connected with other tribal leaders across North Dakota the last two years, especially over developments at the federal level, such as tribal college funding cuts.
“Sovereignty does not mean that we work alone,” the chairman said.

title: ‘Identity returned to us’: How Taiwan’s latest recognised indigenous group is reclaiming its voice
content:
‘Identity returned to us’: How Taiwan’s latest recognised indigenous group is reclaiming its voice
- The Siraya people of Taiwan gained official recognition as the island's 17th Indigenous group, reclaiming their identity after centuries of assimilation and discrimination.
- Recognition enables legal status, government funding, and efforts to revive the Siraya language and cultural traditions, benefiting descendants and future generations.
- Concerns exist among other Indigenous groups about resource competition and political representation, but experts encourage unity to strengthen collective Indigenous rights in Taiwan.
AI generated
TAINAN, Taiwan – As a child, Taiwanese indigenous language teacher Hanna Domok would lie to her classmates and say that her ancestors hailed from China.
Her darker skin made her look different from her peers, who called her derogatory names that meant “savage” or “barbarian”.
“It gave me an inferiority complex. So I would make things up and tell people, ‘No, no, you’re wrong, I am not who you think I am’,” the 54-year-old recalled in an interview with The Straits Times.
“I would tell them that my grandfather immigrated to Taiwan from China,” said Domok, who also goes by her Chinese name Mu Li-chun.
Her experience as a member of the Siraya, an Austronesian-speaking indigenous group native to south-western Taiwan, is not unique.
For centuries, the Siraya as well as other lowland plains – or Pingpu – indigenous communities often kept their background a secret to avoid social stigma and discrimination; many were forced to adopt Han Chinese customs and languages and assimilate.
But things have come a long way since the late 1980s during Taiwan’s transition to democracy, following the lifting of martial law in 1987.
On July 30, after decades of activism, the Siraya people finally won legal recognition from the Taiwanese government as the island’s 17th officially recognised indigenous group. There are 26 known indigenous groups in Taiwan, including those that are not recognised by the government.
Taiwan’s indigenous communities, which are traditionally divided into highland and lowland groups, make up about 2.7 per cent of the island’s 23.3 million people. They claim thousands of years of history on the island before the first foreign settlers arrived in the 17th century.
Taiwan’s first foreign settlers were the Dutch (1624-1662) and the Spanish (1626-1642), who built trading posts along the coast. To secure labour for farming, the Dutch encouraged the immigration of Han Chinese workers from mainland China, which marked the first significant wave of Chinese migration.
Han Chinese settlers grew to dominate Taiwan numerically, culturally and politically during the Qing Dynasty (1683-1895), and the indigenous groups became a minority discriminated against by the Chinese majority and forced to adopt Chinese surnames and pay heavy taxes. When the Kuomintang (KMT) government arrived from the Chinese mainland in 1949, indigenous people were forced to adopt Mandarin Chinese and suppress their cultural customs.
There is no official data on how many people of Siraya descent are in Taiwan, but the city government of Tainan, where they historically resided, recorded more than 11,800 people as Siraya in 2016.
The Siraya are also the first group to secure recognition under the Pingpu Indigenous Peoples Identity Act, which was passed in 2025 to redress the historic erasure of Pingpu groups. The other 16 groups are recognised under the Status Act for Indigenous Peoples.
The Siraya’s historic recognition will likely pave the way for more lowland plains indigenous communities to receive the same treatment in the future. But while the landmark ruling is cause for celebration, Siraya community leaders and activists say substantial work remains for full cultural and administrative integration.
“It feels incredible, because it’s like our identity has been returned to us,” said Domok from a Siraya-owned cafe in Tainan. “A lot more work needs to be done, but at least we can say that we have secured an entry ticket now (into legal parity).”
Taiwan President Lai Ching-te welcomed the news, having previously supported the Siraya people’s fight for cultural and legal recognition during his tenure as mayor of Tainan (2010-2017).
“This is a historic moment for the Siraya people and an important milestone in the pursuit of historical and transitional justice for indigenous peoples,” he wrote on Facebook on Aug 1, Taiwan’s Indigenous Peoples’ Day.
The milestone is not merely symbolic. Official recognition provides a clear legal basis and central government funding to restore the Siraya language and protect traditional customs such as the Siraya Night Festival, which honours their ancestral spirits while being an expression of thanks and blessings.
Eligible descendants can also begin to register at household registration offices to receive Plains Indigenous status on their official documents.
“Making our status official means the world to us,” said Vukin Takalomay, 28, a Siraya rights activist and language teacher.
“At university, even members of other Taiwanese indigenous groups would question my claim as a Siraya indigenous person. They’ll say I cannot possibly claim such a thing if it’s not made official,” he told ST.
While highland indigenous groups such as the Atayal and Bunun, who traditionally reside in Taiwan’s isolated mountainous areas, have been legally recognised since the Japanese colonial era (1895-1945), plains indigenous groups have struggled to receive recognition because they were deemed to be highly assimilated into Han Chinese society.
Their perceived loss of distinct cultural markers comes from centuries of intermarriage, language shifts and cultural integration with the Han Chinese settlers they lived alongside in the lowlands.
However, Siraya language and customs were largely suppressed not by choice but by a succession of dominant ruling powers.
As far back as the late 17th century during Qing Dynasty rule, Siraya families faced educational and societal pressure to adopt Chinese surnames and speak Chinese dialects. Then, when Japanese became the primary language of instruction in public schools under Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945, the Siraya language fell out of regular use altogether, and it was declared linguistically “extinct” by 1908.
Indigenous languages were further suppressed under the KMT government, with locals subjected to the regime’s strict Mandarin-only policy.
“If you spoke anything other than Mandarin, you could get punished in class,” said Lo Chao-teng, 71, chairman of the Tainan Siraya Cultural Association.
“The teachers would record it on the blackboard to humiliate you, and you could get beatings,” he added.
Linguists and language teachers have in recent years worked to reconstruct and promote the Siraya language, one word at a time. As the Siraya language has had no native speakers for such a long time, linguists relied heavily on historical texts, including a copy of the Gospel of Matthew, a book of the Bible, translated into Siraya by a Dutch missionary during the Dutch colonial period (1624-1662).
In 2008, activists published a comprehensive glossary containing thousands of Siraya words.
“There were certain words that we kept hearing from our elders but we didn’t even realise that they were Siraya words,” Domok said. “It’s amazing being able to learn these words again as my language, and teach them to the next generation.”
A few times a week, the freelancer teaches primary school-aged children Siraya words through songs in private lessons. “One of my seven-year-old students recently told me, ‘I can sing these Siraya songs by myself, I don’t need you to guide me any more.’ That made me so happy.”
Official recognition of the Siraya is expected to provide a legal and financial foundation to expand language revitalisation programmes, building on local efforts in Tainan where multiple schools already offer classes.
Jolan Hsieh, an indigenous studies expert at Taiwan’s National Dong Hwa University, who is also known by her Siraya name Bavaragh Dagalomai, noted the significance of learning one’s native language.
“Through learning the language, we can learn more about our history and culture, and that will make our identity stronger,” she told ST. “When you have that, more people can recognise and celebrate your group as distinct and just as valid as other indigenous groups.”
That is important given that official recognition of the Siraya has led to some anxiety among other indigenous communities over the possible dilution of government resources and benefits allocated to them, she said. For instance, there is a fear that it may become more difficult for them to secure political representation in the future.
Taiwan reserves six seats in its Parliament for indigenous people, which are directly voted on by eligible indigenous voters.
As the potential population of Pingpu descendants is estimated to be quite large, existing recognised indigenous groups fear they could easily overwhelm the vote, effectively squeezing their tribes out of parliamentary representation.
At the moment, officials are working on amending laws regarding political participation, social welfare, healthcare, education and other supporting measures for the Siraya, according to the Council of Indigenous Peoples, a Cabinet-level government agency.
“There is some concern that the more indigenous people are recognised, the more people there will be coming in to fight for a small share of resources,” said Hsieh.
“But actually I like to see it from the other perspective – the more of us there are, the more we can work together and negotiate for our collective rights.”

title: El rap indígena se convierte en un escudo para defender la Amazonía ecuatoriana
content:
- Jóvenes de diferentes nacionalidades indígenas de la Amazonía ecuatoriana apelan a la música para denunciar los impactos de las actividades extractivas en sus territorios.
- Cada tema es interpretado en la lengua originaria de su autor y algunos tienen subtítulos y pasajes en español para tender un puente hacia oyentes de otras culturas.
- Mongabay Latam presenta las historias de cuatro raperos indígenas: Willan Gualinga (Taki Supay) de la nacionalidad kichwa de Sarayaku; Misael Elías Criollo Grefa (Misa17), a'i cofán; Raúl Vargas (Robenban), kichwa de Pastaza, y Tzitzanu, sapara.
- Con su música están llegando a escenarios nacionales e internacionales: el tema “Ingi Tsampi”, de Misa17, suma más de 400 000 visualizaciones en TikTok a un mes de su lanzamiento.
La primera vez que Willan Gualinga se subió a un escenario fue en su comunidad, Sarayaku, en la Amazonía ecuatoriana. Recuerda que le sudaban las manos, le temblaba el cuerpo y su boca no podía pronunciar todas las palabras que se amontonaban en su mente. Tres años después de su debut, se presentó con la misma canción en el Festival Rizoma 2026, en la ciudad amazónica de Puyo, donde ya no eran decenas, sino miles de espectadores los que coreaban sus letras en idioma kichwa.
Esta vez su cuerpo se movía al ritmo y, sobre todo, con la fuerza necesaria para acompañar el mensaje que estaba transmitiendo: “Allpamanda kawsay manda jatarishun” o “levantémonos por la tierra y por la vida”, en español. Este es el nombre de su primer tema y la frase que repetía a todo pulmón durante su presentación. La canción se enfoca en los relatos de los abuelos sobre los orígenes de Sarayaku y, al igual que sus otras composiciones, pone el foco en las amenazas a su pueblo.
“A través de la música podemos transmitir los conocimientos de nuestros antepasados y, sobre todo, defender el territorio”, dice este joven de 23 años, conocido artísticamente como Taki Supay. Como él, una nueva generación de artistas amazónicos están usando el rap como una herramienta para visibilizar las amenazas que afectan a los diferentes pueblos y nacionalidades indígenas de la Amazonía ecuatoriana y, sobre todo, para demostrar por qué es necesario proteger la selva.
Leer más | Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
“El rap es hablar de lo que sientes, de lo que está pasando y de nuestra lucha”, agrega Misael Elías Criollo Grefa, más conocido como Misa17. Él es el primer rapero de la nacionalidad a’i cofán de Ecuador y su tema “Ingi Tsampi” ya suma más de 9000 visualizaciones en YouTube y más de 400 000 en TikTok a un mes de su lanzamiento.
En el sur de la Amazonía, las letras del grupo Zona Verde, compuesto por Raúl Vargas (Robenban) y Alejandro Moya (Naruman), impulsan las demandas de sus comunidades kichwa y shuar de Pastaza por el acceso a agua limpia. En la misma provincia, pero en el territorio sapara, Tzitzanu rapea en contra de la industria petrolera y a favor de mantener viva su cultura.
Todas estas canciones transmiten su amor por los ríos, la selva, los animales y todo lo que les rodea. Pero, sobre todo, están basadas en las experiencias que vivieron los cantantes desde que eran niños, cuando empezaron a acompañar a sus padres y abuelos en la defensa de su hogar, en su oposición a diversas actividades extractivas que dejaron sus impactos ambientales en el territorio.
Cada uno canta en su lengua, lo que para ellos representa otra forma de resistencia, de mantenerse fieles a su identidad y de llevar sus saberes a otras partes del planeta. Aunque el rap de los cinco ya ha trascendido fronteras, el camino no ha sido fácil. La ausencia de estudios de grabación en la Amazonía y los altos costos de producir los videos son algunos de sus obstáculos.
A eso se suman los riesgos de exponerse públicamente a los impactos que generan las actividades económicas que quieren instalarse en sus territorios y que, según dicen, los convierte en blanco fácil de agresiones o represalias. Sin embargo, estos jóvenes confían en que esta nueva forma de resistencia, a través del arte y sus rimas, en lugar de traer más enfrentamientos, será motor del cambio que llevará el mensaje a un público más amplio, despertará conciencias y motivará a otros jóvenes a involucrarse en la defensa de la Amazonía.
Rapear para sobrevivir
A Carla Vera, docente universitaria y periodista musical, no le sorprende que el rap haya ganado popularidad en estos territorios. “Es un género que se acopla a la potencia de los discursos y de la resistencia indígena. Va en contra de la opresión, promueve la liberación, es directo y genera ese sentimiento de empoderamiento en quienes lo hacen y en quienes lo escuchamos”, dice.
Para entender el contenido de sus canciones hay que remontarse a sus orígenes. El rap surgió en el Bronx, uno de los distritos marginales de Nueva York, en la década de los 70. Las rimas cargadas de mensajes de protesta contra la situación del país, en un contexto de racismo, precarización laboral y maltrato policial, irrumpieron en la escena musical.
En la actualidad, este género mantiene esa esencia y la connotación política de sus mensajes. Para Vera, también es entendible que el rap esté ganando más popularidad en este momento, ya que responde a las amenazas crecientes que enfrenta la Amazonía.
Según datos de MapBiomas, recopilados por la Fundación Ecociencia y entregados a Mongabay Latam, el 71 % de la minería en Ecuador se encuentra en la región amazónica. De esta, casi la mitad (44.5 %) está en territorios indígenas. Por otro lado, las concesiones petroleras están en el 63 % de los territorios de pueblos y nacionalidades amazónicas.
Leer más | Ecuador: juez ordena frenar minería en el río Ortega y nombra a una comunidad como su guardiana
“No quiero ver nuestros ríos contaminados, no quiero ver nuestra selva acabada, no quiero enfermedades por la culpa del petróleo, no quiero ver más muerte en mi territorio”, rapea Misa17 en su canción “Ingi Tsampi”, que significa “nuestra selva” en su lengua A’ingae. Con una camisa que conserva la forma y los rasgos de su vestimenta tradicional, pero más holgada, para darle un toque más urbano, y con el número 17 atrás, Misa lanza una frase tras otra sin detenerse a respirar.
Este joven de 19 años nació en Dureno, una comunidad a’i cofán ubicada en Sucumbíos, en el norte de la Amazonía, que se ha opuesto al ingreso de las empresas petroleras Texaco y la estatal Petroecuador.
Uno de los rostros más visibles en esa resistencia fue su tío, Eduardo Mendúa, quien fue asesinado en febrero de 2023. “Eduardo vive y la lucha sigue, fuerza, fuerza en honor a nuestro líder”, recita Misa17, mientras detrás de él, en el video musical, aparece una imagen del difunto defensor.
Desde que empezó a escribir sus canciones, hace dos años, ha encontrado un refugio en el rap. Al reconocerse como una persona más reservada, la música se ha convertido en el canal perfecto para expresarse. Aunque al inicio sus padres no lo apoyaban en este camino, al ver su esfuerzo y sus resultados, ahora son sus principales seguidores.
Gracias a su videoclip, el mensaje de este rapero ha llegado a otros países. “El mundo se va a dar cuenta de todos los problemas que pasamos en mi comunidad y algún día llegará más ayuda”, dice con una sonrisa, confiado de que sus deseos se convertirán en realidad.
Robenban también espera que, a través de sus canciones, se pueda difundir la importancia de proteger la selva, especialmente la cuenca del río Puyo, que es el que pasa por su hogar, la comuna San Jacinto, en Pastaza. Actualmente, las comunidades de esta zona están impulsando una acción de protección para exigir la descontaminación de este cuerpo de agua, afectado sobre todo por las descargas de aguas residuales.
Junto con Naruman, Robenban está escribiendo una canción sobre esta problemática y espera publicarla en los próximos meses. Su idea es narrar los impactos en la salud de las comunidades y en el turismo, que es su principal fuente de ingresos. En sus otras canciones, Robenban ya abordaba temáticas similares. “Se escucha el llanto de los peces mientras los ríos se secan”, rapea en su tema “Decepcionado y triste”, que es una crítica a los gobiernos por destruir la selva y “crear guerras”.
Leer más | TEDxAmazônia llegó a Ecuador para reunir a científicos, artistas y líderes indígenas
El contenido romántico era el que más le llamaba la atención cuando inició su carrera, pero al ver los procesos de resistencia de sus mayores, decidió enfocarse en “promover la protesta consciente para defender la selva a través de la música”. Al escuchar a unos amigos improvisar canciones, conoció lo que era el rap. Así, empezó a imitarlos, sin imaginarse que, una década después, tendría seis temas propios en YouTube.
Su afición se convirtió en una profesión hace seis años, cuando conoció a Naruman, de nacionalidad shuar, y formaron Zona Verde, un nombre que hace alusión a su hogar. El grupo ya se ha presentado en diversos escenarios de la Amazonía y en ciudades de la costa ecuatoriana como Guayaquil. Además, cuentan que tienen seguidores en países como Colombia y Estados Unidos, que les envían mensajes y están pendientes de lo que pasa en sus territorios. “Queremos que los niños y la gente adulta llegue a entender que vivimos gracias a la tierra, a las aguas, a los árboles y no debemos destruirlos más”, explica este rapero kichwa de 28 años.
Una lengua universal
Al tener un integrante shuar y otro kichwa, las canciones de Zona Verde tienen frases en ambas lenguas y en español. En el caso de Gualinga (Taki Supay), sus letras son exclusivamente en kichwa y en el de Misa17, sus rimas son en a’ingae, con subtítulos y algunos fragmentos también en español. “Este ritmo me gustó apenas lo escuché, pero quería hacerlo en mi idioma”, asegura este rapero a’i cofán, cuya lengua está en peligro de desaparecer. Él está convencido de que esta es una forma de incentivar a los más jóvenes a seguir practicándola.
A Tzitzanu le ocurre algo similar, ya que el sapara también está en riesgo de extinguirse. Las manifestaciones culturales de esta nacionalidad, que vive en la frontera entre Ecuador y Perú, fueron proclamadas en 2001 como Obra Maestra del Patrimonio Oral e Inmaterial de la Humanidad por la Unesco.
Su lengua fue reconocida como un repositorio de saberes y “memoria viva de toda la región”. Cuando integraron la lista de la Unesco, sólo cinco personas, de más de 70 años, hablaban el sapara a la perfección. Ahora, solo queda una abuela.
Tzitzanu es parte de la nueva generación de jóvenes sapara que están aprendiendo su lengua con el fin de evitar que desaparezca. Cuando era un niño, acompañaba a su padre, que es maestro de la lengua sapara, a las distintas comunidades de esta nacionalidad para entregar libros, diccionarios, rompecabezas y juegos para motivar a las personas de este territorio a que retomen este elemento trascendental de su cultura. Ahora, se esfuerza por mantener su lengua viva a través del rap.
Sin embargo, para este joven, de padre sapara y madre achuar, es importante rapear en varias lenguas para que el mensaje llegue a más personas. “Hablar en nuestro idioma es interesante, pero nosotros tenemos claro lo que pasa y lo que necesitamos es dar a conocer nuestra visión al mundo de afuera”, explica.
Tzitzanu, que significa “el primer hombre que llegó a la tierra a enseñar la ciencia y el arte”, honra su nombre desde 2015, cuando un primo le enseñó lo que era el rap y desde ese momento decidió que esa sería su arma para defender sus derechos y los de su hogar, que forma parte de la Comunidad Ecológica Cultural Yakuruna, un proyecto de turismo vivencial ubicado en la Amazonía de Ecuador, en la provincia de Pastaza.
“Me gusta porque puedes expresar muchas cosas en poco tiempo”, cuenta el cantante de 28 años. La oposición a los impactos del petróleo en su territorio también es uno de los temas protagonistas en sus canciones. “Somos una revelación, evolución, revolución en contra de su traición, explotación y destrucción”, se escucha en “Enraizate” o “Aiteka kaja pawetsa kaje” en sapara.
Contagiar las rimas
Tzitzanu también busca que otras personas de su comunidad ingresen al mundo del rap. Por eso, les comparte canciones de otros raperos y les explica el impacto que pueden tener estas letras.
Por su parte, Gualinga dice que “hay que dar un mensaje más claro, que muestre cómo todo está cambiando y cómo podemos perder nuestro conocimiento”. Este joven kichwa conoce de cerca lo que es la oposición al establecimiento de las actividades extractivas en territorio indígena. Su comunidad, Sarayaku, ha sido reconocida internacionalmente por resistirse al ingreso de una empresa petrolera, que intentó instalarse sin consultar a su pueblo.
El caso llegó a la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, que en 2012 emitió una sentencia en la que se reconocieron violaciones a los derechos colectivos de este pueblo.Ya han pasado más de 14 años y aún no se ha cumplido con algunos puntos de la sentencia, como el retiro de los explosivos que la empresa instaló en 25 000 hectáreas del territorio de la comunidad.
Gualinga tenía nueve años cuando se emitió la sentencia y ese fue uno de los eventos que le marcó, ya que le ha impulsado a buscar más formas de dar a conocer lo que está pasando en su tierra.
“Mi sueño es tener un estudio en Sarayaku donde los jóvenes puedan venir a hacer música y grabar lo que realmente les apasiona”, cuenta este rapero que conoce de cerca las dificultades de producir estos materiales en la Amazonía.
Tanto Gualinga como Tzitzanu, Robenban y Misa17 cuentan que el proceso para publicar un video o grabar sus canciones es costoso, necesitan equipos que no son comunes en la zona y tienen que viajar a ciudades como Puyo o Lago Agrio, ya que solo ahí están los estudios.
Esto se ha convertido en un obstáculo para que estos artistas publiquen sus canciones. Misa17, por ejemplo, ha escrito 12 temas, pero ha logrado sacar un video. El objetivo de todos es buscar formas de instalar más estudios cercanos a las comunidades para motivar a los niños a seguir este camino. “Vamos a crear una comunidad de raperos para seguir resistiendo”, dice orgulloso el cantante a’i cofán.
Su anhelo es que los niños de las comunidades ya no necesiten de ídolos externos, como fueron para ellos Canserbero o Santa Fe Klan. Con cada verso en kichwa, a’ingae, shuar o sapara, esta generación está construyendo sus propios referentes y demostrando que la selva también se defiende con música. El mayor desafío ahora, dice Gualinga, es perder el miedo, no solo a presentarse en los escenarios, sino a recitar con fuerza su mensaje.
*Imagen principal: Willan Gualinga, conocido como Taki Supay en el mundo artístico, se dedica al rap desde hace tres años para difundir los conocimientos ancestrales de su pueblo, al igual que las amenazas que los acechan. Foto: cortesía Willan Gualinga

title: En Arizona inició la construcción del muro fronterizo de Trump pese a la oposición de la tribu Tohono O’odham
content:
La construcción de un nuevo tramo de 100 kilómetros de muro fronterizo con México, impulsada por la administración del presidente estadounidense, Donald Trump, comenzó en Arizona pese a la oposición de la Nación Indígena Tohono O’odham, que considera que el proyecto viola su soberanía.
Tohono O’odham cree que el nuevo tramo de muro amenaza el medioambiente y resulta innecesario ante la caída del “95 %” en las detenciones migratorias en ese sector.
“Siempre hemos protegido nuestra tierra, nuestra comunidad, mucho antes de que esta nación fuera establecida y aún hoy nuestro deber es seguir protegiendo la tierra”, dijo a EFE Verlon José, presidente de ese territorio tribal, sobre el proyecto Tucson 5.
Por décadas, este resguardo indígena que comparte parte de la frontera entre Arizona y México se ha opuesto a la construcción de un muro físico dentro de su territorio, al considerar que afectará el tránsito de sus propios miembros, muchos de los cuales viven a ambos lados de la frontera y la cruzan con frecuencia para participar en ceremonias religiosas, peregrinaciones o visitar a familiares.
La comunidad también advierte que la construcción del muro podría destruir sitios ceremoniales considerados como “sagrados” y cementerios ancestrales.
La Nación Tohono O’odham interpuso una demanda contra el proyecto, al considerar que la construcción de una barrera de doble capa de acero y concreto, de unos 9,1 metros de altura, viola su soberanía al alterar los límites de sus terrenos, pero el pasado agosto una jueza federal en Washington falló en contra de la tribu al determinar que no pudo demostrar que el gobierno de Trump estuviera violando su soberanía.
La decisión se basa en un decreto emitido en 1907 por el entonces presidente de Estados Unidos, Theodore Roosevelt, que establece una franja de terreno de 18,3 metros de ancho a lo largo de la frontera con México, desde California hasta Nuevo México, considerada como “terreno de uso federal” con el propósito de combatir el narcotráfico.
Despliegue operativo y reclamos por derechos ancestrales
Semanas después de ese fallo, contratistas y agentes armados de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) se presentaron de forma sorpresiva a finales de agosto dentro del territorio tribal.
De acuerdo con CBP, actualmente se realizan trabajos de medición y toma de muestras de tierra en el área, donde ya se observa la presencia de maquinaria pesada.
El comisionado de CBP, Rodney Scott, anunció la reactivación del proyecto Tucson 5, que, según aseguró, permitirá “cerrar” uno de los corredores irregulares más utilizados para el tráfico de drogas y de inmigrantes indocumentados en la frontera con México.
Sin embargo, José indicó que siempre la Nación Tohono O’odham ha cooperado con el gobierno federal en la vigilancia de la frontera, permitiendo la entrada de agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza y cooperando con sus operaciones de seguridad nacional.
“En los últimos dos años los arrestos se han reducido en un 95 %, no vemos por qué la necesidad ahora de construir el muro”, enfatizó.
“Esto no se trata de la construcción de un muro o de seguridad nacional, se trata de la violación de los derechos de la Nación Tohono O’odham, su cultura y sus sitios ancestrales”, dijo a EFE la congresista de Arizona Adelita Grijalva.
Grijalva junto con otros congresistas demócratas han hecho un llamado a CBP pidiendo un alto a la construcción del proyecto.
Alerta ambiental en el manantial de Quitobaquito
En medio de la disputa se encuentra el manantial de Quitobaquito, en el sur de Arizona, y aunque está fuera del territorio indígena, es un sitio de importancia cultural para este pueblo, que lo consideran un lugar sagrado.
Además su laguna, que está en terrenos del gobierno federal, es un refugio para especies amenazadas, entre ellas la tortuga de Sonoyta y el pez pupo de Quitobaquito.
José asegura que el resguardo mantiene su lucha legal en los tribunales y ha apelado la decisión de la corte.
También señala que miembros de la tribu observan diariamente los trabajos que realizan los contratistas y agentes de CBP, y que algunos incluso encienden fogatas por las noches para llevar a cabo ceremonias pacíficas.
“Existe una gran frustración, pero también desilusión por la falta de respeto a nuestra cultura, es como si nuestras creencias y nuestros antepasados no tuvieran ningún valor”, lamentó José en declaraciones a EFE.

title: ‘The Asholio Heritage’: Documenting history, identity and life of Asholio people
content:
By Prisca Sam-Duru
