Presented as a rich and priceless compendium, “The Asholio Heritage,” by an accomplished and seasoned journalist, Ben Adam Shemang, is a historical masterpiece that takes readers on an interesting journey into almost everything they need to know about the Asholio people in Southern Kaduna, Nigeria.
The book by the pioneer Director of Training with the Voice of Nigeria (VON), Shemang who retired as Director of News (VON), brings to light, who the Asholio people are, what stands them out, as well as some of the people’s identity being threatened by modernisation.
In other words, The Asholio Heritage explores the cultural identity, farming practices, and social structure of the people.
Shemang, a graduate of Ahmadu Bello University (B.A. English), who holds postgraduate diplomas in journalism and law, a master’s in criminology and security studies, and currently a PhD student in Criminology and Security Studies, brings his training as a journalist into the compilation.
“The Asholo Heritage,” was published in November 2025 by NIRPRI Publishing Press, Abuja. The 409-page book is a product of profound research on Asholio life, history, culture, tradition, and custom.
The epoch-making history book on the Sholio people, is structured into 22 chapters made up of provocative topics and themes, including the people and history of Sholio, political organisation, clans and rulers, arbitration and alternative dispute resolution, language and linguistic variations, settlement patterns, religious modes of worship, cultural dances, family and marriage systems, games and leisure, music and musical instruments, customary practices, beliefs, economic activities, mathematics/counting, genealogy, etc.
In the “Introduction,” the author explains that the book wasn’t written to cause disaffection or injury to anyone considering that it delves deep into diverse aspects of Asholio people’s ways of life which aren’t documented.
Rather, the book was written “with the intention to provoke “debates, further insights and more literary works by critics, scholars, students, researchers and authors about the people,” adding that it “contains many parts of the history, politics, sociology, geography, economic development, the phonetics and phonology, the language, culture, religion, belief system, architecture etc, of the Asholio people,’ noting that it also provides insight into the Sholio land and immediate neighbours.”
In other words, “The book as it is in my submission, tends to define Asholio people with the hope that incoming authors and researchers can pick aspects or parts of this book and develop them into different books and that will be interesting reading titles in my thinking.”
“The Asholio Heritage” also features the totems and taboos of the Asholio people, such as why females are forbidden from eating eggs. As documented in chapter nineteen, “Way back, when a new house is to be built, it is started with just one stone at the centre of the proposed compound. The stone was called “afang agban”, meaning that the Asholio people started building a new compound with a granary (agban). The emphasis on the granary was the fact that the family must never go hungry.
Chapter one subtitled, “The Asholio People”, dives into who the people are, disclosing that Lutswe was the father, founder, and leader of the Asholio people. “…Lutswe came in the Alutswe clan, people who are said to be the first people to live in what is today known as Sholio land.” According to the author, the Asholio people are divided into four clans- Alutswe, Abvuat, Azam, and Aswua. The clans are listed in order of seniority without any of them being superior to the others.
It is noted in this chapter that modern scholars and colonial records have spelt the names of the clans quite differently without being able to change who they are; all these names refer to the same people who call themselves Asholio.
The author also reveals in the “Introduction” the different names the Asholio people are known with. He wrote, “The people we are talking about call themselves Asholio while outsiders call them Moroa or Marwa. So, some documents will have it as Moroa, Moro’a or Marwa.
In chapter two, titled ‘History of Asholio People,’ Shemang gives profound and diverse accounts of the origin of the Asholio people. Under subtitles such as ‘Vak as origin of Asholio’, ‘Bauchi origin theory’, ‘Origin from colonial sources’ and ‘Zaria and Katsina origin story,’ the book documents the diverse theories and accounts about the Asholio people.
The book captures the ‘Political Organisation’ of the Asholio people in Chapter Four, in which the author traces the leadership structures of the people from the pre-colonial era. Subtitles in this chapter include; ‘Pre-Colonial Period’, ‘Colonial Period’, Post-Colonial politics in Sholio land 1960- date, Asholio (Moroa) Development Association, Sholio Town Hall and Chat Community Bank. He follows this chapter up with “Some of the Paramount Rulers (YAAGWAM) of Sholio”, which is the title of Chapter Five.
While Chapter Nine deals with ‘Language and Linguistic Variations’ of the Asholio people, chapter eleven documents the impact of civilization on the people. The two major impacts are in the areas of cultural erosion and “Changes and substituting names of settlements”.
The people’s religion and modes of worship, their sacred places and heroes and heroines, diverse cultural dances, family and marriage (which delves deeper into the relationship between grandparents and their grandchildren), games and leisure, the different musical instruments used for entertainment, the different practices, totems and beliefs of the Asholio people, etc, are all captured from chapter thirteen to chapter nineteen. Interestingly, the Asholio people have their own unique mathematics symbols.
This is documented in chapter twenty-one titled, ‘Mathematics (fe) and its importance. This section is presented with two subtitles, ‘Mathematics Symbols’ and ‘Counting in Sholio Language’.
The author’s attempt to make the book appealing to the reader pays off as he employs coloured illustrations, images, and photographs like the one used for the cover page.
He goes further to dedicate a total of sixteen pages in between pages 266 and 267, for photographs and illustrations showing the people’s kitchen utensils, wild fruits, traditional method of storing cold water, how the people dressed in the 70s, traditional dancers, their huts, and a whole lot more.
The ‘References’ section is an indication that ‘The Asholio Heritage’ is a well-researched and referenced book. It is quite suitable for the avid reader and scholars. Any reader who is traditionally and culturally inclined will find the book a historical companion.
As Fr. Benjamin Yakubu Bala, also known as fr. Bamba wrote in the Foreword, Shemang’s book will serve as a rich reference material to many.
“The heritage of a people is preserved in documentation. Unfortunately, there is not much documentation available on Asholio. Therefore, this book is a modest contribution by Shemang in this regard. Considering that there is not much written on the Asholio heritage, the author made good use of oral sources and personal experience and a few available documented sources.
“The author pays tribute to documentation by colonial masters. Some were apt while others contained uncompleted and unbalanced truths. In this book, you will see how the author was able to respectfully blend the colonial narratives with the realistic experiences of the people from local sources,” fr. Bamba wrote.
‘The Asholio Heritage’ is highly recommended to the Nigerian public, particularly every indigenous person of Southern Kaduna. Tourists and tourism entrepreneurs will find it a vital document.
To lovers of history, the book is priceless. It is a must kept on the shelves of homes, schools, and public libraries.

title: Small Welsh football club's victory over Italian giants brought to life on stage
content:
Small Welsh football club's victory over Italian giants brought to life on stage
- Published
Almost 40 years after Merthyr Tydfil FC stunned Italian footballing giants Atalanta in the European Cup Winners Cup, the remarkable story is being brought back to life on the theatre stage.
The comedy Just One Cornetto focuses on the weeks leading up to the match at the club's Penydarren Park, when Merthyr defeated the team from Bergamo 2-1, in the first round of the competition.
Disappointment was to follow with the thousands who had travelled from Merthyr to northern Italy having to suffer a 2-0 loss, which meant Atalanta would go through, eventually reaching the semi-finals of the competition.
But the drama of that first match, and the attention on it at a time when English clubs were banned from European football, means it will go down in Welsh footballing folklore.
The play has been written by local writer Anthony Bunko, and premiered on Thursday at the Coliseum theatre in Aberdare.
It was a dramatic game, with Merthyr's winner only coming in the 83rd minute thanks to a Ceri Williams free-kick deflecting off an Italian player, but Bunko believes the play is about much more than that.
"It's a football story. But it's not so much of a football story. The football is right at the end. It's a bit like the Full Monty, where the dance is right at the end. And with this play, the football is right at the end."
The plot follows a boy called Decker, and his efforts to fulfil a promise to take his grandfather's ashes to the game, but it is also about the wider community.
"It's all about the characters and their struggles to overcome. You've got Italians who come over, who are quite apprehensive. You've got the committee, who have got to go from an amateur to professionals. You've got a bit of a love story in it, because the Italians come over and fall in love with a Merthyr girl."
On the night at least 8,000 supporters were crammed into Penydarren Park, but Bunko admits that although he lives in Merthyr, he wasn't one of them.
"I was playing rugby at the time, so it passed me by", he said.
"But the last couple of years, I've been going up to Penydarren Park, and they always end up talking about that game. And I see all the photos on the wall. And I just thought I'd love to do something about it."
"I'm a proud Merthyr boy anyway. And I just wanted to fetch that part. Because the town gets a big kicking off everybody and I just wanted to show the communal side of it and how good it is."
Ben Evans plays the part of Kevin Rogers, the only Merthyr-born player in the team that beat Atalanta, and the man who scored in the 38th minute to go 1-0 up.
With many of those players expected to be at the opening performance on Thursday, Evans says he is excited, despite the added pressure on the cast.
"It's such an honour. I've been very, very lucky to speak to the marvellous Kevin Rogers, who I said to him that I hope I didn't let him down. And he's such a nice guy," said Evans.
"It's very much a Welsh thing that I probably didn't get starstruck meeting Rowan Atkinson or Anthony Hopkins and Michael Sheen. I got more starstruck meeting Gareth Bale and Ryan Giggs and Kevin Rogers and Ceri Williams."
"So, there will be a few extra nerves maybe. And I hope that I do Kevin and all the players justice."
Evans agrees that the significance of sporting events goes far beyond the results on the pitch, emphasising their impact on communities.
He added: "I was only three in '87, but in Wales especially, we hold on to these historical moments. Being from West Wales, we still talk about when Llanelli beat the All Blacks and that was a long time ago," Evans said.
"When we first came into the rehearsal space, we spoke not even about the match, but about Merthyr in 1987 and the problems that were going on economically and how this night gave the town hope. And it's something to make you believe, isn't it?"
Director Neil Maidman attended the famous fixture at Penydarren Park.
"It was absolutely amazing. I was a sixth former at the time. It happened on 16 September. My 18th birthday was on 17 September, so I attended the match the night before," he said.
"Looking back on it, that week was so instrumental in my entire life. I started my first job a few days later and then I actually met my future wife a few days later."
"To be doing and directing this play about that time, it's quite surreal, really."
The independent production looked in jeopardy at one point, as director Neil Maidman and Bunko struggled to secure funding for the project, "which was disappointing", said Bunko.
It's a mirror image of the events of 1987, where club chairman John Reddy led a campaign to raise tens of thousands of pounds, with an army of volunteers working day and night to renovate the stadium, in order to ensure the match could be played in the town.
"We weren't going to put [the play] on, and then the community got together, from business people and volunteers and we got enough money to actually put it on", Bunko said.
"We could then pay the actors good money and we could get the props and the costumes and everything we want."
"But it just showed our little punk rock spirit, and we got money from somewhere else, and on Thursday night we're going to have 500 people in here [The Aberdare Coliseum], which will be a good experience."

title: Thousands support petition against proposed amendments to Treaty references in legislation
content:
Thousands support petition against proposed amendments to Treaty references in legislation
A Ngāti Kahungunu petition calling for a halt on government plans to amend references to Te Tiriti o Waitangi in legislation has attracted more than 20,000 signatures.
Ngāti Kahungunu chair Bayden Barber told RNZ that any legislative or constitutional changes affecting Te Tiriti should involve genuine consultation with Māori and the public.
Iwi representatives are planning to deliver the petition to Parliament on horseback, with the first group of riders departing Friday morning from Waimārama Marae.
Barber said Waimārama was the home of Harawira Mahikai Te Tātere, a Ngāti Kurukuru chief who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi at Waipūreku in 1840.
"We will ride from Waimārama, and connect with riders from Heretaunga, Ahuriri and Wairoa at the Tukituki River. From there, we'll travel through Havelock North.
"We will continue through Ngāti Kahungunu heartland, travelling past Pukehou marae, on to Waipawa, Waipukurau, Rākautātahi, Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua (Dannevirke) and Te Whakaoriori (Masterton)."
Barber said the trek aims to send a simple yet powerful message that cannot be ignored.
"We want to send a message to this Government that we are serious about protecting Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the founding agreement of this country. Not only to this Government, but whoever is there come November 7."
"Te Tiriti o Waitangi is what makes our country unique - the coming together of two peoples, Māori and Pākehā, working for the benefit of all - and it must be upheld. If you haven't already signed the petition, please do."
Te Taiwhenua o Tāmaki nui a Rua representative and Ngāti Kahungunu deputy chair Hayden Hape said this petition is important given the current climate.
"This petition is especially important as we have experienced continued attacks on Te Tiriti o Waitangi within government legislation, basically absolving the government of its responsibility to uphold Treaty precepts and principles."
Government response
In a statement, Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said the Government does not agree or accept its legislation is weakening Treaty obligations.
"Over the last 30 or 40 years, Parliament has made all sorts of references to the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. Sometimes it's 'honour', or 'have regard to', or 'give effect to', or 'take into account'.
"We need to create some consistency here, in the interests of increasing certainty and supporting compliance. A core foundation of our success as a nation is predictability in the law."
Barber said the horse trek will bring together tangata whenua, whānau, hapū, iwi and supporters from across the lower North Island in a highly visible journey to deliver a message that Te Tiriti o Waitangi must be protected.
The riders are expected to arrive in Wellington next Tuesday where the petition will be presented to Ikaroa-Rāwhiti MP Cushla Tangaere-Manuel at midday on the steps of Parliament, with the intention of presenting it to the House later that afternoon.

title: Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
content:
Photography as a Bridge to a Vanishing Time
Fukushima’s Old Farming Rituals Come to Life in Haga Hideo’s Photography
Guideto Japan
Lifestyle Culture- English
- 日本語
- 简体字
- 繁體字
- Français
- Español
- العربية
- Русский
Worshipping Tanokami: The Deity of Abundant Harvests
Before becoming a professional photographer, the pioneering folklore photographer Haga Hideo (1921–2022) worked as a translator at a news agency. That career came to an end in 1952 when the agency disbanded. For a change of scene, he headed to Fukushima Prefecture, where his father was from. While staying with relatives in what is now the city of Iwaki, he encountered a New Year ritual performed among farming families.
Prior to Japan’s rapid economic development in the years after World War II, folk beliefs in the tanokami rice deity were alive and well in many parts of the country. In Fukushima, the family patriarch and his eldest son would gather the straw from the rice harvested the previous fall to create a yorishiro, an object to beckon a deity, to welcome Shōgatsu-sama, the spirit thought to bring bountiful crops. In spring, this spirit would reappear in the rice paddies to make the rice ripen; it would then leave after the fall harvest, returning to the mountains where it dwelled.
The idea of an invisible deity responsible for the bounty of nature inspired Haga, who turned his camera lens to deity-welcoming ceremonies and their carefully crafted ritual implements and offerings. Casting a closer eye on this unadorned spiritual culture, he was reminded of marebito, the concept of a divine spirit visiting from the “other world” that he had learned about from the folklorist and ethnologist Orikuchi Shinobu (1887–1953) during his university studies.
Passing On the Traditions of Iwaki
In the foreword to Tanokami: Nihon no inasaku girei (Deity of the Rice Paddies: The Rice Cultivation Rituals of Japan), Haga’s first collection of photos taken in Iwaki, he explained why he had chosen to pursue this work there.
“For 2,000 years, the Japanese people have grown rice, around which the belief in tanokami and associated rituals has developed. Many Japanese customs and myths have been influenced by tanokami, providing insight into how rice cultivation rituals are reflected in daily life and social structures . . . Today, modern science has made good harvests possible without the intervention of tanokami. Progress in agricultural technology and the modernization of farm life are rapidly eroding traditional village society, in which religious beliefs, crop production, and entertainment were intertwined. This is a last opportunity to record the rituals associated with rice production for posterity.”
As Haga had foreseen, the rituals around rice growing were rapidly becoming simplified or had disappeared altogether. Meanwhile, the significance of rites centering around tanokami, such as Hiroshima Prefecture’s Mibu no Hana Taue and Ishikawa Prefecture’s Oku-Noto Aenokoto, has been recognized with their collective inscription by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Haga, who made recording folklore for posterity his lifework, passed away in 2022 at the age of 101.
Iwaki, where Haga got his start as a folklore photographer, is today on the verge of losing its traditional farming culture. The Iwaki City Museum of Folklore and Traditional Housing, which opened in 1999, is leading efforts to preserve what is left of those traditions. The museum collects and displays all manner of artifacts related to local life.
Five traditional thatched-roof houses, dismantled and transported from various parts of Iwaki, have been re-erected in the museum’s vast grounds. Meticulously preserved, they reproduce a premodern farm village. On display inside the houses are farming tools of the era; visitors can also try their hand at working in the fields and paddies outside. Iwaki schoolchildren visit here as part of their social studies lessons, and on weekends, adults can participate in workshops to learn about the local culture.
In the summer of 2026, Haga’s son Haga Hinata visited the folklore museum to donate 46 film rolls’ worth of digitalized photo data, to help teach local history. Sorting through the collection, the museum selected photos of folklore entertainment that had died out more than 30 years before, including them in a special exhibit during the summer.
According to curator Ōta Yūhi, “Photos depicting farming in Iwaki in the postwar years are very rare, and they are invaluable for scholarly research. For example, the folklorist Seki Keigo [1899–1990] remarked that he had understood narikizeme, the act of hitting a fruit tree with a knife to cast a spell to ensure a bountiful crop, from a written description, but that Haga’s photo was the first time he had actually seen the action performed.”
A special exhibit planned for the fall on the theme of “straw” features donated photos illustrating Shōgatsu-sama, torigoya, and other traditions. The photos will also be used for school lectures by outside speakers and are included in the Iwaki Digital Museum showcasing cultural resources. Haga says “I’m very happy that the folklore museum values local folklore and that I was able to entrust it with my father’s photos.”
Rich Folklore Traditions Live On
Haga also called on the Fukushima Museum in Aizu-Wakamatsu to donate the digitalized contents of 138 rolls of film containing photos taken throughout the prefecture. His father’s photos had been included in an exhibition that traveled to Beijing and Rome in 2012, the year after the Great East Japan Earthquake. Haga’s presentation took place on the occasion of the return of the exhibition to the Fukushima Museum.
At the ceremony, Ōsato Masaki, the museum’s curator in charge of folklore, displayed the actual ritual implements and crafts that the photos had recorded. He explained: “Along with actual physical examples, photos are vital for explaining traditional rituals. Haga Hideo’s photos, especially those in which he focused on capturing the essence of those rituals, are priceless.”
In addition, several film strips were digitalized in chronological order, giving a good idea of the sequence of events taking place. The 1960 photos showing festivities in the town of Miharu are particularly interesting.
One sequence shows the moment a bride enters the groom’s home, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion. According to Ōsato, “Haga must have negotiated beforehand with the family, since he took photos from inside the home.” He expressed surprise that the sequence of photos “shows the go-between and a female neighbor removing the bride’s umbrellalike wicker headgear and guests chanting the celebratory ‘Takasago’ song from the nō play of the same name. These are the kinds of photos depicting a ceremony that one might expect to see in school textbooks on folklore.”
Presenting the collection, Haga said, “Fukushima’s festivals are an important element in human relations. They haven’t really been in the public eye since the March 2011 earthquake, but I hope that these photos will make local people proud of their folk culture.”
A similar collection of digitalized photos, taken in the 1950s, was gifted to Kagoshima Prefecture’s Amami Ōshima in the summer of 2025; activities relating to the collection have been ongoing there. The Amami Museum held an exhibit commemorating the donation of the photos this summer and is also planning a traveling exhibition to other parts of Japan, starting with Kobe, targeting former residents of Okinoerabujima, one of the Amami islands. Perhaps a similar activity can be organized in Fukushima to communicate the local culture to younger generations.
(Originally published in Japanese. Reporting and text by Fujiwara Tomoyuki of Nippon.com. Banner image: A man carrying the straw bundles used in the Shōgatsu-sama New Year ritual, at left, and a man striking a fruit tree in the narikizeme rite. © Haga Hideo.)

title: 푸른 하늘의 날
content:
‘푸른 하늘의 날’은 유엔의 공식기념일 중에서 우리나라가 제안해 채택된 첫 번째 기념일이다.
2019년 8월 국가기후환경회의(위원장 반기문)의 국민참여단은 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’의 제정을 제시한 바 있으며, 이를 바탕으로 문재인 대통령은 2020년 9월 유엔 기후행동 정상회의에서 ‘세계 푸른 하늘의 날’을 국제사회에 제안했고, 이에 우리 정부가 결의안을 공식 제출했다.
같은 해 12월 제74차 유엔 총회에서 매년 9월 7일을 ‘푸른 하늘을 위한 국제 맑은 공기의 날(International Day of Clean Air for blue skies)’로 지정하는 결의안이 채택됐다.
이 결의안은 유엔 제2위원회(경제·개발·금융)에서 채택된 최초의 대기오염 관련 결의이기도 했다.
우리 정부는 지난 2020년 8월 18일부터 ‘각종 기념일 등에 관한 규정’을 개정해 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’을 국가기념일로 지정, 기념식과 함께 각종 기념행사를 진행한다.
유엔환경계획(UN Environment)이 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’ 기념일 준수를 촉구하는 역할을 담당하는 국제기구로 지정됐으며, 2020년 유엔환경계획(UNEP)에서 정한 제1회 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’ 주제는 “모두를 위한 맑은 공기(Clean Air for All)”다.
환경부와 외교부는 국가기후환경회의, 지자체 등과 함께 9월 7일 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’을 전후해 ‘푸른 하늘 주간’을 운영하고, 미세먼지 등 대기오염의 심각성과 그 영향에 대한 경각심을 일깨우는 다양한 행사를 선보인다.
유엔기구에서도 9월 7일과 8일 사이 다양한 기념행사가 개최된다.
미국 뉴욕 유엔본부에서는 사티아 트리파시 유엔환경계획 사무차장 주재로 기념식이 열리고, 케냐 나이로비 유엔환경계획 본부에서는 잉거 앤더슨 유엔환경계획 사무총장 주재로 고위급회의가 열린다.
한편 2026년 개최되는 제7회 ‘푸른 하늘의 날’ 주제는 ‘기후와 맑은 공기를 위한 행동(Action for Climate and Clean Air)’ 이다.

title: De oceaan is geen scheiding maar een brug op het literaire festival Read My World
content:
De oceaan is geen scheiding maar een brug op het literaire festival Read My World
Geeft een relevant perspectief ter verduidelijking. Beweringen worden geredigeerd voor leesbaarheid en evidente onjuistheden
Literair festival Dichter Theoresia Rumthe en mensenrechtenactivist Defe Wabiser willen via verhalen uit West-Papoea en de Molukken bruggen slaan met ‘broeders en zusters’ in Nederland.
Het zal 2017 zijn geweest, rekenen ze terug. Toen troffen Theoresia Rumthe en Defe Wabiser elkaar toevallig in een bibliotheek annex boekwinkel in Bandung, West-Java. „Soms heb je van die mensen waarvan je voelt dat ze later nog eens je pad zullen kruisen”, zegt Wabiser over de ontmoeting. En zo geschiedde. Bijna tien jaar later werken de twee vrouwen uit het oosten van Indonesië – Rumthe van Maluku (de Molukken) en Wabiser van West-Papoea – samen aan het literaire festival Read My World, dat vanaf donderdag in Amsterdam plaatsvindt.
Rumthe is dichter en leidt een literair platform. Wabiser zet zich als activist in voor bescherming van het leefgebied van inheemse volken. Read My World focust dit jaar op de Molukken en West-Papoea en naast gasten uit beide delen van Indonesië zijn ook schrijvers en kunstenaars uit de Molukse en Papoeaanse diaspora en van daarbuiten uitgenodigd. Het festival beoogt met verhalen, gedichten en andere kunst en cultuur een brede uitwisseling tussen de beide volkeren, hun diaspora en andere geïnteresseerden te bevorderen.
Gedeelde geschiedenis
In ‘Oceanic Solidarity’ vonden Rumthe en Wabiser een overkoepelend thema, vertellen de co-curatoren in een videogesprek. „De oceaan is de plek waarover vanaf 1951 zo’n 12.500 Molukse KNIL-soldaten en familieleden uit de Molukken en andere delen van Indonesië met hun gezinnen naar Nederland werden gebracht”, zegt Rumthe. Het Koninklijk Nederlandsch-Indisch Leger (KNIL) bestond uit Nederlandse en inheemse militairen en vocht om koloniale belangen te beschermen. „De zee werd zo een brug, een plek die onze geschiedenis draagt. De zwart-wit foto’s van die reis laten ons die geschiedenis steeds opnieuw beleven.” De dichter ziet de oceaan door die gedeelde geschiedenis niet als „iets dat ons scheidt, maar juist als iets dat ons verbindt.”
„Voor mij is de oceaan een universum dat we delen”, zegt Rumthe. „De oceaan is niet alleen een fysiek gegeven, maar staat ook voor kennis; het staat voor een thuis, een cultuur, maar ook migratie, geschiedenis en diaspora.” Onder jonge kunstenaars in Indonesië bestaat een sterke wens om verbonden te zijn met „de broeders en zusters in Nederland”, merkte Rumthe eerder bij een literair festival dat ze op Ambon organiseert.
Het is niet alleen de verbinding met de voormalige kolonisator en de Molukse en Papoeaanse diaspora (die begin jaren zestig in Nederland arriveerde nadat Nederland Nieuw-Guinea als kolonie had opgegeven) die inmiddels in Nederland leeft, ook gemeenschappen in Indonesië zijn onderling altijd met elkaar verbonden door het water. „In onze cultuur is de oceaan vanzelfsprekend gemeenschappelijk”, zegt Rumthe. „Bij de oceaan zijn mensen nooit alleen. Ze leven er samen, ze vissen er samen. Ze helpen elkaar.”
Gemeenschappelijke vijand: de VOC
Verbindingen tussen de Molukken en Papoea bestaan ook dankzij het water en gaan ver terug, weet Wabiser. „Onze voorouders stonden begin 1600 voor een gemeenschappelijke vijand, die heette de VOC.” De Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, de handelsonderneming die in de 17de en 18de eeuw met grootschalig geweld onder meer grondstoffen en specerijen uit Azië haalde en verhandelde, kwam niet naar Papoea maar wel naar de Molukken. Deze twee gebieden dreven handel met elkaar. „Maar de VOC probeerde dat bestaande handelssysteem te vernietigen en conflict te creëren tussen de koningen van Maluku en mijn voorouders in West-Papoea”, vertelt Wabiser.
Ook vandaag de dag zijn er gemeenschappelijke vijanden die de bevolking van Papoea en de Molukken bedreigen, ziet Wabiser in haar werk. Het wordt inheemse gemeenschappen heel moeilijk gemaakt om hun mensenrechten op te eisen. „Tegelijkertijd geeft de Indonesische regering juist heel makkelijk concessies af voor palmolieplantages in de gebieden waar zij leven.” Ze bouwen die op moerassig gebied en hebben dus materialen nodig om wegen aan te leggen. En die zijn niet voorhanden in Papoea dus die halen ze van de Kai-eilanden, waar kakak [oudere zus] Theoresia’s familie vandaan komt.”
Vrijheden onder druk
Indonesië bevindt zich op een moeilijk moment, vertellen Rumthe en Wabiser. Hun (t)huis wordt op allerlei manieren bedreigd. Vrijheid van meningsuiting en andere vrijheden staan onder druk en net als in Europa brandden de afgelopen maanden ook in Indonesië talloze hectaren natuurgebied af. Dat komt naast klimaatverandering door de activiteiten van de Indonesische staat en diens zakenpartners, die natuurgebieden openstellen voor palmolie- en suikerrietplantages en mijnbouw. Plantages zijn extra vatbaar voor brand en zodra concessies aan bedrijven zijn afgegeven is onduidelijk bij wie de brandpreventieverantwoordelijkheid ligt.
Wabiser hoopt dat ze kunnen bouwen op de samenwerking van hun voorvaderen uit de tijd van de VOC, want de strijd tegen de verwoesting van een leefgebied is al eens eerder gevoerd. „Wat in West-Papoea gebeurt, gebeurt ook in andere delen van Indonesië. Omdat de vrijheid van meningsuiting beperkt is, is het veiliger om via kunst ons thuis en onze cultuur te beschermen.” Zo nodigde Wabiser Samuel Yohanes Glenn M uit, een kunstenaar die met natuurgeluiden en het verzamelen van Papoeaanse culturele objecten zijn cultuur levend wil houden en er opnieuw betekenis aan wil geven.
Tijdens Read My World wil Wabiser nieuwe verbonden smeden met de Papoeaanse diaspora en andere geïnteresseerden, „vrienden die dezelfde waarden en principes hebben om ons thuis te beschermen en die dat ook via kunst doen.”

title: Suspension
content:
Article begins
We started the Rowasu’u collaborative digital archive—a project that returns decades of anthropological research materials to the communities they document in Central Brazil—in 2023. Our A’uwẽ (Xavante, Indigenous) collaborators are used to projects that are proposed but never started, launched but fizzle as institutional priorities shift, or take years for regulatory approval. The leaders of the six participating A’uwẽ communities are experts in the landscapes of government projects, NGO initiatives, and the fickle interests of Brazilian and foreign researchers. Experience with waiting, however, has not made the NSF’s April 2025 cancellation of our three-year collaborative research award any less difficult (or detrimental) for them, us, or the project. The defunding of Rowasu’u awakened a familiar and strange temporality: suspension.
For us, the non-A’uwẽ project team members, waiting is familiar, but the starkness of our defunding was a shock that ushered in an unsettling phase of uncertainty. At a time when austerity and precarity are reconfiguring careers and research, suspension entails contradictory, confusing, and at times unexpected affective challenges. The cancellation means loss of focus and momentum. Moreover, with each passing day, delays mean the very real risk that another elder knowledge-holder may pass, together with the wisdom that community researchers seek to protect and strengthen.
We had already had a long wait to begin. A year of regulatory delays followed five years of consultation and two years of grant writing during the pandemic. We finally launched Rowasu’u in July 2023. Our opening event made the wait worthwhile (figures 1 and 2). As we shared slideshows of photos from the 1970s, it immediately became clear that the digitized materials offered a forum for young A’uwẽ researchers to engage their Elders with curiosity. We explored how the Mukurtu platform would allow them to enrich historical photographs, audio recordings, and researchers’ publications with contemporary A’uwẽ perspectives. Members of the A’uwẽ Oversight Committee extolled the potential Elders saw in this repository of history and traditional knowledge: it would be a resource for future generations and cultural continuity. We and they were ecstatic with the communities’ engagement; our first days were marked by discussions of photographs of ceremonies that had not been practiced for decades and conversations about what kinds of materials might support the enduring fight to protect land and livelihoods.
With the NSF funding, we introduced a prototype of the archive and began training the twenty A’uwẽ researchers who were nominated by their communities (figures 3 and 4). They learned to use digital technologies for recording and archiving elders’ narratives. The communities formed an oversight committee consisting of elders and leaders who provide guidance and decision-making authority over the archive structure, contents, and community participation. Over five periods of fieldwork, we prioritized digital literacy and the work of building a slow archive together.
When we received the cancellation on April 18, 2025, it shocked us, even if we ought to have seen it coming as DOGE publicly set its sights on cancelling projects that used language related to social justice and race. Abruptly, with one of us in the middle of an archival research trip, our plans and ability to follow through on our commitments were thrown into question. We were forced to call off upcoming fieldwork, frustrated by processes related to federal terminations, and forced to notify our A’uwẽ team members that expected salaries would not arrive. Incredulity, disappointment, and anger commingled with a sensation of mid-air pause. For all the momentum that we had finally built, would the communities trust us to continue to steward the project and the collections through a period of suspension? Would our conviction about the necessity and urgency of the work manifest in new funding, and on what timescale? It became challenging to bring the future of the project back into focus.
Community members’ and leaders’ responses to the defunding have been multiple and heterogeneous. Despite our best efforts to convey our continued dedication, many are confused about the project’s future. Some interpret the sudden change as “business as usual” for any project with warazu (non-A’uwẽ). Others accept the suspension with resignation. They see the disappearance of funding as yet another inevitable delay associated with collaboration. For many A’uwẽ project members, the funding cut has been hard to disentangle from the idea that the project itself had been called off. Although we had really just begun to implement a vision of a long-term ongoing collaboration, years in the making, some A’uwẽ have interpreted the unfunded interlude as the project’s end. One leader even asked us to return to T.I. Pimentel Barbosa to hold a project “closing ceremony.” The project was something to commemorate with celebration, even if its successes barely scratched the surface of its potential.
The cancellation unsettled carefully negotiated relationships of trust and obligation along well-worn paths. Our fight now is to ensure that Rowasu’u does not join the ranks of other abandoned, sometimes-damaging projects that A’uwẽ are familiar with. One community still hosts a cement building, the remnants of a planned documentation center that was built but never finished. A lawsuit against the construction company may or may not still be languishing, but the publicly funded museum behind the project has moved on and reallocated funds following a change in federal administration. Development projects have promised profit and food security, only to leave similarly transformed landscapes and diets in ruination. We worry that the rapid, unanticipated funding interruption may put us into the undesirable category of those deemed “untrustworthy.” These are often outsiders who arrived in communities unbidden, full of good intentions but replete with unrealistic promises and expectations. (Is that us too, now?)
On April 12, 2026 almost one year after the defunding of our work, Angélica Wautõmõ’uptabi’õ Xavante passed to the realm of the ancestors (figure 5). Far too young, only 58 years old, she was mother and aunt to two of our researchers. She joined a number of other elders who have passed since the project began. In the community of Sõrepré Angélica was one of the people who had recorded the most memories and reflections during the funded portion of the project. She spoke of traditional foods, women’s labor of cotton spinning, and ceremonial life. Angélica led project researchers to document collecting practices for edible tubers of the cerrado (Brazilian savanna). She took with her to the next world a lifetime of wisdom and embodied skill. While recordings of Angélica’s voice are precious supplements to our rich memories of her, they are also reminders of what else might have been had we been able to follow the momentum of our work. The sensation of suspension is of pause, of interruption, of uncertainty and frustration, but it is also one of profound loss.

title: [Magazine] En Turquie, le dernier gardien d’un royaume disparu
content:
Âgé de 86 ans, Mehmet Kusman a passé la majorité de sa vie à préserver un souvenir vieux de près de 3 000 ans : celui du royaume d’Urartu et de sa culture. Autodidacte total, il a consacré plus de vingt ans à déchiffrer sa langue et continue de veiller sur l’héritage du royaume.
L’index pointé, il glisse sur les inscriptions martelées dans le basalte noir et lit d’une voix rauque : «Avant moi, il n’y avait rien. Mais par la puissance du dieu Haldi j’ai fondé cette ville.» Mehmet Kusman, 86 ans, a dédié sa vie à la forteresse de Cavuştepe, dans l’est de la Turquie, et à l’apprentissage de la langue d’Urartu, qui emprunte son alphabet cunéiforme à l’assyrien, pour célébrer les dieux et les souverains du royaume disparu. Le pas vif et l’esprit alerte malgré les ans, et le vent brûlant qui fouette les herbes sèches autour des fondations du temple dédié au dieu des dieux, Haldi, il a coiffé son visage tanné d’une casquette acquise à Los Angeles : «USA 2009», a-t-il tracé au feutre noir en cunéiforme.
Engagé comme manœuvre sur les fouilles archéologiques de Cavuştepe après son service militaire dans les années soixante, Mehmet Kusman tombe sur une première stèle, raconte-t-il. «L’inscription était très belle.» Le chef du chantier le dissuade néanmoins d’apprendre cette écriture «très difficile». «Qu’il me dise non m’a blessé. Je me suis acharné en pensant : de mon vivant, j’apprendrai», raconte-t-il.
Dès lors, Mehmet Kusman, malgré son manque de formation, relève les inscriptions sur les fouilles conduites dans l’est de la Turquie, mais aussi en Iran et en Arménie, sur lesquels s’étendait le royaume d’Urartu. En trois ans, affirme-t-il, il maîtrise l’alphabet. Mais «il m’a fallu 22 ans pour maîtriser 650 mots» de vocabulaire. Les universitaires saluent l’enthousiasme et le dévouement de Mehmet Kusman, comme une sorte de curiosité locale.
L’octogénaire se targue d’être «l’un des sept derniers en Turquie à parler la langue d’Urartu», «l’un des États les plus puissants du Proche-Orient ancien, entre les IXe et VIIe siècle av. J.-C.», souligne Erkan Konyar, professeur d’histoire ancienne à l’université d’Istanbul. Plus récent que les grands royaumes mésopotamiens d’Assur, Sumer et Babylone, Urartu a su fédérer les communautés tribales des montagnes autour d’un État centralisé, bâtissant des forteresses, des capitales provinciales, des réseaux d’irrigation et de vastes capacités de stockage au service d’une économie agricole, détaille-t-il.
«Mehmet Kusman a consacré sa vie à Cavuştepe et, malgré sa retraite en 2005, il continue de veiller sur elle. Pendant soixante ans, il a vécu au milieu des fouilles et enseigné à des milliers de visiteurs à l’histoire d’Urartu», souligne le Dr Konyar, spécialiste de la capitale fondatrice du royaume, Tuspa, dans l’actuelle forteresse de Van. Mais l’expert tient à nuancer le terme de «langue», car les historiens manquent d’indications sur sa prononciation.
Je suis le descendant des Urartéens. Ils ont disparu, mais ils ne sont pas tous morts
«Les inscriptions disponibles permettent de la comprendre jusqu’à un certain point, mais il nous manque du vocabulaire et des textes. Seul le sens de certains mots est connu avec certitude. Aussi, personne ne peut dire qu’il parle l’urartéen», explique-t-il. Alors, que dire des syllabes traînantes égrainées avec conviction par l’autodidacte Mehmet Kusman : «Shi Ni E Ni Ye Su Si Si….». Par sa passion, le vieux gardien est devenu une célébrité locale qui s’est rendu pour des conférences «en Amérique, cinq fois, en Allemagne, aux Pays-Bas, en Belgique», énumère-t-il, un rien cabot, disant envisager «d’aller au Japon».
«Malheureusement, très peu de personnes en Turquie savent lire et analyser les inscriptions», relève Mehmet Isikli, directeur du département d’archéologie du Proche-Orient à l’université d’Ankara. «Même à l’époque d’Urartu, les gens ne parlaient pas cette langue : elle était seulement écrite», abonde-t-il.
À 35 km au nord de Van, avec une vue plongeante sur le lac, le Pr Isikli poursuit les fouilles de la forteresse d’Ayanis, la dernière des grandes forteresses avant l’effondrement du royaume. «Nos fouilles nous renseigneront peut-être sur la fin d’Urartu», avance-t-il, en mentionnant «les traces d’un très puissant tremblement de terre». «La première inscription qui atteste de la fondation du royaume d’Urartu, en assyrien, a été découverte à Tuspa, sur la forteresse de Van. Cavuştepe est venue bien après», explique-t-il.
«Mehmet Kusman assure une sorte de publicité pour Urartu, mais rien à voir avec un travail universitaire : il connaît seulement quelques signes alphabétiques, ou quelques lettres, et des informations très, très générales à leur sujet», estime le Pr Isikli. «Je l’admire», assure-t-il néanmoins. «Il a travaillé dur et mis en lumière la culture d’Urartu.»
Dans sa petite cabane de pierres à l’entrée du site de Cavuştepe, Mehmet Kusman n’en démord pas. «Je suis le descendant des Urartéens, leur petit-fils. Ils ont disparu, mais voyez : ils ne sont pas tous morts», clame-t-il crânement, se levant pour accueillir des visiteurs.

title: Veterans who died by suicide honoured at memorial
content:
Veterans who died by suicide honoured at memorial
- Published
Hundreds of people have gathered at the National Memorial Arboretum for the dedication of a permanent tribute to veterans and armed forces personnel who have died by suicide.
The Elysium Memorial, at the site in Elrewas, Staffordshire, is the first permanent memorial of its kind to be built in the UK.
More than 1,300 military veterans and personnel have taken their lives in the last 30 years, with the memorial aiming to provide a place for contemplation for those affected by the loss of a friend or loved one.
Edward Mackenzie, co-founder of the Elysium Memorial Foundation, which is behind the project, said he was "blown away" by the number of people that had turned up.
More than 300 motorcyclist rode to the arboretum from Burton-on-Trent on Sunday, with a convoy organised by community organisation Wheels for Wishes.
Mackenzie, who served in the army for more than 30 years and has lost over to 20 friends to suicide, including his best friend, said seeing those veterans' being recognised "means everything".
"This is why I did it, I did for for the friends, the families, the comrades, those that we've lost to suicide," he told the BBC.
"There's a lot of families here today that have been thanking me for achieving this memorial so I'm incredibly grateful."
There were 277 cases of veterans taking their own lives between 2006 and 2025, according to the Ministry of Defence.
"Any death by suicide is a tragedy that is felt across our community, and our thoughts are with those who have been impacted by the loss of a loved one," a spokesperson said.
"The welfare of our armed forces is at the heart of everything we do - more than £25m invested into Op Courage in the last year and our £50m Valour programme gives veterans in England access to specialist NHS mental health services and access to essential care, continuing our steadfast commitment to provide our forces and their families the wellbeing support they deserve."
Following the ceremony, people at the arboretum were invited to lay their own wreaths at the memorial.
Mackenzie said he was "very emotional" about the size of the turnout.
"I'm lost for words a lot of the time and I hope that this memorial will really help towards the mental health and families and basically taking the word suicide out of the shadows," he explained.
"I think that we still have amazing work to do to try and help everyone."

title: ‘The drought has left its mark’: Slovenia’s potato lovers lament low yields
content:
‘The drought has left its mark’: Slovenia’s potato lovers lament low yields
Hundreds gather to share roast potatoes in northern Slovenia as think tank warns ‘chips are down’ across Europe.
Prekmurje, Slovenia – Lipovci, a village of about 1,000 residents in the flatlands of northeastern Slovenia, transformed into a hub celebrating a beloved national dish.
The air carried a sweet, juicy aroma as it hosted the 26th international festival of roasted potatoes.

- list 4 of 4‘Poor bear the impact’: Sugar prices soar in India, souring festive season
Hundreds of people and more than 50 societies were united – farmers and avid potato eaters from across the country, roasting their own versions of this national dish one September morning.
“I’m a potato guy, through and through,” Matjaz Lavric, from the capital, Ljubljana, who has attended the festival for the past 15 years, told Al Jazeera. “Life just isn’t the same without them … When I’m home, potatoes are always on the menu.”
His recipe’s key ingredient is tarragon. “I’d happily eat them as a main course.”
But local potatoes are getting harder to come by.
Estimates by the Chamber of Agriculture and Forestry of Slovenia suggest a loss of between 30 and 90 percent for this year’s potato harvest – the yield having been hit by Europe’s severe droughts.
In 2025, Slovenia produced only about a third of its total potato consumption, a rate that keeps dropping due to other factors including higher fertiliser prices, restrictions on pesticide use and low purchase prices.
Janez Jambrosic, a small farmer from the southern town of Velike Lasce, lost half of his potato harvest this year.
“The drought has left its mark,” he said.
He makes a lighter version of the dish, using vegetable oil instead of pork fat.
Lavric, whose potatoes were dug up from a friend’s farm, said this year’s lot was smaller.
“It took us much longer to peel them,” he said.
Others said the drought also hit their corn yields, used for feedstock, and in some cases wiped them out almost entirely, as well as their wine-making grapes.
“The harvest was maybe a bit worse than in other years,” said Marija Bev from Dobrna in the country’s east.
The drought was most severe in the first half of August. As temperatures soared, the weather hit later potato varieties hardest.
Bev grows potatoes for her family’s needs, and dug hers up at the end of July.
“They’d already survived the worst of the drought by the time we put them in the cellar,” she added.
‘The chips are well and truly down’
The shortages extend far beyond Slovenia.
Analysis released on Thursday by the United Kingdom-based nonprofit Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) suggests that the summer drought is likely to knock about 3.1 million tonnes off the potato harvest in some of the world’s largest exporters, such as Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands.
“For potato growers on the front line of climate change, the chips are well and truly down,” said the think tank’s food and farming analyst Tom Lancaster.
“As we move into autumn, the impact of the record-breaking summer heat and drought on food and farming becomes clear … As one of Europe’s thirstiest crops, it was inevitable that the potato harvest would be hit hard, and we are starting to see that now in industry yield estimates, down 20 percent in some cases.”
Slovenia’s sector is characterised by small farms that families operate part-time, often passed down through generations.
In 1767, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, who ruled the region at the time, issued a decree on the planting and cultivation of potatoes, a measure farmers initially resisted because they grew potatoes only to feed their livestock.
Now the potato has become so ingrained in local culture that there is even a Slovenian saying: Telling someone they “have potatoes” means they’re lucky.
Petra Molek, from Carinthia, presented two versions of the roasted potatoes alongside other women farmers from her village. One was roasted in pork fat, the other in sausage fat.
“The potatoes we used were dug up two days ago, from her field,” she said, pointing to one of her colleagues. She feels fortunate as the potatoes were good growers, despite the conditions.
“It depends a lot on the type of potato and the location of the field,” she explained.
Marija Kovac, also from Carinthia, said roasted potatoes are a regular feature of the daily menu at home.
“On our farm, we always have roasted potatoes, any day of the week,” she said, handing out paper plates to offer a tasting of their version of the dish.
The gathering, which started as a tongue-in-cheek event in the early 2000s, is held every year in a different location across Slovenia.
Its founders run a society with a mission: To elevate roasted potatoes from their usual side-dish status to a main dish.
The group’s emblem features the potato bug, the growers’ biggest “frenemy” – a killer but also, like the organisers, a potato lover. At one point, attendees sang a hymn praising the national dish. Debates on the taste of the dish buzzed around the stands, alongside the sounds of the accordion.
“We all pretty much know how to make roasted potatoes,” said Bev. “But the main point is to have fun.”

title: Daughter brings her father’s cendol legacy home
content:
Old telephones, lamps and a retro radio fill its interior, while diners enjoy bowls of cendol and ABC outside beneath the raised house.
This is Warung Cendol Wak Paad, now run by second-generation owner Siti Zulaika Supaad, who’s keeping her family’s legacy alive.
Her father, Supaad Musran, began selling cendol in 1990, raising Zulaika and her six siblings with the income he earned. As each child grew older, they took turns minding the stall whenever their parents needed a break.
“I started helping out at the stall when I was in Standard Six and enjoyed it,” Zulaika told FMT Lifestyle.
Those hours nurtured her love for her father’s business and sparked her entrepreneurial spirit. She later sold cendol during school Canteen Days and at university.
The stall closed in 2004 when Supaad fell ill. Two of Zulaika’s sisters later sold cendol, but neither venture lasted. Still, the story of the family’s cendol business had another chapter waiting to be written.
Zulaika graduated in heritage studies during the pandemic, but struggled to find work and contemplated starting a business.
“I thought about my family’s business and asked my father whether he still remembered the cendol recipe,” recalled Zulaika, 29.
He did, and he encouraged her to go ahead, especially since former customers wanted him to revive the business. Some had enjoyed his cendol as schoolchildren and longed to taste it again.
In June 2021, Zulaika began selling cendol near her father’s former stall. His business never had a name, so she called hers “Warung Cendol Wak Paad” in his honour.
Zulaika, who is of Javanese heritage, explained that “Wak” means “uncle” in Javanese, while “Paad” is the name by which her father is affectionately known.
Zulaika stayed true to Supaad’s cendol and ABC recipes. Nothing pleased her more than hearing long-time customers say her cendol tastes just like her father’s.
As the business grew, Zulaika saw potential in the family’s old home, which was largely unused. Remembering how alive it once was, especially during Hari Raya, she longed to fill it with warmth again.
Some customers warned the house’s quiet location near a dead end would hurt the business – but Zulaika trusted her instincts.
After renovating the place, she opened in October 2021 and expanded the menu.
To create a nostalgic atmosphere, she travelled to Indonesia and Egypt for retro décor items. Others in the house are cherished family keepsakes – her father’s old ice shaver, her mother’s trays and a wooden bench that belonged to her late grandfather, Musran Surajak.
Fun fact: Zulaika’s roots in the area run deep: Musran established the street where her father first sold cendol and where her business now stands.
Indeed, the cendol does not disappoint, combining fresh santan with green cendol as well as palm sugar syrup and red beans prepared in-house. You can also opt for cendol with corn or glutinous rice.
For something richer, the decadent ABC Coklat comes crowned with roasted peanuts and chocolate sauce, while the creamy Jelly Cocktail Susu brims with a variety of fruits.
Savoury favourites include nasi lemak with fried chicken and house-made sambal as well as Penang laksa. The mee bandung is equally satisfying, with prawns, egg and more in a gravy.
Lighter bites include fruit rojak, a traditional Malay pancake called lempeng and crispy tempeh served with sambal kicap, a spicy soy dipping sauce.
Today, word has spread beyond Klang, drawing visitors from Kelantan and Johor. Even Singaporeans and Koreans have stopped by.
“I’m proud and happy that I am able to keep my family’s legacy alive,” she said.
“I hope customers will enjoy the cendol and the atmosphere I have created – as though they’re enjoying a bowl of cendol in a kampung or in their grandmother’s home,” she concluded.

title: Mónica Ramírez Is Teaching Migrant Women How to Organize
content:
Growing up around the rows of corn and soybeans in Fremont, Ohio, Mónica Ramírez spent her earliest days being looked after by her maternal bisabuela, or great-grandmother, Virginia Guardiola. From her home in town, Guardiola served as an informal, one-woman welcome committee for farmworkers who arrived in Fremont, disoriented and alone. Guardiola would tell these newcomers where to find jobs and fill them in on what they needed to know about Ohio.
From her great-grandmother, Ramírez says she learned “the importance of having information to share, so that people could actually get jobs—and get safe.” Ramírez saw the vulnerability of those who followed the harvest to a place like Fremont. Many were women living far from their families, who often worked without legal status, which made it risky for them to speak out against exploitative foremen in the fields or predators in the worker barracks. It mattered, she says, for them to have “trusted community members.”
Some 40 years later, Ramírez is an internationally recognized attorney and feminist, with degrees from Ohio State and Harvard. The founder of the advocacy group Justice for Migrant Women, Ramírez has made powerful allies, including celebrities like Eva Longoria and America Ferrera; she was Laura Dern’s guest at the Oscars in 2018. Yet to this day, she still lives within miles of the agricultural fields in Fremont.
When Ramírez founded Justice for Migrant Women in 2014, she’d spent a decade as an attorney helping farmworkers fight for their rights in court. But Justice for Migrant Women is not a legal aid clinic. Instead, it performs the service Ramírez saw her bisabuela perform in Fremont: it provides information. Ramírez helps workers access the knowledge they need to organize and fight for their own rights.
She sees herself more as a neighbor than a charity giver, and the neighborliness goes both ways. One of the women who most inspired Ramírez was a farmworker named Bernice, who had been sexually victimized in a labor camp and later evicted. Homeless and injured, Bernice decided to return to her home county rather than file a criminal complaint, despite Ramírez’s offer to fight for her. In all their calls, Bernice always began conversations by asking Ramírez the same question: “Are you happy?” For Ramírez, it was a model. Today, she says she starts every new conversation by considering the dignity of the person she is speaking with, taking account of the fullness of their life.
Ramírez sees a role her organization can play in the twists and turns of politics and culture, working to ensure that Justice for Migrant Women is there for people who need support as the political landscape shifts and new challenges arise. In 2017, as the Me Too movement took off, Ramírez helped write the “Dear Sisters” letter, which ran in TIME under the headline “700,000 Female Farmworkers Say They Stand With Hollywood Actors Against Sexual Assault.” It read, in part: “Even though we work in very different environments, we share a common experience of being preyed upon by individuals who have the power to hire, fire, and blacklist.” And amid the Trump Administration’s mass deportation campaign, as some farmworkers feel they have to choose between enduring sexual abuse in silence or coming forward and risking the trauma of detention and family separation, Ramírez is working in community meetings and trainings to help them understand their rights.
One of Ramírez’s projects, the “Humans Who Feed Us” dinner series, brings people together and highlights the interdependence of our broader communities. In Ohio and around the country, she sets large tables for farmworkers, line cooks, delivery drivers—immigrant workers who support the nation’s food system—and then invites business leaders and other community members to join them.
“We’re too far apart, and I think that that space between us is what’s leading to hate and misunderstanding,” Ramírez says. She sets the table the way her great-grandmother would for any newcomer in town. “Back in the day,” she says, “people relied on their neighbors.”

title: Conservation’s Blind Spot: Why Language Matters for Biodiversity
content:
To many visitors a mangrove forest appears as a stretch of trees standing between land and sea. But if you walk through the same forest with a local fisher returning with the tide, a honey collector searching for wild hives, or a boatman who has spent a lifetime navigating its creeks, another landscape comes into view. What seems to be a single landscape is understood as many. Diverse names distinguish places where fish breed, honey is gathered, storm surges lose their force, or tides behave differently.
Across the eastern and western seaboards in India, coastal communities have developed distinct names for tidal forests that reflect ecological function as much as geography. In Bengal, Sundarban evokes a forest historically associated with the sundari tree and its life-sustaining tidal ecology. Along the Godavari–Krishna delta, the Telugu expression mada vanalu refers to brackish tidal forests that nurture fisheries and soften the impact of cyclones. Tamil and Malayali people use terms built around kandal to distinguish salt-tolerant coastal habitats, while related expressions across the Konkan and Gujarat coast identify creek-edge forests, honey-collecting areas, and other ecosystems.
These names are far more than local expressions. They reflect generations of close observation about how the forest functions and how people have learned to live with it.
Much of this vocabulary is quietly disappearing. In administration, education, and even conservation practice, diverse coastal landscapes are increasingly gathered under a single term, mangroves. The forest remains, but the distinctions that once helped people recognize its ecological diversity begin to fade.
Conservation has become notably good at measuring environmental change. Forest cover, species recovery, and habitat loss are monitored with increasing precision. Still, an irony remains. Even as technologies sharpen the view of nature, the ecological languages through which Indigenous peoples have long interpreted these ecosystems and processes are becoming less visible.
Before ecosystems disappear, the ability to read them often begins to erode.
Conservation routinely monitors species richness and habitat extent but rarely asks whether the vocabulary needed to recognize those habitats is itself surviving. That is conservation’s overlooked blind spot. Protecting biodiversity is not only about safeguarding species and habitats; it also requires sustaining the languages that enable people to understand the many distinctions within an ecosystem in the first place. Conservation cannot fully succeed while the ecological languages that make landscapes intelligible continue to disappear.
When Conservation Loses Resolution
Ecologists classify habitats by their vegetation, hydrology, and species, while people who have lived in these landscapes for generations have long relied on another system of classification — language. Their vocabularies did not evolve to describe nature in the abstract. They emerged from everyday interactions. In tidal forests people learn to distinguish places shaped by tides, soils, fisheries, storms, and seasons, allow them to understand differences that matter.
The problem arises when these locally evolved classifications are absorbed into broader, standardized terminology. A common vocabulary undoubtedly makes administration, education, and scientific communication easier. Yet it also carries an unintended consequence: Ecosystems begin to appear simpler than they really are.
India’s mangrove coast illustrates this shift.
These are not simply regional names but ecolexicons that condense generations of environmental observation into everyday language.
As this mosaic of ecological vocabularies gives way to the single label mangroves, something more than linguistic diversity is lost. It’s like reducing the resolution of a satellite image: The coastline remains visible, but its finer ecological distinctions begin to disappear.
This process may be understood as linguistic flattening — not merely a dilution of linguistic richness and a loss of words, but also the gradual loss of ecological resolution. Long before a language falls silent, it can lose the nuances that once helped people read landscapes.
Language as Conservation Infrastructure
Linguistic flattening also weakens the systems that have long governed how people interact with ecosystems.
Language is often treated as a medium of communication, yet in many Indigenous societies it functions as something more fundamental. It carries practical rules, ethical obligations, and ecological boundaries that are learned not from policy manuals but through everyday speech, stories, and customary practice. In this sense, language is part of conservation infrastructure.
The Māori understanding of harakeke (New Zealand flax) offers a striking example. The central shoot, or rito, represents the child, while the surrounding leaves symbolize parents and grandparents. This is more than a metaphor. The vocabulary itself shapes harvesting practices: Inner shoots are never cut, because removing them threatens the life of the plant. Only the outer leaves are taken, allowing regeneration to continue. Even the flowering stalks (kōrari) are managed with care so that nectar remains available for native birds, supporting pollination and the wider ecosystem.
This appears to be a biocultural expression but in practice is a sophisticated system for managing relationships between people and nature. The language does not simply describe ecological relationships; it instructs people how to behave within them.
Similar patterns are found across Indigenous societies, where names, stories, and customary expressions regulate seasonal harvesting, identify sensitive habitats, and define responsibilities towards land and water.
Conservation recognizes the value of Indigenous knowledge, yet it often overlooks the languages through which that knowledge is organized, remembered, and transmitted. Protecting place-based knowledge while allowing the languages that sustain it to disappear is rather like preserving a library after removing its catalogue. The books may still exist, but their meaning becomes increasingly difficult to recover.
Vanishing Languages, Vanishing Environmental Archives
Modern conservation depends heavily on data. Satellite imagery tracks forest loss, climate models project future change, and ecological surveys measure species abundance with precision. Yet most of these records span only a few decades. They rarely capture and interpret the much longer histories through which communities have understood environmental changes.
That longer record often survives in language. Across Indigenous societies, names for plants, animals, winds, tides, and seasons are not arbitrary labels but accumulated observations refined over generations. They preserve knowledge of when rivers shift their course, when particular fish arrive, how flowering responds to rainfall, which plants indicate groundwater, or where storms repeatedly reshape the coast. Much of this information was never written down because it did not need to be. It remained alive in speech, memory, and everyday practice.
When a language slips away, the environmental archive becomes fragmented, and we lose part of nature’s archive. Individual observations may still be recorded by researchers, but the wider system that connected them — linking species, habitats, seasons, and human experience — is gradually lost.
Conservation then faces an unusual paradox. We invest heavily in collecting new ecological data while allowing centuries of carefully accumulated environmental knowledge to disappear unnoticed.
Seen in this light, language loss is not simply a cultural concern. It also represents the quiet erosion of one of conservation’s oldest and least recognized ways of understanding nature. Protecting biodiversity therefore also means sustaining the living archives that have preserved ecological memory across generations.
Conservation Literacy Beyond Species Lists
Conservation governance has made important progress globally in recognizing Indigenous peoples as partners in biodiversity protection. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework calls for respecting and applying traditional knowledge in biodiversity governance, while IPBES has repeatedly shown that indigenous and local knowledge strengthens conservation outcomes. Likewise, UNESCO’s International Decade of Indigenous Languages (2022–2032) emphasizes that these languages sustain knowledge systems shaped through long relationships with place.
Yet an important gap remains. Conservation frameworks celebrate traditional knowledge but rarely ask how that knowledge survives across generations. Knowledge does not exist independently of the language through which it is observed, evolved, organized, and passed from one generation to the next. A conservation strategy that values Indigenous knowledge while overlooking Indigenous languages risks protecting the product while allowing the process that continually renews it to fade.
This calls for a broader understanding of conservation literacy. Alongside species inventories, habitat maps, and ecological monitoring, conservation should also recognize the value of ecolexicons, the place-based vocabularies that enable Indigenous communities to distinguish habitats, seasonal change, and ecological processes.
Supporting community-led language documentation, multilingual ecological education, and regional diversity of Indigenous vocabularies are therefore not simply a cultural exercise. It strengthens the knowledge infrastructure of future generations to interpret and care for the landscapes they inherit.
Reading Nature Before It Falls Silent
Biodiversity conservation has long measured success in hectares restored, species recovered, and habitat protected. These remain essential benchmarks. Yet this understanding argues that another measure deserves attention: whether the languages that enable communities to understand, interpret and care for those landscapes are also surviving.
A forest is more than the trees it contains. It is also the vocabulary through which generations have learned to read its tides, seasons, species, and silences.
The next frontier in conservation is not simply protecting more land but protecting the many ways in which people understand that land. Every ecological language that survives preserves a way of noticing what others might overlook while their disappearance reduces the world’s ability to see nature in all its complexity.
Conservation cannot claim to protect the living world if it allows the languages that have long interpreted that world to disappear unheard.
Long before a forest falls silent, its words often do.
