title: Ponto Novo recebe 4º Festival de Sementes Crioulas da Bahia
content:
Uma década após a sua primeira edição, o Festival das Sementes Crioulas na Bahia chega ao seu quarto encontro reunindo cerca de mil pessoas entre camponeses, guardiões e guardiãs da agrobiodiversidade, pesquisadores e movimentos populares do campo e da cidade. Organizado pelo Movimento dos Pequenos Agricultores (MPA) e pela Cooperativa de Produção e Comercialização Camponesa (CPC-BA), o evento acontece no Assentamento Terra Nossa, no município de Ponto Novo, norte da Bahia, nos dias 18 e 19 de setembro.
Com o lema “Sementes Crioulas: Da Resistência Camponesa à Soberania dos Povos”, o evento coloca no centro do debate a defesa das variedades tradicionais como escudo no enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas e ferramenta essencial para garantir comida saudável na mesa da população trabalhadora.
Em um cenário de secas severas e desequilíbrios do regime de chuvas que afetam o semiárido e toda a região nordeste, a preservação genética cultivada pelos povos tradicionais ganha contornos de segurança e soberania alimentar. Diferente dos pacotes tecnológicos industriais, as sementes crioulas são selecionadas e adaptadas naturalmente aos biomas baianos, Caatinga, Cerrado e Mata Atlântica, há gerações.
Para Saiane Santos, dirigente do MPA na Bahia, o festival demarca a urgência de encarar a autonomia das sementes como questão pública. “Este ano trazemos essa discussão sobre o papel da semente crioula na defesa da soberania alimentar articulada à questão climática. O avanço das mudanças do clima impacta diretamente a vida do campesinato. Para nós, a semente é indispensável para pensarmos a autonomia e a soberania dos povos, garantindo comida boa de verdade no prato do povo”, afirma.
Além das discussões locais, o encontro impulsiona a atualização do Plano Nacional de Sementes do MPA, que organiza casas, campos e bancos comunitários de sementes pelo país, e pauta a criação e fortalecimento de políticas públicas voltadas ao setor junto aos governos estadual e federal.
Ponto Novo, terra de luta e transição agroecológica
A escolha do local do evento reflete a disputa dos modelos de desenvolvimento para o campo. O Assentamento Terra Nossa nasceu da luta pela terra iniciada em 2008 e abriga atualmente 60 famílias, 30 organizadas pelo MPA e 30 pelo Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST).
Localizado em uma área de perímetro irrigado historicamente ocupada pela lógica das monoculturas convencionais, o território se tornou um polo de resistência e experimentação camponesa, onde as famílias desenvolvem projetos de transição agroecológica irrigada voltados para a diversidade e a produção de alimentos sem veneno.
“Fazer esse festival em Ponto Novo tem muita simbologia para nós. É um território onde o MPA faz a luta pela terra desde 2008, e hoje estamos desenvolvendo um projeto de produção agroecológica irrigada justamente para fazer o contraponto com o modelo do agronegócio, que foi muito difundido nessa área”, pontua Saiane.
Programação
O primeiro dia de atividades reúne cerca de 500 delegados vindos em caravanas de mais de 60 municípios baianos para momentos de estudo e formação técnica e política. A programação conta com debates sobre soberania alimentar e enfrentamento ao agronegócio; produção própria de bioinsumos e transição agroecológica; educação do campo e saúde coletiva; questões jurídicas e direitos territoriais; o papel das infâncias e da juventude camponesa na guarda das sementes.
No segundo dia, o espaço é aberto à comunidade regional com a realização da Feira das Sementes Crioulas e da Sociobiodiversidade da Bahia, que promove trocas diretas de variedades de milho, feijão, fava, tubérculos e manivas entre agricultores de diferentes biomas. A jornada encerra com um grande ato político e intervenções culturais de samba de coco, forró pé-de-serra e poesias populares da região.
Sobre o Festival
A iniciativa teve início em 2016, em Feira de Santana, a partir de uma articulação pioneira entre o campesinato e a Universidade Federal do Recôncavo da Bahia (UFRB). O processo seguiu com o 2º Festival em Brumado (2018), marco do lançamento da campanha “Adote uma Semente”, e com a 3ª edição em Jacobina (2023), que vinculou a produção de sementes ao combate emergencial à fome no estado.

title: What even is an ‘Asian’? And why are we bundled together?
content: Tze Ming Mok introduces a new book that explores through art, activism, research and lived experience what it means to be Asian in Aotearoa. The following has been abridged from the original introduction to Between Dreams. During the “Inv-Asian” migration wave of the early 1990s, you could see the Asians at school clustering together in class and lunch break. We didn’t know if we liked each other yet, because we didn’t speak the same languages or dialects. There was just an unspoken agreement that we wouldn’t try to hurt each other. This is how you make friends, I think. Spivak’s strategic essentialism is one way of Being Asian, but it also requires thinking through what your strategy is in aid of. To not get bullied, yes. What about the rest? Can we imagine something better? To make a real life for ourselves, with agency, humanity and validation of our specificity? What even is an “Asian” and why are we bundled together, at lunch, in statistics, in books, in a blur of ill-fitting stereotypes? On the streets of Aotearoa, “Asian” is a racialised term specific to East Asians or “yellow” Asians. Meanwhile, Stats NZ defines “Asian” through a far vaster sweep of continental geography that takes in 60 percent of the world’s population – from Samarkand to Chennai, from Pyongyang to Bali. What about West Asia? You’ll have to ask the Iranians. At a grassroots organisational level, pan-“Asian” community activism in the diaspora is often based on strategic alliances within state-determined funding of diversity, policy and community initiatives – the confines and definitions of which can be grating. But activism and community work inside these confines can also be generative, collaborative and specifically dependent on articulating difference within our tenuous alliance. We grind away for recognition of the term “Asian” as not simply inherently absurd, but – in the way we need to use it – as inherently diverse. We do so in order to deploy it meaningfully in public policy, in political analysis, in collective struggles and in our histories of ourselves. “Asians” do not always have a shared ethnic history, language, religion, tradition or migration cohort. Oft-times, our homelands have been or are still at war with each other, even as others cannot tell us apart in the suburbs of Auckland. But more often, we do have a common history or experience of migration, arrival, settlement and daily life that has been governed by a racial and colonial logic marking us out for a clear purpose, which I will state bluntly: To return an advantage to colonial capital through replacing more expensive and better-organised labour. The historical arrival of Asian peoples in Aotearoa is inseparable from the British drive for colonial expansion through Oceania, with New Zealand being just one outpost. Aotearoa Asians inhabit multi-levelled, multi-cohort, multinational diasporas connected by what Ballantyne would call the “webs of empire” – the giant bureaucracy of governance and trading interests – or what Wallerstein would call the capitalist world system – where legacies of racial ideologies, oppressive rule, and extraction of value from bodies and stolen lands in one part of the system wash up repeatedly on the shores of another. Asian presence in Aotearoa is often the historical result of being filtered along these webs, in order to return value to the imperial centre. The historical transportation of Asian bodies to the Caribbean, South-East Asia and the South Pacific, including Aotearoa, was required to extract valuable material and agricultural resources from freshly acquired colonial lands – sugarcane, cacao, rubber, tin, gold. A century later, national immigration policies extract valuable human resources from the erstwhile Asian periphery and reallocate it to the neocolonial core that has grown up around the New Zealand settler state – nurses, doctors (including my parents in the 1970s), builders, teachers, IT workers. Stories of New Zealand Asian achievement and nationalist dedication abound, but leave a bitter taste. Audre Lorde says you cannot dismantle the master’s house using the master’s tools. But, we whisper to ourselves, with our postcode envy from Mount Roskill to Botany, but – but – but what if I am the tools? Is this all we have been doing this whole time? Tooling away industriously, hewing to the structure of white supremacy? Inhabiting the role of “middleman minority” used by the white state as a political, economic and administrative buffer against other groups denied power? To the contrary, this book shows how organising, agitating, joining rebel alliances and going in deep cover to challenge the dominant order has also always been the story of Asians in Aotearoa. Much of our early story here takes place at the shifting borders of the periphery, where existing accounts repeatedly reveal natural alliances between those who were “together on the margins”. This includes ease of intermarriage between Asian labour and Indigenous people under white colonial rule that excluded and oppressed them both, as shown by the commonplace nature of Chinese ancestry among Aotearoa Samoans due to the history of indenture, or the well-documented whānau relationships and community connections between Māori and early Asian market gardeners similarly marginalised within the Pākehā settler-state. Stories in Between Dreams include the recent reconnection between old-generation Chinese and the iwi who extended kaitiakitanga to the Ventnor remains, as explored by fourth-generation Chinese New Zealander Christopher Fung, bringing this relationship full circle over a century. Matua Moana Jackson’s example of the Taranaki Parihaka exiles in the caves of the South Island creating a protective cordon around Chinese gold miners inspired activist group Asians Supporting Tino Rangatiratanga (ASTR) in their kaupapa of reciprocity, mutual aid and solidarity with Māori. Fung is one of several ASTR alumni and affiliates who are contributors to this book, and to the 2021 public submissions on the New Zealand history curriculum consultation that inspired it. Rev. Mua Sofi Strickson-Pua (right) and his younger brother Sofi Ulugia-Pua outside their childhood home in Scanlan Street, Grey Lynn, 2019. (Photo: Taylor Aumua) Post-war social movements had undercover Asians working alongside Māori and Pasifika in new ways. In their story of their Chinese-Samoan father – the unionist, community leader and broadcaster Sofi Pua – activists Mua Strickson-Pua and Sofi Pua Junior sense the echoes of indenture in Sofi Pua Senior’s advocacy against the Dawn Raid deportations, and their own protests against the Springbok tour. As part of a 1970s intellectual and radical milieu, Pua was a friend of James K Baxter, as was former Jerusalem commune member “Burma Bill” Maung, a political exile and former senior Burmese government administrator. Maung famously leveraged his cultural capital and high-level connections to become an intermediary between the New Zealand government and dispossessed Māori in gangs in the 1970s. Instead of representing the interests of the white elites as a middleman, Maung literally acted as an agent of Black Power. The removal of New Zealand’s informal “White New Zealand” immigration policies in 1987 led to a rapid increase in Aotearoa’s Asian population. This initially led to an ugly surge in anti-Asian racism in the 1990s, mirroring that of a century earlier. In the 1990s, Manying Ip, a 1970s generation Hongkonger and academic, was the most prominent anti-racist advocate to speak out against this backlash, although the Chinese community in particular was split between new migrants with little political voice, and older communities trying to distance themselves from the new “rich foreigners” being targeted. This new idea of “rich Asians” taking over Aotearoa was a totalising fantasy intended to mobilise the savage political force of racial resentment. This fantasy has been erasing the reality of Asian working-class and migrant labour struggle for decades. In a unique and important contribution to Aotearoa’s history scholarship, unionist Sun-Min Elle Park and curator/union delegate Grace Gassin highlight our long history and ongoing record of fighting for workers’ rights in Aotearoa, both within and outside of a trade union movement that has not always welcomed us as members. Grace Gassin, editor of Between Dreams. (Photo: Supplied) Aotearoa Asian communities built and consolidated throughout the 2000s, creating new alliances across the migrant cohorts, with a crucial bridging role played by 1.5-generation migrants coming to adulthood. The increasing ease of online communication had coincided with a demographic tipping point, and previously isolated progressive and radical Asians rapidly began forming networks throughout media, academia, community-based activism, the public and third sector, and the arts – a critical and diverse “Embedded Asian Underground”. At this point in 2026, the majority of Asians in Aotearoa have no direct ancestral or familial connection to early Asian settlers and their stories of survival and solidarity. Post-1987 community histories underline the modernity of the Asian diasporas. Staying connected to identity in a politically and socially conscious sense is less about upholding an unattainable ideal of cultural and linguistic authenticity frozen in time, and more about continuing to engage in solidarity with the contemporary social and political life of countries in the Asian region itself – as much a part of normal day-to-day life as the extended family group-chat. The nature of Ong & Nonini’s diasporic “ungrounded empires” should not only be seen as the transnational relationships created by capital flows – but also networks of resistance to dictatorship, authoritarianism and colonial capitalism. Stories and objects from these newer generations in this collection show that to be Asian in Aotearoa is to also participate and resist in ways that are specific to Asia and the Asian regional context. Sometimes this relates to the West’s imperialist or neoimperialist legacy of war, as Rebekah Jaung explores in her chapter on the memorialisation of the Korean war. Sometimes it is about our own homelands’ imperialism over others in the region. Pan-Asian solidarity here is a precarious balance between historical colonisers and the historically colonised, transported to a new colonial framework in the Pākehā settler state. The Asian region’s geopolitical shifts in the last twenty years have ensured that bland liberal generalities are inadequate for even understanding what has historically been the largest single Asian population in Aotearoa, the ethnic Chinese. In a piece that strikes at the heart of the matter, former journalist Keith Ng reflects on his return to Hong Kong to join the city-state’s 2019 street revolution – a final mass show of defiance and identity before the descent of a new Iron Curtain. The first Lennon Wall along the stairway to the Hong Kong Central Government building in Admiralty, 2014. (Photo: Wikicommons /Wpcpey CC SA.) New moves from the old Biggest Empire in the region may already be splitting “Asian” solidarity unless we redefine the terms on which solidarity is based. Aotearoa has seen emerging, contingent alliances between those affected by the Chinese government’s new claims on the Chinese diaspora, and by its repressive rule at home. Similarly , those against the current Indian government’s turn to Hindutva fundamentalism, its persecution of Muslims, and the dismantling of Asia’s oldest secular democracy, have been coming together in a rebel alliance. We are still part of an intergenerational struggle to build, win and maintain post-Cold War democracy across East, South and South-East Asian countries, and to uphold those values in the diaspora. “Out here”, these once regional progressive solidarities have transformed into a global, transdiasporic collectivity – sometimes jokingly referred to as the Milk Tea Alliance, or simply the Asian anti-authoritarian left. As I write this, a quarter of a century after the historical turning point of 9/11, we are witnessing a global resurgence of the far right, a collapse in democratic political norms, and a rapid decline in reality-based social and political discourse in the West. Political institutions only upheld by convention have proved no match for bad actors capitalising on the rapid peak and decline of the mass public sphere promised by social media. The canaries in the coal mine are dead; fascism is here. More Reading Yes, the post-war consensus has collapsed. But that consensus – around liberal democracy, human rights and a humane welfare state – was never one that extended to Asian countries or Asian people. We had to fight for it, and some of us fought and lost – if not us personally, then our parents, our grandparents, our aunts and uncles, our cousins, our old neighbours and our friends. Aotearoa needs, right now, to learn from those of us who know what it is to fight for justice and lose. To give up and leave. We’ve seen things you people wouldn’t believe. We have gathered like dew, disappeared like mist and re-formed as tears. All these “losers” and descendants of losers can tell you what the true cost of surviving is. But some also still hold on to what drove us to get into trouble in the first place, and what the purpose of survival is at all: to keep our identity, our values, and our stories alive. Even if it has to be in some other place – even in some place like this. Between Dreams: Resistance and Representation in Asian Aotearoa edited by Grace Gassin ($50, Te Papa Press) is available to purchase from Unity Books. Gassin is delivering the Julie King Memorial Lecture at WORD Christchurch on Sunday August 6, details here.

title: Tamil Nadu's 70-YO Palmyra Tree Climbers Find New Income Through a Professor's Tourism Trails
content: As the sun rises over the dry stretches of southern Tamil Nadu, silhouettes begin appearing against rows of towering palm trees. Some carry ropes coiled around their shoulders. Others carry sickles and woven baskets. For generations, these climbers have scaled palmyra trees before dawn, tapping sap, harvesting fruit, and collecting leaves that would eventually become everything from jaggery and handicrafts to sweets and roof coverings. Today, many of them are in their seventies. And that worries Dr Preethi Hari Babu. “Without community support, the tree cannot be protected. That is the charm of the palmyra — the community and the tree survive together,” says the 30-year-old tourism researcher and assistant professor from Chennai, whose doctoral research has focused on understanding how Tamil Nadu’s state tree can be revived through tourism and community engagement. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” Dr Preethi says. “I have hosted three tours. In each tour, nearly 20 to 30 people participated. Most of them did not know about the community and their livelihoods. They were overwhelmed to learn about them, purchased the products, and even saved their contacts to place orders in the future,” shares Dr Preethi. A journey that began in a classroom For Preethi, the journey into the world of palmyra did not begin in forests or farms. It began in classrooms. After completing her bachelor’s degree at Ethiraj College and later pursuing an MBA in Tourism, she entered the tourism sector, believing that every place has something unique that shapes its identity. While working with a nature conservation NGO in 2019, she joined a trail focused on palmyra landscapes. That changed everything. “When I understood the benefits of the tree and saw communities trying to revive it, I realised there was so much more to explore,” she says. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research. The idea stayed with her long after the trail ended. Eventually, while pursuing her PhD in Tourism from Mizoram University, which she completed in 2025, she turned the palmyra tree into the centre of her research — not just as a species, but as an ecosystem connecting livelihoods, ecology, culture, and identity. More than just a tree Across Tamil Nadu, palmyra trees stand along roadsides, fields, and coastal landscapes. But according to Preethi, reducing them to scenery misses their significance. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. “There are edible and non-edible products. There are handicrafts, exports, climbers who harvest products, and women who make jaggery. It creates employment at many levels,” she explains. Large communities depend on the tree directly for income. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Women’s collectives produce palm jaggery and craft products. Climbers harvest sap and fruit. Artisans weave leaves into baskets and utility products. Entrepreneurs make jams, squashes, and sweets from palm fruit. And then there is the environmental role. The tree helps reduce soil erosion, supports water retention, and acts as a habitat for multiple species. In coastal and dry landscapes especially, these ecological functions become critical. “It is not only useful for people. Many species survive because of these landscapes too,” she says. Where livelihoods climb trees During her fieldwork across Kanyakumari, Thoothukudi, and Villupuram, Preethi spent time with climbing communities whose relationship with palmyra stretches across generations. “There are huge climber communities, almost like fishing communities. Their identity and livelihoods are deeply connected to this tree,” she says. One such climber is 32-year-old Anto Brito, whose family has worked with palmyra trees for generations. “My grandfather was a climber, and my father was also in this profession,” he says. “After my studies, I got a job elsewhere, but I did not find satisfaction there. Here, I am physically fit, I am with my family, and I enjoy the work.” But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) His family remains deeply involved in the palmyra economy. While Anto climbs the trees and harvests sap and fruit, his parents prepare food products made from palmyra produce. Together, they also run two shops that sell handicrafts and food items derived from the tree. But what struck Preethi most was how invisible many of these value chains remain. Many people know palm fruit. Few know how much more exists. From neera-based beverages to jams, squashes, jelly, adhirasam, and paniyaram, communities continue creating products that rarely receive mainstream attention. For climbers like Anto, the work remains seasonal but can provide a meaningful income. Between April and October, he harvests enough sap to produce around two to three kilograms of karupatti (palm jaggery) a day, earning roughly Rs 1,000 daily during the season. “In a day, I climb more than 10 trees,” he says. “During the COVID period, I used to climb nearly 20 trees a day.” One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. To change perceptions around palmyra products, Preethi began organising palmyra trails and community events. One of them was a fruit festival organised with local communities and hosted at Madras School of Social Work, where artisans and producers from Villupuram showcased dishes made from palmyra produce. “About 150 people came and tried the food. Many had never tasted these products before,” she says. The moment that changed perspective One experience continues to stay with her. As part of her extended research, Preethi travelled through remote islands in Indonesia for 15 days, studying how communities there interacted with similar palm ecosystems. Instead of feeling distant, it felt familiar. “I was proud that this potential already existed in Tamil Nadu,” she says. Communities there used palm trees for food, crafts, and even musical instruments. “That was when I realised this tree connects communities across Asia. The community involvement travels with the tree.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. (Photograph: Gio Shravan) Rote and Sabu are remote islands in Indonesia. They conserve the palmyra — known locally as lontar — in every possible way. “More than conservation, I can say they co-exist with the tree. Sasando is a traditional harp-like musical instrument native to Rote Island, made from lontar. It is considered a symbol of identity, culture, heritage, and pride. You can see its influence everywhere on the island, from heritage monuments to modern décor inspired by its shape. There is even a Sasando-shaped building that serves as the official residence of the Governor of East Nusa Tenggara in Kupang. “Sabu Island is mostly covered with grasslands and lontar palms. The majority of people depend on the tree for their livelihoods. They make intricate handicrafts such as baskets and handbags, while also preserving their traditional products. “Namata village in Sabu has conical lontar-thatched houses, where visitors can observe animist and ancestral worship practices. Visitors can also experience ikat weaving and watch climbers collect sap from the trees, locally called tuak. The area is underdeveloped in terms of infrastructure, amenities, and sanitation facilities, but it is remarkably well-maintained and organised.” The benefits are directly shared among the community and supported by the government. For Preethi, it serves as one of the strongest examples of community-based tourism. How tourism can help revive community livelihoods For Preethi, tourism is ultimately about empowering communities by sustaining their livelihoods. “Community-based tourism can create additional economic opportunities while helping communities showcase their culture and knowledge systems,” she says. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. The benefits, she believes, extend far beyond tourism revenue. Visitors could experience both the edible and non-edible worlds of the palmyra ecosystem — tasting fresh palm products and traditional foods while also learning how leaves are transformed into handicrafts, utility products, and decorative items through skills passed down across generations. Women who already play a central role in producing jaggery, food products, and handicrafts could earn directly from visitors without relying on middlemen. They could price their products themselves, run their own enterprises, and continue living and working within their villages instead of migrating elsewhere in search of employment. “Tourists are not only visitors; they become consumers who understand the work, effort, and knowledge behind these products through direct experience,” says Preethi. That experience also creates a deeper understanding of the communities whose livelihoods depend on the palmyra and of the ecosystem that supports them. Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. They know the birds and insects that inhabit the trees, understand seasonal cycles, and recognise changes in flowering and fruiting patterns that come only from living alongside the landscape for decades. “They can narrate these experiences as stories, making the journey more memorable while sharing traditional ecological knowledge associated with the tree,” says Preethi. In her vision, tourism becomes a platform not only for conservation but also for collaboration. Palmyra artisans in Tamil Nadu could exchange ideas with palm-based craft communities elsewhere in the world through co-learning platforms, helping revive traditional practices while encouraging innovation in products and design. She also imagines dedicated celebrations that place the tree at the centre of public attention. “Why not have an exclusive Palmyra Day celebrated globally?” she asks. “The tree deserves recognition for everything it supports.” Greater visibility, she believes, could also encourage more research and development around palmyra products, crafts, and sustainable livelihoods. The outcome, according to Preethi, is not simply economic development but social development as well — one that supports inclusive growth, circular economies, and sustainable tourism models rooted in local ownership. Tourism, she argues, can strengthen the relationship between climbers and the trees they depend on by creating value through cultural experiences, palm-based products, and ecotourism. As communities begin earning more from the living tree, they gain stronger reasons to conserve palmyra landscapes, preserve traditional climbing skills, and protect the biodiversity that exists around them. A tree that cuts across faith What also fascinated her was how the palmyra quietly crosses religious boundaries. Muslim families use palm leaves during wedding decorations. Christian households use them for decorating homes. In Hindu traditions, sweets wrapped in palmyra leaves remain part of festivals like Karthigai Deepam. “It connects people in ways we do not always notice,” she says. The challenge no one talks about For all its benefits, the future of palmyra remains uncertain. The biggest concern is not the tree itself. It is the people. “Most climbers today are around 70 years old,” says Preethi. The younger generation increasingly avoids climbing work due to safety concerns, low earnings, and changing aspirations. As climbers disappear, traditional knowledge risks disappearing with them. “You cannot separate conservation from communities,” she says. “If we want the tree to survive, the people connected to it also need support.” Unlike conventional tourism experiences, palmyra communities carry generations of ecological knowledge that exists nowhere else. Her answer lies in tourism. Not mass tourism, but experiences rooted in local knowledge — trails, festivals, food experiences, and community-led storytelling that create livelihoods while reviving interest in traditional systems. Because for Preethi, saving the palmyra is not only about protecting a tree. It is about protecting everything that climbs with it — livelihoods, culture, memory, and communities that have spent generations looking up at these tall silhouettes and seeing not just trees, but survival.

title: In Odisha, drum-making traditions echo the rhythms of farm life
content:
In Pahandi, a small village in Bijepur block of Odisha’s Bargarh district, the rhythm of a traditional baja or drum begins long before it reaches a festival ground. It begins with the earth.
Of the roughly 530 households in the village, most depend on agriculture, growing paddy, millets, green gram, ground nuts and other crops. But for eight households of the Chamar community, making traditional drums and other percussion instruments has supplemented their livelihoods for generations.
For Judhisthir Sagar, locally known as “Kutru”, the two occupations have always existed alongside each other. He inherited the craft of making baja from his ancestors, along with the practice of farming.
“Making drums and musical instruments is our identity,” said Sagar while tightening the strips of a newly made mrudanga, a two-headed percussion instrument widely used in traditional music. “We have been doing it for generations. It is our livelihood. We are proud to continue it.”
Apart from the mrudanga, other percussion instruments made in Pahandi include the godi mrudanga, udand khol, madol khol, dubi-tabla, pankuch, dhol and nisan. Each has a different shape and sound and a place in the cultural life of western Odisha.
From soil and hide to sound
The craft begins with the khol, the body of the instrument.
The soil used to prepare the khol is carefully chosen. According to craftsman Baisakhu Rana, red or black soil without stones or other impurities is preferred.
The other essential material is animal hide, usually from goats or cattle. The hides are sourced from various parts of Odisha and, at times, from outside the state.
The process brings together materials closely connected to rural life. Soil comes from the agricultural landscape, livestock provide an important raw material, and the knowledge of transforming these materials into instruments has passed from one generation to another.
Once the basic structure is ready, the drum is decorated.
Amitabh Naik, 40, has been making traditional baja for more than six years. He learnt the craft from his paternal uncle and uses Sambalpuri printed canvas, bamboo strips, coloured threads and soil to decorate the instruments.
“My uncle taught me this work,” he said. “I have been doing it for more than six years now. I enjoy making the instruments, especially when I see them being used in our festivals.”
The connection with Bargarh’s textile tradition is hard to miss. The district has a large community of handloom weavers. Sambalpuri textiles are among Odisha’s Geographical Indication-registered products.
In Pahandi, that textile aesthetic becomes part of a musical instrument. Here, agriculture, livestock, textile traditions and music meet in the making of a baja.
Depending on its type, an instrument can take three to five days to complete. Its price varies according to the quality of the hide, its sound and the intricacy of its decoration.
Sagar says instruments made in Pahandi have travelled to districts of Odisha and other parts of India. Some have even reached Australia and Singapore through word-of-mouth orders and references.
But the value of these instruments goes beyond the markets they reach.
Instruments with a place in village life
A baja acquires meaning when it is played.
The mrudanga, godi mrudanga and udand khol accompany kirtans and nama yajnas, devotional chanting of the names of god. The madol khol is used during Karamsani Puja at harvest time, while the dhol and nisan accompany the Dalkhai dance and festivals such as Sital Sasthi, at which the wedding of Shiva and Parvati is re-enacted; Nuakhai, which celebrates the harvest; and Durga Puja, which marks the victory of the goddess Durga over the demon Mahishasura.
These occasions are closely woven into the social and agricultural calendar of western Odisha.
Nuakhai, for instance, is associated with the new harvest and the sharing of newly harvested food. Music and rituals bring communities together during these occasions, making the instruments an important part of village life.
Bargarh has a rich folk music and dance tradition that includes Sambalpuri, Sanchar, Pala, Khanjani Bhajana, Dulduli, Karamsani and Danda Nrutya. The traditional percussion instruments made by artisans such as those in Pahandi provide the rhythm for many such performances.
From village workshops to distant stages
Naresh Bhoi, a young folk musician from Bargarh, is a member of the Kalagram Adi Dhun Group, which promotes Odisha’s traditional musical instruments through performances. The group was founded by Rabi Ratan Sahu, an artist from Padampur in Bargarh who promotes folk culture through music. Sahu has been a research fellow with the Ministry of Culture and a general council member of the Odisha Sangeet Academy.
The group has performed at Rabindra Mandap in Bhubaneswar and Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in New Delhi, as well as in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.
“Traditional instruments help carry the sound of western Odisha to audiences who may be unfamiliar with our folk traditions,” said Sahu. “A baja does not end its journey at the workshop. An artisan makes it, a performer brings it to life, and a festival gives it meaning.”
Keeping a tradition in motion
Traditional crafts face pressure from changing lifestyles, mass-produced alternatives and shifting market preferences. However, Pahandi’s drum makers continue to find work because their instruments remain part of rituals, festivals and performances.
Their knowledge is also sustained within families. Older artisans teach younger members, while performers continue to use the instruments in new settings.
The village remains rooted in agriculture. Its fields provide food and livelihoods, while its workshops sustain other form of rural knowledge. Soil, livestock, bamboo, textiles and inherited skills come together in objects that eventually become part of a festival, ritual or performance.
That makes Pahandi’s story larger than the survival of a traditional craft. It is a story of how different parts of rural life remain connected.
Some of the information for this article was provided by Abhishek Singha, who works as a District Project Coordinator with the Watershed Support Services and Activities Network, Bhubaneswar.
Pritesh Sundar Roy, Susant Sekhar Choudhury, Abhijit Mohanty and Bikash Das work for the Watershed Support Services and Activities Network.
